events.title: Flock Once Touted Its Cameras as ‘Made in the USA.’ Now It’s Not So Clear
events.summary: Flock CEO Garrett Langley has said the company made its first license plate cameras in his Atlanta home, permanently scratching his dining table with drill marks. A decade later, where the company assembles its signature—and fiercely debated —product has become more of a mystery. For years, Flock touted publicly that its devices were produced in the United States. But more recent marketing materials from the company reviewed by WIRED no longer specify where its cameras come from. One US manufacturer that previously identified Flock as a customer quietly removed a mention of the company from its website earlier this year as public backlash against the company’s surveillance technology grew. The startup has become the subject of a nationwide protest movement that has prompted dozens of local governments to abruptly stop using its cameras. Congress is also considering legislation that would cut federal funding to states that fail to limit use of Flock and other license plate readers. While police have argued the cameras are crucial tools for deterring and solving crime, activists have criticized Flock for enabling officers to track the cars of their exes , share footage with immigration authorities , and follow the movements of pedestrians . But Flock’s manufacturing supply chain has received scant attention, even though where its hardware is produced could have implications for US national security. WIRED spoke with current and former Flock employees and supply chain analysts, reviewed data from US import records, and watched past marketing videos featuring Langley to piece together the first account of how its hardware pipeline has evolved. Flock’s cameras largely rely on suppliers around the world that provide non-custom parts, which are also used in products from other companies. “Our value is in the aggregation and the packaging of all of these things … in a nice waterproof, consumer-friendly device,” Langley said in one marketing video from 2021. Import records collected by ImportGenius show the company has been increasingly bringing “commodity” cameras, radar systems, and other components over from Primax Electronics in Thailand. Primax is based in Taiwan, but has manufacturing facilities in China, Thailand, and elsewhere. “My understanding is that these are components, but it looks like Primax manufactures whole security camera solutions,” ImportGenius’ analyst Lynn Hughes says. “Quite a few shipments include ‘Radar’ in the product description which might be related to the radar sensor pods they’re attaching to their cameras.” Flock didn’t respond to most of the detailed questions WIRED asked for this story, though it did provide some general information. “All products that Flock builds are National Defense Authorization Act compliant,” Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said in an email, referring to a US law that effectively bars government contractors from using parts made by a handful of Chinese tech companies over security concerns. Cris van Pelt, creator of the anti-Flock advocacy project Have I Been Flocked, says that while where the cameras are made may have relatively minor implications for US communities, the lack of transparency about their origins underscores a broader problem . “It all speaks to the fact that there is no real oversight, and that tens of thousands of literal and figurative black boxes are being installed on American roads,” van Pelt says. “If any part of the supply chain is compromised, we would never know. That’s a much bigger problem than where the final product is assembled.” The earliest Flock prototypes were made using cameras ripped out of Android phones bought on Alibaba, which were then attached to batteries and soldered onto a solar panel, Langley recalled in one video. The goal was to prove that a useful device could be created from parts collectively costing between $200 to $300. (WIRED reported earlier this week that Flock’s cameras continue to use smartphone-style processors and leave significant data unencrypted.) As Flock began securing contracts with homeowners associations, it shifted into a corporate office that also doubled as an assembly line. Langley described the setup as fun, but also unprofessional and arduous—pallets of parts shipped in from China had to be dragged a quarter of a mile through the building multiple times a week. Around 2020, Flock moved its assembly line to a WeWork-style warehouse facility in Atlanta, according to a marketing video produced by the space’s operator. A handful of Flock employees cranked out as many cameras as they could, with engineers assembling the main camera device and less technical staff attaching solar panels and mounts. Rather than opening up warehouses, Flock stored cameras in self-storage locations across the country for its installation crews to retrieve as needed, according to two former employees.

events.title: Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting
events.summary: Illustration by Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: Records obtained by ProPublica, iStock. Two Oregon lawmakers want to end an unusual exemption in the state’s records law that has kept the public from learning how hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer money is spent on subsidized housing — and the effort has already landed key industry support. Rep. Pam Marsh, chair of Oregon’s House Committee on Housing and Homelessness, told ProPublica that she plans to introduce legislation next year to eliminate a law that shields key details of state spending on low-income housing . The southern Oregon Democrat said she didn’t realize the documents were being kept secret until reading about it in a ProPublica story. She said previous leaders of her committee told her they were also unaware. “I think this is an issue that will have very broad interest,” Marsh said. State Sen. Khanh Pham, a Portland Democrat and chair of the Senate Committee on Housing and Development, said she also wants the Legislature to tackle the issue in its next session. Meanwhile, a lobbying group for low-income housing developers, lenders and related businesses, Housing Oregon, said it strongly supports repealing the secrecy provision; the organization has asked the state to disclose more about projects that it funds in the meantime. “Oregon’s affordable housing providers share the public’s interest in ensuring that public investments in housing are used effectively, responsibly, and with visibility,” said Kevin Cronin, a spokesperson for the group. “The questions raised in your recent ProPublica article regarding development costs deserve serious attention.” Cronin said Oregon can increase transparency around development costs “while still protecting genuinely proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” “More consistent reporting of costs and outcomes will help policymakers, providers, researchers, and the public understand where the system is working and where it needs improvement,” Cronin said. ProPublica highlighted Oregon’s secrecy around low-income housing in August. Since 2021, our story noted, Oregon has given developers an unprecedented $1.4 billion, and the cost of developing each low-income apartment has nearly doubled, to $540,000. Dozens of projects are lined up for another $850 million in future state funding, and costs are expected to continue rising. Read More Oregon Is Spending More Than Ever on Low-Income Housing. A State Law Keeps the Details Secret. “We are spending, as you said, a lot of money on the development of affordable housing,” Marsh said. “We really need to understand what it is that we’re funding, how much it costs, why it costs that much, and be able to justify the investments that we’re making.” In other states, researchers and journalists have used the financial records from subsidized housing projects to investigate their spiraling costs and the drivers behind the growing price tag. Marsh said after reading the ProPublica story that she “pretty much immediately” looked up the provision in Oregon public records law that officials cite for keeping cost details secret. She said financial documents that show where a project’s money is coming from and what it’s going to should be public and easily accessed. She said she would like to see them posted online as part of the public materials that Oregon’s Housing Stability Council receives for each project before awarding subsidies. Pham, in a written statement, said: “It’s imperative that Oregonians can trust that our state government is investing in affordable housing as cost-effectively as possible. I appreciated ProPublica’s reporting on Oregon’s inadequate public records law that hinders our ability to monitor how affordable housing funds are being spent, and I’m hopeful legislators can address this next year.” Oregon’s Sunshine Committee, which reviews public records exemptions and recommends ones that could be rolled back, is also examining the exemption for housing financials as a result of ProPublica’s coverage, co-chair Charlie Fisher said. It’s not clear where opposition to repeal efforts, if any, might arise. Officials in Washington and California, where the details of state spending on subsidized housing are available to the public, have said it hasn’t interfered with low-income housing efforts. Oregon Housing and Community Services, the state housing agency that persuaded lawmakers to create the records exemption in 1997, cited the law in redacting major sections of developers’ cost reports that ProPublica requested in May. The agency’s current executive director, Andrea Bell, told ProPublica in July that she is committed to transparency but that the agency is following the law as it stands today.  Asked to comment this week about whether the agency would support efforts to change the law, a spokesperson said by email that state agencies don’t take positions on bills. “OHCS appreciates the opportunity to review the legislation” that’s introduced in 2027, the spokesperson wrote. The post Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: 3 big takeaways on aging, beauty, and work from Maye Musk’s new memoir
events.summary: Maye Musk shares her insights on aging, beauty, and work in her latest memoir, "Timeless." Shea Kastriner/USTA via Getty Images Maye Musk reflects on starting over and late-career milestones in her new memoir, "Timeless." In it, she wrote that embracing her gray hair opened doors she never expected. At 78, she sees aging as an expansion of possibility, not a narrowing of it. Maye Musk may be best known as the mother of Elon Musk , the world's richest person. But at 78, she has also built a career of her own as a dietitian, model, author, and public speaker. In her latest memoir, "Timeless," released September 15, Musk looks back on her childhood, divorce, and years as a working single mother of three, as well as the career breakthroughs she found later in life. Here are three lessons from the book on getting older, beauty standards, and why Musk sees no reason to slow down. Some of life's best chapters can come later Maye Musk said most of her career achievements came later in life. PATRICIA DE MELO MOREIRA/AFP via Getty Images In the memoir, Musk wrote that she admired people who thrived from a very young age, and considered herself a late bloomer. "Maybe that's an understatement. I bloomed so late that most of the things I'm known for didn't happen until after I turned fifty," she wrote. Musk wrote that she didn't walk runways in New York, Paris, or Milan until after 50, and her Times Square billboards came when "most people my age were considering retirement." Her later years brought a string of new opportunities. In 2017, Musk became CoverGirl's oldest spokesperson at 69. Two years later, at 71, she published her first memoir, "A Woman Makes a Plan: Advice for a Lifetime of Adventure, Beauty, and Success." "And at seventy-four — white hair, wrinkles, life experience, and all —I became the oldest cover model in Sports Illustrated history. I still smile thinking about it," Musk wrote. She held this title until Martha Stewart made the cover at 81 the following year. Aging isn't something to conceal Maye Musk said she learned to embrace her grey hair and her wrinkles. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Musk wrote in her memoir that she stopped bleaching her hair when she was nearing 60, after feeling down. As her white roots grew in, she cut her hair short and found she loved the new look. Her agent, however, was not impressed. When she saw Musk's new hair and photos, she warned that she would "never work again," Musk wrote. Instead, Musk realized her contract allowed her to send her new photos to agencies outside New York City . Fifteen signed her and booked her for work across Europe and the US. She also caught the eye of a Time magazine casting director, who noticed Musk walking her dog every morning, leading to a photo feature inside the magazine. Elsewhere in the memoir, Musk recounts her initial hesitation over appearing in Sports Illustrated's Swimsuit Issue, because her agents had long told her she did not have a "swimsuit body." "Even at my smallest, my bottom never did that thing the magazines usually look for in a swimsuit model — smoothly transitioned into my thigh without a fold — and it certainly didn't do that now," she wrote. She worried about showing her wrinkles and cellulite, but her daughter encouraged her to do it, so she reconsidered. "What was I so afraid of? Men never worry about their wrinkles; they add gravitas. Overweight men still walk proudly in their little speedos. Women gain five pounds and we hide behind our towels. All those years of indoctrination from agents and the industry — it was time to throw all that nonsense out," Musk wrote. "I would walk proudly and show the world how happy and healthy I was in my swimsuit, and my seventy-plus-year-old body." There's no deadline for meaningful work Maye Musk said she continues to keep up with nutrition research, even though she no longer practices. In this photo, she is pictured with then-University of the Free State Vice-Chancellor Francis Petersen after receiving an honorary doctorate in dietetics in 2023. University of the Free State. Musk's work as a dietitian has remained important to her, too. In the memoir, she wrote that her alma mater, the University of the Free State in Bloemfontein, South Africa, awarded her an honorary doctorate in dietetics in 2023. Although she no longer practices, Musk has continued to keep up with nutrition research. "Once a dietitian, always a dietitian. I'm even still registered. Every five years, I pass seventy-five exams to keep my accreditation current. It takes some time, but I enjoy staying up-to-date on nutritional science research," Musk wrote. Reflecting on aging, Musk wrote that she has come to see it as an expansion of possibility, not a narrowing of it. "Reinvention isn't reserved for the young; it's reserved for the brave. And courage can arrive late and still change your life," Musk wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Flydubai expects higher fuel costs, travel curbs and aircraft delays to limit growth
events.summary: Soaring jet fuel prices, international travel advisories and aircraft delivery delays are frustrating flydubai 's growth plans, with higher fuel costs being passed on to customers. The airline has hedged a “big part” of its position against higher jet fuel prices. Still, the rising costs are reflected in its air fares, chief executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai on Wednesday. Jet fuel is the “biggest headache” because sudden price swings make it hard to cash in on higher air fares due to the fuel market's unpredictability, he added. “Your fare has to reflect your cost,” Mr Al Ghaith said. “Whenever the costs increase – in this case, the fuel – our fares are reflecting the fuel price.” The majority of Flydubai's aircraft deliveries have also been postponed to year-end, with its Boeing 787s coming in 2028 after repeated delays in 2026 and 2027, leading to added costs in terms of crew training and route openings. The jet delays have not offered operational relief during the travel disruptions from the Iran war, he said. “We are totally not seeing any benefits from aircraft delays because we want to be at full capacity to start business when it comes back with a vengeance,” Mr Al Ghaith said. The travel advisories imposed by some western governments on several Middle East countries during the regional conflict are having a “big negative” impact on inbound travel, particularly from Europe, he said. “We believe that as soon as all of these restrictions are lifted, the traffic will come back,” Mr Al Ghaith said. Growth outlook The airline boss is optimistic about the airline's recovery from the seven-month conflict, betting that demand will return quickly once restrictions ease. Flydubai is already operating at 85 per cent of its capacity and expects to return to prewar levels, or exceed them, by the end of 2026 as it takes delivery of 11 aircraft. “We really had a very good summer; it encourages us that a full recovery is around the corner,” he said. The airline now flies to 130 destinations out of its prewar network of 140. Markets such as Eastern Europe are recovering faster than others, with forward bookings “almost back to normal”. “Our biggest disadvantage currently, especially in Europe, is all of these advisories that are still ongoing,” he said. Mr Ghaith said the airline was not behind its prewar growth target. “We are taking all the aircraft that we are supposed to take; we are manning up for this operation because you have to be ready for the day after when the business will come, and it will come with a vengeance.” The airline still expects to make a profit despite the higher costs and travel disruptions, with no redundancies and continued hiring. “We always work on a target that we will make money. This is always in our DNA,” he said. “Our cash flow is as strong as it was before the war.” Mr Ghaith declined to quantify the cost of seven-month war disruptions, saying it is “significant but it is manageable”. “If we end up making money, even a little money, and sustaining our size, that is a target, because then when the business comes back, you will be bigger to absorb most of it,” he said. In 2027, Flydubai plans to take delivery of up to 17 aircraft. “We are very confident that it will be a great year for us,” Mr Al Ghaith said. Looking ahead, the airline continues to invest in its long-term growth with an order book of 300 planes, a focus on expanding its premium products and a recent foray into cargo. Its incoming Boeing 787s and Airbus A321 jet deliveries will open new destinations, with China a “big part” of its future plans, Mr Al Ghaith said.

events.title: Trump’s Saudi ambassador pick faces early hurdles
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump’s pick for ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Texas, is staring down a potentially difficult confirmation fight due to hurdles from a tight Senate calendar and skepticism among Republicans. Hunt’s nomination this week came just months after he finished third in the Texas Republican Senate primary. Hunt had entered the race against Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Attorney General Ken Paxton, turning the contentious contest into a three-way fight. Now Trump has tapped Hunt, a former Army officer who served twice in Saudi Arabia as a diplomatic liaison, for the high-profile diplomatic post. Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., could be an obstacle to Hunt’s confirmation and is likely to block Hunt’s nomination from moving as part of any large, en bloc nomination package. Tillis has previously used nominations as leverage to press the Trump administration on other issues; he’s currently holding up Kari Lake’s nomination to be ambassador to Jamaica, for instance. Asked about Hunt’s nomination, Tillis told Semafor, “I gotta look into the details.” “Right now, with the limited number of session days that we have left, if they don’t get into an en bloc package, they’re going to die,” Tillis continued. “That’s how I’m holding Kari Lake. I mean, there’s some people saying, ‘Please let her go to Jamaica,’ but the reality is once she gets Senate confirmed, she could go other places in acting roles. And that’s what I’m not going to allow.” “The truth is, the odds that I’ll let him go as an en bloc nominee are almost zero, but it needs some more work,” he said. The timing could also give Tillis additional leverage. The Senate is in its final legislative sprint through October before adjourning ahead of the midterm elections, meaning it would be difficult to fit a confirmation hearing, committee vote, and potential floor vote into the remaining calendar. If Hunt’s hearings slip until after the midterms, the calculus could change entirely — particularly if the Republicans lose seats in the Senate. Unified Republican support could also be a challenge. Asked about Trump’s pick, Cornyn told Semafor he is an “interesting choice. An interesting choice in many, many ways.” He declined to weigh in further. When Hunt ran against Cornyn and Paxton in the Texas Republican Senate race, the contest grew increasingly bitter as the primary unfolded. Cornyn’s campaign called Hunt “ fake MAGA ,” and Hunt responded by saying Cornyn’s record “ reads like a registered Democrat .” Cornyn’s reaction — after the two Republicans spent months attacking each other on the campaign trail — adds further uncertainty as Hunt seeks Republican support. Other members of the Foreign Relations Committee were cautious. Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Semafor, “I don’t know him well enough, so looking forward to seeing more.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, told Semafor, “You’re that first person that’s mentioned that name.” To be sure, Hunt has some early support: fellow Texan Sen. Ted Cruz told Semafor, “I think Wesley’s terrific.” Know More Hunt also has a potential vulnerability in his own record, particularly given the country he has been nominated to serve. In December 2025, Hunt posted a video describing his time as a diplomatic liaison officer in Saudi Arabia after the US operation that killed Osama bin Laden. Hunt said he stopped going to work for two weeks because he feared bin Laden sympathizers in Riyadh could target American forces. “These are our allies that we are working with every single day, and we were actually fearful of our lives,” Hunt said at the time. “Now, imagine letting people, with that mindset, come to our country, and you wonder why we are waking up to having dead national guardsmen… the mentality of these people never ended. It never stops. The jihad never ends. We are the infidel.” The comments could become a focus of questioning when Hunt appears before the Foreign Relations Committee. Hunt’s office did not respond to a request for comment. In a post on X after the nomination was announced, Hunt said he was “profoundly grateful to President Trump for his confidence in me and for the extraordinary honor of being selected.” Step Back Trump nominated Hunt at a time Saudi Arabia faces increased military pressure from Iran-backed forces. Houthi fighters in Yemen have increased attacks against targets in Saudi Arabia, and the kingdom’s East-West oil pipeline, a key route for Saudi crude exports, has shut down amid attacks. With Saudi Arabia facing intensified security challenges and seeking increased US support, Hunt’s nomination could be a welcome signal to Riyadh by telegraphing the importance of the relationship. There is also a broader shortage of confirmed US ambassadors in the Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, having a confirmed ambassador in Riyadh would provide another direct channel to the Trump administration, and in the case of Hunt, one with an extensive military background and close ties to congressional Republicans.

events.title: Senators sought to add AI antitrust exemption to defense bill
events.summary: The Scoop Senators had secured a narrow antitrust exemption for AI companies in annual must-pass defense policy legislation earlier this year before negotiations over the measure were delayed, according to people familiar with the matter. Senators included the national security-focused antitrust exemption as part of a larger so-called manager’s package of amendments to the bill, which the leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee file each year. Specifically, the package would have included a proposal from Sens. Jim Banks , R-Ind., and Adam Schiff, D-Calif., granting AI companies a limited antitrust exemption for sharing intelligence with one another and coordinating defenses against Chinese spying and distilling of AI models, and addressing other risks to advanced systems such as cybersecurity incidents. The package had approval from Armed Services Committee leaders, Sens. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., and Jack Reed, D-R.I., the people said. Senate Democrats blocked debate on the annual bill over the summer in objection to President Donald Trump’s handling of the Iran war. It would have to survive negotiations with the House. The effort, which hasn’t been previously reported, takes on new relevance as AI companies, led by Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, advocate for a different type of antitrust exemption that allows them to coordinate on pacing the development of their technologies. That idea, fueled by concerns about risks posed by the fast-advancing technology, has drawn criticism from members of the Trump administration, as well as members of Congress from both parties. “You have a basic obligation to make your products safe. Do not demand antitrust waivers or liability waivers in exchange for that,” Trump’s former AI adviser, David Sacks, said in an interview with Bloomberg earlier this week. Know More While Amodei has suggested an antitrust waiver for coordinating on capability slowdown, the proposal from Banks and Schiff is decidedly narrower. It focuses on Chinese espionage and distillation, or the practice of an AI model training on a more sophisticated model to steal techniques. An earlier announcement of the proposal said it would allow for “coordinating responses to risks involving loss of operational control over advanced AI systems” — which the people said relates to incidents like the Hugging Face attack by OpenAI agents — and letting researchers share information with one another. Lawmakers enacted a similar policy for companies through the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act , which protects companies from antitrust liability when they share cyber threats with government agencies or one another. It’s unclear whether the current debate over AI safety — or potential White House opposition — will change the fate of the provision. If it passes the Senate, the defense bill will need to be reconciled with the House’s own version before it can reach Trump’s desk. Not everyone in the AI industry is lobbying for the broader carveout as pushed by Amodei: OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, recently said such an exemption for labs to be able to coordinate on pacing was unnecessary. John Connell, Google’s vice president of government affairs and public policy, said in July that the bill from Banks and Schiff would “give the AI industry clear rules of the road to share threat intelligence and collaborate on much-needed standards and benchmarks.”

events.title: Backpacker cuts slammed as 'low blow' for farming and tourism
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Albanese government's backpacker limits will hit hard, farming and tourism leaders say Working holiday-maker numbers will be cut significantly under changes announced by the Albanese government. ( ABC Kimberley: Tom Forrest ) Backpacker numbers will be slashed and visa eligibility tightened under the federal government's immigration changes. Working holiday-makers are crucial for staffing farming and tourism businesses across Australia. Industry leaders say the changes are a "low blow" at a difficult time. Federal limits to backpacker numbers have sparked fears in regions reliant on holidaying workers for farming and tourism. On Thursday Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined an overhaul of the working holiday-maker visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers seeking to extend their stay and reducing overall numbers. A cap of 45,000 will be applied to those looking to stay a second year, down from the 57,000 who qualified this year. Tony Burke announced the changes in an address to the National Press Club on Thursday. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Those seeking a third year will be capped at 5,000, down from 31,000 this year. Mr Burke said the government would prioritise migrants that have skills Australia needs in areas such as construction and agriculture. Backpackers provide a significant source of workers in regional communities across Australia. ( Pixabay ) People who successfully secure an extension in the ballot will be required to undertake regional work. Mr Burke said backpackers could not be exempt if the country was serious about lowering net overseas migration. "Drastic cuts, wherever you make them, hurt the economy in every part, in every area," he said. But the National Farmers’ Federation (NFF) has warned the government is putting Australia’s food security, regional economies and farm safety at risk if it pushes ahead with its plan without "urgent" consultation. Hamish McIntyre called the decision a "low blow" for farmers. ( Supplied: National Farmers Federation ) The lobby group's president, Hamish McIntyre, said farmers were furious that the time-frame for processing visas would now take up to three months, as opposed to days. “This is a low blow for farmers and the businesses that produce Australia’s food and fibre,” he said in a statement. "A three-month processing target leaves farmers completely stranded, with harvest already underway in parts of Queensland and the main season only weeks away." Federation chief executive Mike Guerin also warned of rising food prices if the industry struggled to find workers for harvesting. "We will see a lift in the price of food. We will see emptier supermarkets," he said. Slowdown leaving farms without workers Esperance farmer Mic Fels said the slowdown of backpacker visa applications, which began last month, meant some farmers were going without the seasonal workforce needed to bring crops in. “I think 'reform' is probably a generous word. I think 'deform' is perhaps a better one," he said. Mic Fels says the loss of workers across the agricultural sector will be disastrous. ( ABC News: Emma Field ) Mr Fels, who contested the WA seat of Swan at last year's federal election, said assurance the government would prioritise applications for skilled agricultural workers was welcomed. But he said the situation was time-sensitive. “If we saw hundreds of applicants coming through over the next week, I think that would give everybody some breathing space,” he said. Mr Fels said there were concerns across the sector that a lack of workers could lead to dangerous practices that the industry had attempted to stamp out. “After COVID, when we just had all these inexperienced workers on farms and the death rates on farms doubled, and it's not hyperbole, this is what we're dealing with,” he said. “These are massive machines with thousands of moving parts. You wouldn't put inexperienced operators on a dump truck on a mine site and say, 'Go for your life', and that's what they're effectively saying." Securing workers is critical ahead of the harvest, Mic Fels says. ( Supplied: Ash Bowman ) Tourism lobby warns of 'severe' impact WA's tourism lobby said the state stood to lose 4,500 backpackers working in peak seasons, costing at least $62 million in tourism spend and 425 local tourism jobs. “The cuts will be most severe for Exmouth, Broome, Kununurra and northern WA, which currently attract backpackers to work in tourism to earn a third visa," Tourism Council WA chief executive Evan Hall said. Tourism Council WA says towns such as Broome will be particularly hard hit.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Yes, the 'Secondhand Software Presentation' does sound like it might be an adverse document... Microsoft AI chief warns Anthropic not to put ideas in Claude's head 1 hour ago Iranian spies hit Windows machines with Chosen Brick data-stealing malware 1 day ago September's Windows 11 patch needs an emergency patch of its own 2 days ago Microsoft account refuseniks have another way of installing Windows 2 days ago Microsoft drafts feel-good AI model guidelines and wants your input 2 days ago The legal spat between secondhand software reseller ValueLicensing and Microsoft took another turn this week: a consent order was published with demands for documents from past and present Microsoft head honchos, and a planned case management conference was canceled. Several requests in the order revolved around a historic, potentially explosive internal document written by Microsoft entitled the "Second-Hand Software" (SHS) Presentation. ValueLicensing and Microsoft agreed to vacate the case management conference ahead of its scheduled date on September 14, 2026. The result is the Consent Order [PDF] , which, unsurprisingly, focuses on locating and asking for the disclosure of Microsoft documents that may bear on the reseller's allegation that the company offered incentives for customers to shift to subscription services in return for not selling their pre-owned licenses. The confidentiality designation applied to several documents in the case has also been lifted. In addition, there are many references to a June 2013 document that Microsoft disclosed on December 22, 2025, entitled "Second-Hand Software Presentation" (SHS Presentation). June 2013 was a busy time for Microsoft: it had launched the Office 365 subscription service two years previously , but there was a question over what to do about those customers with perpetual licenses that Microsoft wanted to move into the brave new world of "an always-up-to-date cloud service, at a predictable monthly subscription." While the content of the SHS Presentation has yet to be made public, the Consent Order treats it as a "Known Adverse Document," meaning it is unlikely to be good news for Microsoft. Furthermore, the consent order requires Microsoft to explain by October 31 why it had not disclosed it earlier. This case was filed in 2021 and yet it took until the end of 2025 for Microsoft to produce the presentation. Microsoft was also asked to conduct extensive, unredacted disclosure searches across its corporate mailboxes and SharePoint accounts of high-level executives for search terms including "antitrust," "used licenses," "second hand", and "Value Licensing," between July 3, 2012 and June 1, 2020. It has until November 30 to produce any documents found during the search. Execs whose mailboxes and document repositories must be searched include Richard Chin, currently a Corporate VP at Microsoft responsible for the company's monetization approach and who was a General Manager between 2012 and 2020 working on pricing, licensing, and the business models in the Cloud and AI world. Kevin Turner, who was Chief Operating Officer at Microsoft from 2005 to 2016, is also on the list. As for confidentiality, the consent order stated, "No blanket or default designation of such documents as 'Restricted' or 'Confidential' shall be applied." Instead, it'll be on a document-by-document basis and "limited to the precise words, figures or passages said to be sensitive; and be supported by specific reasons rather than general assertions." "Defendants shall disclose by no later than 4pm on 30 November 2026 any further documents they have identified relating to the same or similar matters addressed in the SHS Presentation." Microsoft will also keep ValueLicensing apprised of its progress every 21 days. Microsoft told The Register it had no comment to make on the Consent Order.

events.title: Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
events.summary: Watch: Tech firms are "essentially seeding a new silicon species" says Microsoft's head of AI Mustafa Suleyman The head of Microsoft AI has warned that without adequate safeguards, the development of AI could lead to the emergence of a new "silicon species" which competes with humans. Mustafa Suleyman said rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" which could create technology that humanity cannot control. Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, the chief executive said it was "right" for people to be concerned about AI, but there were "very practical things that we can do" to control it. The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Anthropic has been approached for comment. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Published 4 hours ago OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms Published 1 day ago Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets. That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us". Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week , external , in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people". In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self. He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations. "They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans." Dario Amodei is the head of the AI firm Anthropic, which Suleyman criticised for treating its AI as if it were human The Microsoft boss said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated. This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology. "We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote. Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone". The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry. Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity. Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. "I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said. Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development. Suleyman's comments reflect Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct , external , a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence". This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control". The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve. events.title: Huawei speeds up launch of new AI chip to take on Nvidia
events.summary: Huawei’s flagship Ascend 960DT chip, originally slated for late 2027, will now be launched in the first quarter. Huawei is accelerating the launch of its Ascend 960DT AI chip to early 2027, aiming to replace Nvidia in China and compete globally with advanced computing power. The company plans to deploy cluster-based SuperPod technology with up to 100,000 chips to boost performance, offsetting single-chip limitations and supporting data centres like DeepSeek. Despite progress, Huawei faces production bottlenecks, US export restrictions, and reliance on Nvidia chips for training AI models, but invests in innovations like LogicFolding and in-house memory design to close the gap. SHANGHAI – Huawei Technologies is accelerating the debut of its next-generation artificial intelligence chip in 2027 by several months as it aims to replace Nvidia in China and compete on the global stage. The company’s flagship Ascend 960DT chip, originally slated for commercial availability in late 2027 , will now be launched in the first quarter, Huawei’s rotating chairman Wang Tao said at the company’s annual summit in Shanghai on Sept 17. Another variant of the new series, dubbed 960PR, will be delivered in the third quarter of 2027, he added. Huawei’s sped-up road map suggests the Chinese networking and chip leader is gaining confidence in advancing an ambitious three-year strategy for developing semiconductors to eventually replace Nvidia. The company, one of several considered key to Beijing’s push to match the US in AI, has since 2025 become increasingly public about outlining its attempts to develop more powerful versions of hardware essential to building data centres and enabling frontier Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI. Wang also highlighted Huawei’s aspiration to offer its AI chips as an alternative to US-origin semiconductors. “Computing power is key to Huawei’s overall AI strategy,” he said. “We will help boost the fundamental of China’s computing power and offer the world a new option with our cluster-based SuperPod technology.” The SuperPod connectivity tech will soon allow as many as 100,000 Ascend chips in a cluster, enabling faster data transmission via Huawei’s UnifiedBus networking protocol. The Shenzhen-based company says its adaptations and networking can make up for shortcomings in single-chip performance relative to the likes of Nvidia. Already, Huawei has been making inroads at home and beyond. DeepSeek is planning to deploy at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT chips at a data centre it is building in Inner Mongolia to operate its models. The company is also exploring foreign markets including Malaysia and Egypt, Bloomberg News has reported. The Chinese telecoms-to-smartphone firm is spearheading Beijing’s drive for self-sufficiency in critical technologies in the face of years-long US restrictions aimed at crippling China’s chipmaking ambitions. It is also leading a Beijing-backed campaign to export the Chinese technology stack abroad at a time when the world’s two superpowers are vying for geopolitical dominance everywhere. Ascend 960 series will succeed Huawei’s current Ascend 950 family of AI accelerators, of which the 950DT favoured by DeepSeek is equipped with faster, higher-capacity memory for demanding AI inference workloads. Another upgraded iteration, Ascend 970, is already planned for 2028, the company previously announced. On Sept 17, Wang said Huawei will launch Ascend 980 in 2029. Each new generation of chips will roughly double the amount of computing power of its predecessor. He also touted Huawei’s nascent optics technology, which enables faster data transmission between AI chips and servers. The company is set to ship its first near-packaged optics (NPO) modules in the coming quarters, he said. NPO speeds up data transmission compared with existing pluggable optic modules, and they also help ensure data integrity. But Huawei’s AI chips are trailing Nvidia’s top-notch offerings. Frontier Chinese AI labs like DeepSeek are still largely relying on the US company’s chips for training their models, which they then operate using more domestic semiconductors, underscoring the challenge Beijing faces to wean itself completely off Western technology. At the same time, Nvidia’s most sophisticated silicon is still finding its way into China via smuggling, albeit in modest quantities. A constraint in production capacity is also preventing Huawei from satisfying explosive demand for computing power in a market that Morgan Stanley estimates could reach 646 billion yuan (S$123 billion) by 2030. Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell processors are not directly available in China. Huawei recently raised pricing for the Ascend 950DT chip by 60 per cent, citing tight component supply in communications with customers. On Sept 17, Wang did not address key issues ahead for Huawei, including how it will navigate manufacturing bottlenecks and ramp up production to meet demand.

events.title: Electricity discount to be given to NI households
events.summary: The one-off reduction will be paid from next month Published 17 September 2026, 00:01 BST All households in Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from next month. It is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market. The schemes are being funded by the UK government and will be applied automatically without the need for an application. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter. The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go. That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up. Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said the money would help families The Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". She said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". Her department agreed the NI scheme with the government and will deliver it to consumers. Last week applications opened for a separate means-tested scheme to provide a £100 voucher to some heating oil users. It is jointly funded by Stormont and the UK government. The electricity scheme reflects two policies which apply in GB: a temporary cut in VAT and the removal of some consumer levies. The UK government decided not to apply the VAT cut in NI as it would have required agreement with the EU which it thought would lead to delay. There are due to be similar bill reductions in the next two years but the size of those will depend on whether the government continues with the VAT cut which was introduced as a temporary measure. It comes as energy prices continue to rise, driven by the US conflict with Iran. Data from the NI consumer council suggests 500 litres of home heating oil currently costs around £560, more than twice the price compared to this time last year. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Frequent class 'splitting' disrupting Canberra students, as union flags further industrial action The Australian Education Union said the government had not provided enough detail on minimum staffing guarantees in its latest offer. ( ABC News: Adam Shirley ) Teachers are set to stop work again next week after the union says a pay and conditions offer from the government failed to meet their demands. Inadequate resourcing and workforce shortages have led to cases where one teacher is managing up to 90 kids due to class 'splitting' and 'collapsing', the union says. One issue raised is a lack of streamlined reporting on workforce shortages, which the ACT's Education Directorate says it is addressing. The Australian Education Union's ACT branch is predicting teachers and other school staff will stop work again next week after what it expects will be a resounding rejection of the government's latest pay and conditions offer. Today, there was minimal supervision for ACT public school students between 9am and 11am as union members met to consider the offer. AEU ACT president Angela Burroughs said a formal response to the deal would be provided next week, but a no vote meant teachers and other school staff would most likely stop work again next Thursday morning. She said members were exhausted by "a prolonged period of inadequate resourcing" in Canberra schools and wanted a guarantee of minimum staffing levels. Angela Burroughs said teacher working conditions were influencing decisions on whether people took up the profession. ( ABC News: Monte Bovill ) Teachers managing up to 90 kids, union says Australia is grappling with a national shortage of teachers . Ms Burroughs explained the profession had become "less attractive" over time as teachers weighed up potential burnout with pay and conditions. Class 'splitting' and 'collapsing', Ms Burroughs said, was an "inevitable consequence" of teacher shortages. Splitting is described as when a teacher is unavailable, and their students are then allocated to multiple available staff. Collapsing is when the class cannot be split into groups, and so the whole class is placed with one teacher. Shortages are forcing different year groups together in one class, the union says. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) "We are seeing one teacher having to teach huge class sizes — 50, 90 in some instances — it has gotten completely out of hand," Ms Burroughs said. ACT public school system to be unified in 'generational shift' The ACT's public education system will be significantly changed after a review of resourcing found schools operated much like "independent small businesses". Ms Burroughs said this could lead to the "most disruptive" cases where very different year groups were mismatched. "It is really hard for the classroom teacher to be able to meet such a diverse range of needs," Ms Burroughs said. Representative body ACT Parents' Veronica Elliot said her organisation surveyed parents and carers at the beginning of 2026, which reported that splitting and collapsing was happening weekly to fortnightly. She said she had also heard of students going a year without a specialist maths teacher. Veronica Elliot said splitting and collapsing remained a big issue of parents and carers. ( ABC News: David Sciasci ) "It does disrupt learning, and we know this is having a big impact on what students are able to achieve, because they just don't have a teacher in front of them," she said. "The issue is that we really don't know how big of a problem it is, because the Education Directorate doesn't collect data on their ongoing vacancies, and also on the splitting and collapsing of classes." She said the data was needed to understand the scale of the problem. ACT Education Directorate Director-General Jo Wood said the directorate was developing a system to show how schools were being affected. ACT Education Director-General Jo Wood agreed improving data collection on workforce shortages was critical. ( ABC News: David Sciasci ) "That automated data system will be the way that we bring visibility to that issue and then we can start to work on some really concrete systems," she said. Ms Wood noted the effects of a declining casual workforce and increased use of leave in a post-COVID era, saying people were being encouraged to stay home when sick. "We're in the flu season at the moment, and we're seeing more people have to access their personal leave," she said. She said the Education Directorate had committed to working with the union and schools to better handle the issue.

events.title: Why Package Digital Twins Are So Hard To Build
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Package twins must track what manufacturing actually builds, not just design intent. Missing process and supplier data can undermine otherwise precise simulations. Coupled physics and ongoing calibration keep models tied to physical reality. A chiplet can be fully characterized, tested, and considered known good, but none of that guarantees it will stay that way after it’s placed into a different package. While the chiplet itself may be unchanged, nearly everything around it can move. A different substrate can alter the mechanical and electrical environment, a different thermal interface can change how heat leaves the device, and a new power envelope can increase how much heat needs to leave in the first place. A thermal path that worked in the first product can cause throttling in the second because the surrounding package and cooling assumptions have changed. By the time the chiplet is assembled into another package, engineers may be dealing with a different system altogether, which is why package models can’t stop at the die boundary, and why the added complexity makes package digital twins so difficult to achieve. That is the basic problem facing digital twins for advanced packaging. They have to predict how known components will behave after integration and eventually inside a larger system. “A chiplet may be characterized and validated in one package or product SKU, then reused in a different package stack, substrate, cooling approach, or power envelope,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of product management at Synopsys . “The chiplet has not changed, but its electrical, thermal, and mechanical environment has.” Fab vs. packaging: A different kind of twin Digital twins are starting to be used in semiconductor manufacturing, but the comparison with front-end fabs needs some clarification. A fab process twin can be enormously complicated, incorporating equipment behavior, process history, and statistical learning. The difference is that much of that complexity remains inside a relatively well-defined manufacturing environment. “A fab process twin is extremely complex, so I would not frame this as fab being easy and package being hard,” Larsen said. “The difference is the nature of the problem. A fab twin is usually deep within one manufacturing environment, one process technology, and one managed flow of equipment, materials, process data, and statistical learning. A package digital twin has to solve a broader integration problem — how a multi-die system is realized across silicon, substrate, assembly, manufacturing variation, test, and reliability learning.” That broader integration problem changes what the twin has to represent. In heterogeneous integration, the package is increasingly part of the system architecture, so electrical, thermal and mechanical behavior cannot be optimized independently. Engineers already have effective tools for each of those domains, but they don’t become a package twin simply by running next to one another. The harder problem is keeping them synchronized around the same physical package as it moves from design to manufacturing. Manufacturing results also need to feed back into those models as the package is revised. “The package, silicon, substrate, materials, thermal solution, and manufacturing assumptions have to be explored together,” Larsen said. “If they are optimized separately, the digital twin becomes a late-stage validation artifact. That is not where the value is.” The boundary also becomes less obvious once the package moves onto a board and into its eventual system. Conditions outside the package can change its behavior, which means some of that context has to travel with the model. “An end-to-end package digital twin requires visibility across the entire lifecycle, from wafer fabrication through assembly, test, and ultimately system operation,” said Joon Ahn, vice president of global factory IT and automation at Amkor . “Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.” Preserving that context would be difficult even if all of the necessary information were sitting in one place. Often, it’s not. The data hole From the OSAT perspective, much of the information needed to describe an advanced package comes from elsewhere. Some of it comes from the foundry, some from substrate and material suppliers, and some is generated only after assembly or test. Even equipment inside the same manufacturing flow may provide different types of data depending on its age and supplier. “For OSATs, an end-to-end digital twin is not a single model, but a connected ecosystem of process, equipment, production, supply chain, and traceability data,” said Ahn. “Packaging performance is influenced by interactions among multiple process steps. Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.” What an OSAT receives can be quite different from what a predictive model ideally contains. Incoming die data may include critical dimensions and wafer-sort results, but not detailed power-density or local stress maps. A substrate may arrive within nominal specifications without showing actual warpage across the production lot, while material data sheets may not capture material-specific behavior in the end device. “The downstream analysis can then look precise while missing the manufacturing reality,” Larsen said. “The missing information is not just more data; it is the context that tells the next tool or team how the data should be used.” That context can be lost even when plenty of data survives the handoff. The problem is that different parts of the supply chain may describe the same physical system in different ways. “The hardest handoffs aren’t necessarily where we have the least data. They’re usually where the data has to move between very different engineering domains,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&D at ASE . “A foundry may describe die behavior one way, a substrate supplier another, and a materials company may provide properties measured under a very specific set of conditions. Then the OSAT has to bring all of that together and understand how it will behave during assembly.” That context becomes even harder to preserve when the information crosses company boundaries. The material supplier knows things about the chemistry that the equipment company doesn’t. The equipment company knows details of the process integration that may not be available to the OSAT or fab. Much of that knowledge also represents intellectual property. “We all have our own data and everybody wants to protect intellectual property,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of marketing and business development at Mitsubishi Chemical Group. “I’ve been in this industry all my life, and when we started we had a different way of collaborating. We were a lot more open as an industry, as an ecosystem.” For a package digital twin,

events.title: Reddit co-founder says tech industry has been 'tone deaf' in explaining AI: 'Misinformation flying around'
events.summary: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian told CNBC the industry has been "pretty tone deaf" in explaining the risks of AI. Ohanian said the AI debate should focus on substantive risks rather than become issues used to score political points. It comes days after warnings from researchers at AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic of the rapid advancement of the technology known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. The tech industry has been "tone deaf" in explaining AI and properly informing the public about real risks, Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian told CNBC on Wednesday. Ohanian said the debate around AI should focus on substantive risks rather than issues that can be used to score political points, arguing that an informed public is essential to navigating the technology. He acknowledged that the tech industry has contributed to the problem by doing a "pretty tone deaf job" of explaining AI, while suggesting that its risks are more mundane than the "Terminator and Skynet" scenarios some fear. Skynet is a fictional self-aware AI system in the "Terminator" movies that saw humans as a threat and sought to wipe them out. The comments come days after warnings from researchers at AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic of the rapid advancement of the technology known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. RSI refers to AI systems helping develop more advanced models, potentially creating a cycle in which increasingly capable systems contribute to building even more capable ones. The concern is that if AI systems take over the process of training new models, their human developers could eventually lose control over how those systems evolve. Ohanian argued that while AI risks are real, apocalyptic "Terminator"-style warnings can distract from real concerns such as agent swarms, when multiple AI agents work together to perform a complicated task. "There are risks, I do think they're more benign, or they're more banal than people are thinking," he said. He compared AI to nuclear energy because both technologies are powerful scientific advances that can cause serious harm but also deliver major benefits if managed responsibly. "I'm hopeful this goes in a healthy direction, and it's just going to require fewer tweets and more, like, thoughtful conversation," Ohanian said. "The doomer tweet was discouraging," he said without specifying, adding it was "frustrating" when "the slogans are actually not real things." Earlier this month, an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic and accused the company and OpenAI of acting irresponsibly when it comes to developing the powerful technology. Jacob Coxon, who has worked as a researcher at both companies, said on social media that he resigned because he was concerned that Anthropic and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives." He said the people building AI "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." For Ohanian, nuance is crucial. "We should have a discussion about the important, like real stuff, instead of these things that maybe score some quick political points… I have faith that we can have this discussion." "It frustrates me because I see all this misinformation flying around, but I do think in the long run, we [will] get it right, and that's what I'm hoping happens. So I'm not terribly worried about that part of it."

events.title: Negative Expansion Materials Resist Warpage
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Warpage is becoming a bigger constraint as package, interposer, and panel sizes grow. Negative thermal expansion (NTE) materials, newly on the market, can help counter warpage. Commercial NTE materials are starting to be used in semiconductor packaging, but broader adoption will depend on temperature range, compatibility of different materials, and uniform mixing and purity. Thermally induced warpage, caused by differences in the rate at which materials expand when heated, is becoming increasingly problematic in large chips and packages. The solution may be to integrate a new class of materials that actually shrink when heated. Rather than relying solely on the few substances that can shrink, companies are focusing on mixtures of materials with a lattice structure that can resist the urge to expand. Using such materials for underfill and as the packaging molding compound can add rigidity for larger packages while keeping warpage in check. Warpage as the enemy Warpage, especially in large packages and panels, occurs because of mismatches between how, for example, a substrate, a die, and surrounding molding compound behave when heated. It’s one of the biggest issues holding back the constant enlargement of package substrates, interposers, and panels. The larger the bonded area, the greater the likelihood that edge connections may be poor or fail altogether. Even before bonding, too much warpage can defeat standard manufacturing equipment features such as vacuum chucks. “The vacuum chucks will pull the warpage down, but if the warpage is too high, then you won’t get a good vacuum,” said Knowlton Olmstead, senior manager of wafer services at Amkor . Anywhere two materials meet with different coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE), warping is likely to some degree. For example, given two layers of material, if the bottom layer has a higher CTE, then it will try to expand to its natural extent. But the material above it will restrict it, assuming they’re well adhered. That will cause the edges of the bottom material to want to curl up. It’s theoretically impossible to stop all warpage if there is a CTE difference. The question becomes how much is too much. If it’s too much, what can you do about it? “We do a certain level of modeling to model the warpage beforehand, and then there’s certain levers you can pull to control the warpage,” said Olmstead. If silicon is one of the layers (as it often is), thinning the silicon can reduce the amount of warping. “You reduce the impact of the low CTE silicon if there’s thinner silicon,” said Mike Kelly, vice president, chiplets/FCBGA integration at Amkor. “In the extreme, you can make it super thin, and then it can follow the shape of whatever I’m attached to. But that ends up being a problem, because nobody wants really thin silicon for managing high power.” Warpage also impacts how new materials may be received, such as glass. “The larger the panel you’re trying to make, the more warpage you will see,” said Lang Lin, principal product manager at Synopsys . “Today we talk about micrometers of warpage, but with glass, it could be even larger — millimeters, maybe.” One approach being explored is to identify or design materials that contract when heated, giving them a negative CTE. “Negative CTE materials could be utilized in a variety of ways to offset expansion,” said Luke Prenger, research scientist IV team lead at Brewer Science . “It might depend on why the expansion needs to be offset to begin with. For things like stress management and warpage reduction, negative CTE materials can be utilized to help better match the CTEs of different materials. An example case of this would be to add filler to a polymer material, which typically has a very high CTE compared to inorganics, to reduce the overall CTE of the polymer matrix so it is closer to that of the metal layers and other components in the device. Reducing or modulating the CTE of organic layers to be closer to the inorganic layers helps in reducing warpage and overall stress build-up in a device.” Going against the grain One of the material interfaces that results in warping is the epoxy molding compound (EMC) used for fillers and underfill. It fills all the major gaps inside the package, so when the temperature changes, it can affect everything it touches. Altering the composition of that compound can mitigate the warping. The key is changing the CTE, with a negative CTE ideal for counteracting an adjacent positive one. Alternatively, mixing a positive CTE material with a negative one can alter the overall CTE of the combination. A variety of materials can exhibit true negative thermal expansion (NTE) behavior, although it often occurs within specific temperature ranges. It may also be associated with a phase change. For example, water behaves normally above 3.98 °C, below which it moves toward freezing. Ice is famously less dense than water due to its molecular structure, and so as more of the water takes on that configuration between 3.98°C and 0°C, it expands up until the final phase transition to ice. Unlike materials exhibiting true NTE behavior, other substances may consist of normal materials encased in a lattice that restricts expansion. The structure of that lattice is important in determining how anything encased in it behaves. “The key is the structure of the filler itself,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of global marketing and business development for the semiconductor business at Mitsubishi Chemical Group. Solids may have a wide range of molecular arrangements. Whereas polymers can be amorphous, inorganic materials typically have some sort of lattice structure. Materials scientists categorize the different structures and study their rheological properties (which refers to the study of how they flow). They’ll describe lattice structures, such as house-of-cards, rigid-rod, or tetrahedral. Each of these structures behave differently and can establish rigidity in one or more dimensions. What’s within the lattice (also called a matrix or a network) can also affect the flow, and the combined NTE materials reflect such a structure — a functional material within a restraining matrix. “It’s more of a network thing than a material thing,” explained Bhatt. “Not everything will form the same network. A carbon powder forms a flocculated network. If you look at a carbon fiber network, that is a reinforcing rigid-rod network. So if you are going to put a carbon fiber into a matrix, it’s like logs in a river. If I use the logs in water, it is going to have little impact on the ability of water to flow. It will restrict it some, but the water is still going to find room between them. events.title: The Silicon Heartland Wants To Be America’s Next Chip Powerhouse
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Major facility investments are driving momentum for the Midwestern semiconductor industry. Workforce development remains a major structural challenge. Quantum investment in Chicago represents a major opportunity for the regional semiconductor ecosystem. The U.S. semiconductor industry has long been concentrated in established technology and manufacturing hubs, but new investments and startup activity are helping expand the industry’s footprint across the Midwest. The prospect of a thriving Midwestern semiconductor industry has long hinged on whether semiconductor companies can leverage the region’s strong base of research institutions and available workforce, logistics, and industrial infrastructure to build a regional ecosystem. Over the last several years, that trend has gained momentum, with Intel and SK hynix bringing landmark facility investments to the Midwest, major bets on the future of quantum computing being made on the shores of Lake Michigan, and significant government investment being funneled toward semiconductor growth and startup support. Defining the Midwestern ecosystem The Midwest has undergone something of a “transformation” in recent years, with signs of a real semiconductor ecosystem beginning to materialize. “There’s always been this culture of innovation, but because a lot of the semiconductor and microelectronics work had existed on the coasts, or had been elsewhere, while the Midwest was really the heart for manufacturing, there’s been this transformation to a technology-based silicon heartland ecosystem,” said Matt Casto, CEO of Midwest Microelectronics Consortium. “New foundry capabilities are being built just north of Columbus, Ohio. Supply chain manufacturers range from water treatment capabilities to semiconductor tools. We’ve got companies in the Midwest and in the state of Ohio now that are doing material growth development. So the building blocks for semiconductor work can connect within that Midwest ecosystem through additional supply chain capabilities. Now is a generational opportunity around advanced technology, and that requires a lot more emphasis on workforce development.” The vision for this developing semiconductor ecosystem rests on a diverse technology production network that can integrate into the region’s existing manufacturing and research base. “One defining characteristic of the Midwest is its emphasis on connecting semiconductor innovation directly to manufacturing and industrial applications,” said Christopher Salomone, account management at Synopsys . “While some regions are heavily concentrated in either semiconductor design or fabrication, the Midwest is building a more integrated ecosystem that includes research institutions, advanced manufacturing, automotive technology, defense applications, and emerging semiconductor production capabilities.” One of the biggest markers of the industry’s Midwestern development has been Intel’s $28B+ “Silicon Heartland” project in suburban Central Ohio. Expected to open in the early 2030s, the facility will create 3,000 new Intel jobs in the metro Columbus area once fully operational. “Intel’s investment helped establish the Midwest as a serious contender in advanced semiconductor manufacturing and created opportunities that simply didn’t exist in this region before,” said Ted Geer, director of state government affairs for Ohio at Intel . “The Midwest has always produced exceptional engineers, researchers, and technical talent through its universities and research institutions. Too often, however, many of those graduates built their careers elsewhere. Today, students and researchers across the region can see a pathway to participate in leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing without leaving the Midwest. Organizations like MMEC are helping build on that momentum by strengthening connections between research, talent development, and the future of domestic microelectronics.” Part of the growing momentum also comes from established regional power players expanding their footprint with long-term growth in mind. “Brewer Science has been rooted in the Midwest since 1981, and our positioning isn’t incidental to the region; it’s strategic,” said Srikanth Kommu, co-CEO at Brewer Science . “We’ve demonstrated that world-class materials innovation and manufacturing can thrive outside traditional coastal hubs, which directly challenges the historical consolidation of semiconductor ecosystems. When you connect that kind of regional leadership to what we’re doing on the ground, like our acquisition of Heraeus Epurio’s semiconductor chemicals business, which brought a production facility in Dayton, Ohio, into our operations, you start to see a materials corridor forming across the Midwest that didn’t exist five years ago. Our deliberate geographic deepening through acquisitions and internal growth, from Rolla to Vichy to Springfield to now Dayton, treats our supply chain and workforce as strategic assets. This model lets us sustain margins while investing in facility upgrades, process improvements, and worker development. The manufacturers who will matter most in this region are those treating this as a 20-year investment in institutional capability, not a response to quarterly performance metrics.” Major Midwest Semiconductor Activities Recently announced, under construction, or recently broken ground | Updated September 8, 2026.
