events.title: Ministry of Justice apologizes after court staff accessed Southport victims' files
events.summary: The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has apologized after court staff accessed documents relating to victims and survivors of the 2024 Southport murders without authorization. For a limited number of people, the material accessed included sensitive personal data assessed as likely to pose a high risk to their rights and freedoms. There is no evidence that the information was shared with third parties. "We are appalled that this happened and recognise the distress it will have caused victims, survivors, and their families," an MoJ spokesperson said. "We apologise to those affected – unauthorized access to court files is completely unacceptable. "This is now being investigated urgently, and the prime minister has asked the Lord Chancellor to oversee this. "All wrongdoing will be met with extremely firm action." The Register asked the MoJ how many staff accessed the files, whether they remained employed, and what their reasons may have been. It did not address those questions. Those affected include members of victims' and survivors' families, all of whom are being contacted directly. The MoJ did not disclose how many people were involved. HM Prison and Probation Service and HM Courts and Tribunals Service are investigating the matter. The Information Commissioner's Office has also been informed. The MoJ breach is the latest in a series of incidents involving inappropriate access to sensitive records connected to the attack. Separately, North West Ambulance Service investigated potentially inappropriate access by some of its staff to records of patients in the Southport attacks. And nearly 50 staff were found to have inappropriately accessed the medical records of some victims treated at Aintree University Hospital, near the place of Axel Rudakubana's attacks. Rudakubana, who was 17 at the time and has since been admitted to a psychiatric hospital, attacked a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport, England, on July 29, 2024, killing three children and injuring eight other children and two adults. False claims about the attack online prompted violent, racially charged riots across the UK. Police made 1,511 arrests in the weeks that followed and brought 960 charges. Rudakubana was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 52 years. ®

events.title: Sunderland gets its Kicks: Nissan to invest £170m to build new hybrid SUV
events.summary: Latest attempt to secure future of Britain’s biggest car factory may be subject to UK weakening EV sales mandate Nissan has said it will invest £170m to build a new SUV at its factory in Sunderland – but said the move was subject to the UK weakening its electric vehicle sales mandate . The new hybrid model, the Kicks, is Nissan’s latest attempt to secure the future of the plant, which employs 6,000 people in Tyne and Wear and is Britain’s biggest car factory. Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s head in Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, said the move would not bring new jobs but was part of “securing and maintaining” jobs at the site , which has been running at 50% capacity. The Kicks will be the fourth Nissan model produced at the Sunderland plant, which already makes the Qashqai, Juke and Leaf. It is already sold in more than 70 markets but has never been built in Europe. The announcement is a boost to Britain’s automotive sector, which was last week hit by the news that Jaguar Land Rover will cut 4,000 jobs. Carmakers have come under pressure from US tariffs, competition from Chinese rivals and high industrial energy costs in recent years. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said the investment and new car model was “a huge vote of confidence in the UK’s manufacturing expertise and automotive future”. However, it also came with an apparent warning from Messina, who said: “Of course we’re going to keep discussing with the UK government because large part of this is subject to the ZEV [Zero Emission Vehicles] mandate amendment.” The government is consulting on cutting the UK’s electric vehicle sales targets for manufacturers. Under the ZEV mandate, carmakers ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero-emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030. But after heavy lobbying pressure from manufacturers, the government said last month that it was considering cutting that figure to as little as 50% by the end of the decade, which it is consulting on until late October. When pressed on whether Nissan would still make the investment if the targets were not weakened, Messina said: “We try to assess always if this is more likely than unlikely.” He added that the company was pushing for a cut to 50% of sales needing to be EVs. “I just want to think that this is done,” he said. “For me, yes, it’s going to happen.” Nissan is separately in talks to share production with the Chinese carmaker Chery, which is looking to build its own cars in the UK, to bring the site closer to full capacity again. Messina said he was putting “pressure internally and externally” to complete the deal which was announced in June . “We are ready to go. We are waiting just that Chery finalises volume and lineup.” Separately, LEVC, the maker of London’s black cabs, said on Wednesday that it will launch its next-generation taxi model next year, built at its factory in Ansty, near Coventry. The Chinese company, owned by Geely, said the new taxi would replace the current all-electric TX range introduced in 2018. Nissan is also lobbying Brussels over the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules, which would require cars to be built within the bloc to qualify for subsidies and public procurement. The company has previously said that it could be forced to close Sunderland if the rules go ahead as currently drafted. Messina said: “You might imagine how much time I’m spending on this to secure that this comes together in order to have Sunderland and the UK part of it. “There are good indications that this will be achieved. We believe strongly, regardless what will be the outcome, that UK cannot be left anyway outside.” Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said the investment was “a major boost for Nissan Sunderland, the thousands of highly skilled jobs it supports and the wider local supply chain”. On Wednesday, McLaren announced it would invest £500m in its UK operations, including a new factory, 1,000 jobs and its first SUV. Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars

events.title: The EU Plans to Ban Social Media for Under-13s
events.summary: The European Union has announced plans to restrict children’s access to social media across member states in a bid to free them from what President of the Commission Ursula von der Leyen described as the “capture [of] their attention, their focus, their minds” by the platforms. The proposal for a total ban on social media for children under 13 was announced in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech, where von der Leyen set out the Union’s priorities for the year ahead. It’s part of an EU Kids Act, which the Commission will unveil fully on Thursday. Children aged 13 to 15 will also not be allowed personal social media accounts but will be able to access social media through mini accounts set up and supervised by parents and guardians, with limited features, for one hour per day. Platforms will also have safe design obligations for users up to 18, with the Union planning to tackle addictive design further in the upcoming Digital Fairness Act in Autumn. “I am aware that many perceive the power of Big Tech as overwhelming and impossible to roll back. I disagree,” von der Leyen told the European Parliament. “We do not have to accept addictive features, we do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content, we do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for-AI generated sexualised images,” she added. “Europe has the power to act; it is us who decide the rules, not Big Tech.” The EU was largely expected to follow other countries in restricting children’s access to social media, which von der Leyen said has been responsible for sleep loss, anxiety, self harm, and even the deaths of European children. Seventeen of the bloc’s 27 member states are already negotiating or preparing draft legislation to protect minors online, including by setting out a minimum age to access certain services. Among those is France, whose top court last month struck down a ban on social media for under-15s because it infringed upon freedom of expression. “Cleaning up that mess, getting everyone on the same page, then running through the EU legislative process,” will probably take until 2029, expects Ashurst Perkins Coie technology lawyer Arnav Joshi. Still, he believes companies will welcome the clarity and simplicity provided by a single set of EU-wide rules. The tiered approach is designed to placate any judicial challenges by being proportionate—a rare example of where “the EU law, by not introducing a blanket ban, is perhaps even a little bit more permissive than others,” he told WIRED, referencing the sweeping social media bans in the UK and Australia . But the measures still force oversight on both guardians and the social media platforms themselves, which could risk privacy infringements. Parental monitoring could be “problematic” says Joshi, who advises global technology companies on children’s online safety, warning: “anything that has deep dive, God-mode style parental access can have a bit of a chilling effect on how children actually use that service and could have issues in terms of their own right to privacy.” The European bloc will also face similar challenges to other countries in effectively enforcing the age limits. Children in Australia have widely been able to circumvent the country’s under-16s ban on social media access. "A key issue is how to carry out the age checks and it’s not straightforward,” Joanna Conway, digital regulation partner at law firm Norton Rose Fulbright, told WIRED. Making age checks accurate, without infringing on privacy rights or harming user experience, is a challenge, she added. The EU introduced an app earlier in the year so members can prove they are over 18 and access adult-restricted sites, which it says can be applied to other age groups. Von der Leyen also acknowledged that Europeans are more widely worried by the “dizzying” speed of technology and its impact on their livelihoods and society. Artificial intelligence “has not yet delivered” value in the real economy—like factories, hospitals, and energy grids—she added, teasing initiatives that will be announced in November to address these concerns across health, transport, agri-food, advanced manufacturing, and defence and space. She also referenced the upcoming Quality Jobs Act, designed to ensure AI helps develop skills, improve the quality of jobs, and “give workers a fair chance,” and said she would invite the main artificial intelligence frontier labs for a discussion on how the EU can support industry efforts to pace the frontier. events.title: Salesforce staggers back to feet after global outage
events.summary: UPDATED An hours-long Salesforce outage on Wednesday hit customers with severe delays, intermittent errors, and inability to access some services, according to the SaaS vendor's status page. The outage hit hundreds of instances throughout the world, including the USA, Japan, India, the UK, France, and Germany. The service disruption was first reported around 0930 BST (0830 UTC) on September 16. An update at 1219 BST (1056 UTC) said the company had validated and rolled out a fix, and customers were seeing service return to normal. However, as of 1500 BST (1400 UTC), the company said that the fix had not completely restored all instances of the problem, and it had "received reports of scheduled jobs not running as expected for some customers who are now able to access the service." A previous update at 1010 BST (0910 UTC) by the CRM giant said its investigation indicated that "requests are stalling while waiting on a response from an internal login service, which is using up available server resources." The vendor added: "Customers continue to experience severe delays, intermittent errors, and inability to access some services. This also affects support case creation." Salesforce's customer list is a roll-call of global giants from all industries, including include Amazon, Walmart, Coca-Cola, Toyota, and IBM. The outage came at a bad time for the SaaS company. Yesterday, it kicked off its annual conference, Dreamforce, in San Francisco. More than 40,000 people are expected to attend in person, with in excess of 200,000 people registered to attend online. Updates to the situation, which is still ongoing as of 1725 UTC, are below. ® Updated at 2020 BTS (1920 UTC) Salesforce says that the incident has now been resolved. Updated at 1722 BTS (1622 UTC): Salesforce says that the impact radius is narrower than they originally thought. They will continue to update impacted instances. Updated at 1650 BST (1550 UTC): Salesforce has completed the next phase of its rollout and narrowed the remaining disruption to a subset of Hyperforce instances. Its first-party environments are unaffected. Mitigation is in place across nearly all affected instances, although the company continues targeted restarts and manual recovery work where the automated fix has not fully resolved the problem. Some customers could still experience delays, errors, and problems accessing services or creating support cases. Updated at 1522 BST (1422 UTC): Salesforce said it was manually restarting instances where the automated fix hadn't fully resolved the issue, and that it was still receiving reports of scheduled jobs not running as expected for some customers who were able to access the service. It also said that the "impact radius" of the problem was "narrower than initially understood." Updated at 1429 BST (1329 UTC): Salesforce said the rollout had not completed successfully on some instances, leaving customers exposed to the original problem. The company is reapplying the fix and warns that some users might need to clear cached data or restart their sessions to recover fully. Updated at 1407 BST (1307 UTC): Salesforce said most instances were recovering as the rollout progressed. Some customers may continue to encounter errors until their instance is manually restarted, and the company has yet to confirm when the incident would be fully resolved. Updated at 1327 BST (1227 UTC): Salesforce said services were returning to normal in regions where the rollout had been completed. The company continues to monitor the deployment while working on a permanent fix. Updated at 1300 BST (1200 UTC): Salesforce said the fix was being deployed region by region and that service was improving, although it had no confirmed completion time. GovCloud customers were no longer affected, but others could continue to experience severe delays, intermittent errors, and problems accessing some services or creating support cases. Updated at 1227 BST (1127 UTC): Salesforce said the fix was being rolled out "fleetwide" and that customers were seeing service return to normal. Updated at 1200 BST (1100 UTC): Salesforce said the fix had been successfully validated on a test instance and would now be deployed across all affected instances. Updated at 1142 BST (1042 UTC): Salesforce said increased load on a core system component had limited its capacity to process requests. The company is testing a fix on one instance and plans to deploy it across its fleet once validated. Updated at 1109 BST (1009 UTC) on September 16, 2026, to add: Salesforce said in its latest update that it is "no longer pursuing restarts as a path to remediation. Customers continue to experience severe delays, intermittent errors, and inability to access some services and support case creation."

events.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
events.summary: WEF report: Progress on gender equality remains 'fragile' Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take 120 years to close. The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%. However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile." The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006. Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels. WEF Managing Director Saadia Zahidi warned that while parity is a foundation for growth and competitiveness, it is "not inevitable." "To accelerate, governments and employers need to learn from the policies that work and apply them faster. A new economy demands a new approach to talent," Zahidi said in a press release to accompany the report. Women still missing in top power roles The WEF found that women remain underrepresented in roles with the largest economic and political influence. They still hold fewer than a fifth of chief executive officer (CEO) positions, while only one in 10 ministerial roles held by women is considered high influence. While the number of ministerial roles led by women has risen 26% since 2008, only one in 10 was considered weighty then — a share the WEF report said was "virtually unchanged today." Despite nearly $1 trillion (€866 billion) being invested globally to develop artificial intelligence (AI), the report also revealed that fewer than one in five AI engineers are women, and they are underrepresented at every level of AI firms. For the 17th consecutive year, Iceland leads the ranking with 93% of the gender gap closed, followed by its Nordic neighbors Finland and Norway. The three nations have made the Top 10, along with Sweden, every year since 2006. Namibia ranked fourth globally, higher than Germany (9th), the United Kingdom (5th) and Australia (8th). The United States dropped five places in the rankings to 47th, with 74.9% of its gender gap closed. The country achieved full parity in education for a second year, ranking first in the world in that area. In the US, women have long matched men in professional and technical jobs, but parity in senior management has fallen by almost 11 points since 2006, the WEF calculated. The political score fell 4.1 points from last year after the share of women ministers dropped from two-thirds parity to one-half. The decline coincided with a lower share of women serving as Cabinet secretaries in President Donald Trump's second administration. The WEF kept the head-of-state indicator for the US at zero as the world's largest economy has never had a female president. India , the world's most populous country, remains at 131st in the rankings, with 64.5% gender parity closed. The report noted India's overall gains amount to a 4.3 percentage-point rise since 2006, which the authors said was mostly due to educational achievement. Women's labor-market participation has barely moved over 20 years, the WEF noted. India's economic parity score has varied significantly since the first report. Parity among professional and technical workers has almost doubled since 2006, to 49.9%. Among legislators, senior officials and managers, however, it is still only 13.1%. In parliament, India has closed 16.1% of the gender gap, up seven points since 2006, while the share of women in long-serving Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet has fallen recently, with parity slipping to 5.9% from a 30% peak in 2019. China , meanwhile, rose seven places to 96th, closing 69.9% of its gender gap. Economic parity is its strongest pillar, at 72.3%, but politics has barely moved in 20 years, with women still accounting for only a fraction of ministers. Namibia's rise in women's political power Large jumps for Namibia, Kenya and Ghana Reaching 84.5% parity in the latest report, Namibia leads the way in Sub-Saharan Africa, climbing four places to No. 4 in the ranking. Namibia has long been well represented by women on the political stage. Last year, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became its first female president. The country also has a female vice-president and the parliament speaker is a woman, too. Other African countries were among the biggest climbers in the 2026 rankings, with Kenya rising 33 places in a year to 65th, Ghana up 32 places to 56th and Angola climbing 30 places to 87th.

events.title: US-Canada trade war further taxes small businesses as costs rise during the Iran war
events.summary: Small business owners in the United States and Canada say a trade war between their countries is hurting sales while they are also dealing with rising expenses from higher fuel costs NEW YORK -- A trade war between the United States and Canada is making it more difficult and expensive for small businesses in the economically entwined countries to operate, according to business owners caught in the crossfire. Canada imposed reciprocal tariffs on about $20 billion (CA$27.6 billion) worth of U.S. goods last week after President Donald Trump placed import taxes on Canadian goods worth the same amount. In response to Canada's action, Trump said the U.S. also would ban imports of wine, whiskey, selected motorcycles and the dairy ingredient whey from Canada. The tariffs so far involve about 5.5% of the neighboring nations' bilateral trade in goods. Analysts say the overall economic impact therefore will be muted. But small business owners who depend on cross-border sales say a tax of up to 50% on their products and ill will created by the conflict have an outsize effect on them, especially when higher energy costs stemming from the Iran war are eroding their balance sheets. The owners of four small businesses, two in the U.S. and two in Canada, spoke with The Associated Press about the ways the trade war is affecting their companies. At Jasper Hill Farm, an artisan cheesemaker in Greensboro, Vermont, co-founder Mateo Kehler said Trump's opening salvo produced an immediate effect: canceled holiday orders from wholesale customers in Canada, whose border is only about 40 miles away. Cheese wasn't among the products made subject to new U.S. tariffs last month. Kehler suspects his hopes for expanding business in Canada are stalling because residents there resent the way the president and members of his Cabinet treat their country, a longtime ally . “The backlash on the market side is actually what’s affecting us the most,” Kehler said. “It’s the rhetoric that has inspired a boycott.” Trump has needled America’s northern neighbor repeatedly since he returned to the White House. First, it was comments last year about wanting to absorb Canada as the 51st state . After trade negotiations broke down in August, he taunted Prime Minister Mark Carney and signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. The lost sales and higher prices for materials and equipment that Kehler buys from Canada are tough to swallow when the war with Iran has made fuel for Jasper Hill Farm's trucks and machinery more expensive too, he said. Some of his suppliers and distributors are adding surcharges to cover their costs, he said. “It’s like death by a thousand cuts, because between the rising cost of energy and the tariffs, the inflationary pressure on the inputs across almost every aspect of our business — from the farming side all the way through to finished goods — is just being ratcheted up,” Kehler said. Revival Stillworks makes equipment for distilling liquor like vodka, agave and whisky and helps design spaces for producing craft spirits from the company's base on Vancouver Island, less than 20 miles from Washington state's San Juan Island. Until last month, the equipment could enter the U.S. tariff-free under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trade pact Trump negotiated during his first presidency. Now, the company's stills, fermenters and other products incur a 50% tax for crossing the border, co-founder Darcy Lane said. The customs charges are considerable because the equipment costs $250,000 to $2 million, Lane said. “We’ve got millions of dollars worth of orders that are supposed to be happening over the next four to six months, and then all of a sudden this happens again,” he said, recalling how a U.S. customer called off a project last year when Trump threatened to put tariffs on some Canadian products. Clients in the U.S. make up about half of Revival Stillworks' business. With rising oil prices during the war driving up shipping costs, many already were evaluating whether they should move forward with projects that involve imported equipment, Lane said. He and his partner are looking into other kinds of work. Since they employ engineers, welders and fabricators, their business could service the local marine industry, Lane said. “Hopefully, cooler heads prevail and everything works out, and we can continue along as business as normal," he said. “But if not, we have to put a contingency plan in place anyway." events.title: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe | Steven Greenhouse
events.summary: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe Not only would the plan do vast economic damage – it assumes that Americans are easily bamboozled W henever Donald Trump gives a speech, it’s filled with so many lies and self-serving exaggerations that when he does utter something true, I see that as a sort of marvel. That’s what happened nearly an hour into Trump’s marathon speech last Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention, when he declared: “Only I can make this promise to you.” Trump said that just before he made a promise that was so shameless and irresponsible that what he said was indeed true: only Trump could make such a preposterous promise. Feeling very generous with other people’s money, the president promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. It certainly looked and smelled like a bribe. I guess that when you’re fearing an electoral debacle because your public approval ratings are in the toilet, because people are furious about your disastrous war of choice against Iran and because so many Americans are hopping mad that inflation has risen even though you promised to cut prices, then you might feel the need to take desperate measures, and that’s what Trump did by offering to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s pocket to help sway them to vote Republican. Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn – that’s more than the Pentagon’s budget and nearly what the US will spend on Medicare this year. Many Republicans and Trump donors rushed to criticize Trump’s $5,000 plan. Joe Lonsdale, a tech billionaire and Republican donor, said he was “strongly against bread and circus bribes ”, while Representative Bob Good of Virginia, former chair of the House Freedom caucus, called Trump’s promise a “ socialist vote-buying scheme ”. What angers me most about Trump’s promise isn’t that it would increase the enormous $40tn federal debt even though the president once promised to eliminate the entire federal debt . Nor am I angriest about the fact that Trump is essentially seeking to bribe the nation’s entire adult population for short-term political gain while in effect passing the cost on to our children and grandchildren. Trump is unconscionably seeking to finance his bribery by borrowing from future generations. But here is what makes me angriest: Trump evidently believes that millions and millions of Americans are such rubes that he can bamboozle them into voting Republican because they would want to get their hands on $5,000. I like to think that Americans are smarter than that and won’t be fooled. When the president made such a shameless proposal, I couldn’t help but wonder: are there no adults in the room with Trump? Is there no one with a sense of shame or fiscal responsibility who will tell him, “Don’t offer this $5,000 bribe. It stinks to high hell, and it’s grossly irresponsible.” Some brutal mockery came from Trump’s one-time ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former House member from Georgia. She hasn’t forgotten that Trump promised last fall that, thanks to his tariffs, every American, except for high-income people, would receive “ a dividend of at least $2,000” . That didn’t happen. Greene also remembers that when Elon Musk said that Doge would chop the federal budget by $2tn, Trump suggested that a sizable chunk of those savings could go directly to Americans . That didn’t happen either. Greene taunted Trump by writing on X, “ $5,000 for the peasants will be in the mail after the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.” Trump egomaniacally called the $5,000 payments a “Trump dividend”, saying the money was available “because of our tremendous strength and success economically ”. But Trump is embellishing big time here; there really hasn’t been economic success during Trump’s second term, other than the much-detested datacenter boom and the stock market hitting repeated records. Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, the trade deficit has jumped over 60% since April, the nation has lost 35,000 factory jobs since Trump’s inauguration and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations. After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the money would come from tariff revenues , while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come from charging wealthy foreigners for visas and from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you.

events.title: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”
events.summary: From Latin America to Southeast Asia, countries are dividing their AI investments between the two superpowers rather than choosing one over the other. Saudi Arabia celebrated the launch of what it calls the world’s most advanced Arabic-language AI model earlier this month. The technology behind it came from China even as the kingdom spends billions building its AI infrastructure with American companies. The Arabic model, Humain-m3, is based on an open-source system from Chinese startup MiniMax. Humain, the state-backed company that commissioned the model, has struck major deals with Nvidia and other U.S. technology companies to build its AI computing capacity. Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds.” Kyle Chan, fellow, John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution Saudi Arabia is not alone. From Latin America to Southeast and Central Asia, countries are buying American chips while adopting Chinese open-source models, splitting key AI projects between companies from two AI superpowers. The trend presents a growing complication for Washington’s competition with Beijing. Even countries investing heavily in American AI infrastructure are not necessarily choosing American technology for every layer of the AI stack. “Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, told Rest of World . Many countries often do not attach the same security stigma to Chinese technology that Washington does, Chan said. “Ultimately, many countries around the world want to keep their options open and not be too dependent on any single source of technology.” In August, Brazil announced an investment worth roughly $444 million into AI, which it effectively divided between Chinese and American technologies. Around $255 million will go toward supercomputing infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro, developed in partnership with China’s Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE and iFlytek. The rest, around $189 million, will go to a separate supercomputer that Brazil is currently tendering, but expecting to source from Nvidia. “The strategy is not to depend on a single company, technology or country,” President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration said in a statement , adding that the investments were intended to strengthen Brazil’s sovereignty over its data. For most countries, technological sovereignty does not mean building an entire AI stack at home, Jesse Marks, a China-Middle East research scholar at the Australian National University, told Rest of World. Competing at the frontier has become prohibitively expensive, leaving governments to decide which technologies they can develop themselves and where they must rely on foreign suppliers. For Saudi Arabia, it would be a “natural decision” to choose Chinese foundations for sovereign AI models if they perform better on relevant benchmarks, even if doing so carries political consequences with Washington, Marks said. The U.S., however, has greater leverage in parts of the stack where its technology is harder to replace, such as advanced semiconductors, networking equipment, and sensitive cloud infrastructure. But Washington will struggle with countries that want AI but cannot afford American systems or software, Marks said. “Outside of the network of American partners who are trusted or can afford it, it’s Chinese AI. It’s open models,” he said. These technological choices are also becoming intertwined with countries’ broader diplomatic relationships. “AI is one of a number of portfolios that middle powers have to consider when negotiating with a partner like the United States,” Marks said. Washington has accused Chinese labs of “free-riding” and training their models from frontier American AI models at an “industrial scale.” China, having rejected those accusations, has warned it would retaliate if Washington implements any curbs on Chinese AI companies. Chinese companies are ramping up efforts to compete with American companies on different layers of the AI stack. In Egypt, Huawei has bid to build AI data centers for the government, according to a source-based report by Bloomberg, competing against a proposal involving Nvidia. A successful bid would give Chinese companies another foothold in a market where AI infrastructure has so far been dominated by American technology. Southeast Asia is another region where China-U.S. competition over technological influence is increasingly apparent. Washington launched the U.S.-ASEAN AI Spark initiative in July, offering financial and technical support to Southeast Asian governments interested in adopting American AI technologies for public-sector use.

events.title: An aging Congress attempts to regulate AI without using it
events.summary: Members of Congress and governors are under increasing pressure to regulate AI , but more than two dozen of them who spoke with Axios said they don't use the technology or have rarely done so. Why it matters: That striking admission — particularly among older, influential lawmakers — comes amid calls for an AI slowdown and warnings within the industry that it could end humanity if left unchecked. Critics argue that it's impossible for politicians to grasp how rapidly the technology is changing — and the threats or scientific breakthroughs it might unleash — if they don't use it or even dismiss it. One House Democrat called it "f*cking absurd," arguing, "Anyone who's overseeing this has to be someone who's a regular user." "That's a real problem," said Rob Flaherty, a 35-year-old Democratic digital strategist who co-founded a group to push his party to move faster in confronting AI. "Understanding what it can do is essential to figuring out what we ought to do about it." "As we begin to legislate on issues related to AI, it helps to have experience using it," said Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), who's 47. Zoom in: Several lawmakers, including those steeped in seniority and in charge of key committees, told Axios they simply haven't tried AI. "Heavens no," said Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, when asked if he uses AI. "Personally? I don't think I've ever used it," said Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), 74, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee. "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating." "I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair. On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that she needs a "primer on AI, and now with the scare that we have out there, it's much more important to be engaged." A GOP senator, speaking anonymously to offer candid remarks about their colleagues, told Axios that the number who use AI is "not very high." That's helped lead to a knee-jerk negative reaction toward AI among several lawmakers, the senator added, as polls show growing numbers of voters turning against it. Some elected officials said they don't utilize AI much personally, though some on their teams employ the technology. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), who's 48, said he uses AI "on the Google, when you can get a little bit of that search summarized for you. But otherwise no. I do not use it in research. We do not use it in our writing." He said that he supports robust regulation and though some in his state government use AI, final decisions must be made by humans. Other politicians were unsure if they've ever used AI — or said they've only done so by accident. "I don't think I do," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), 70, when asked if he utilizes it. "If I Google something, it kicks off an AI thing, but that's about as far as I go." "I don't know. I can't remember," said Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), 88. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), 73, said she doesn't seek out AI on her own, but that "it pops up on my phone occasionally." "Not intentionally," said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), 68. "The only AI use that I'm kind of familiar with is an AI tool attempting to summarize email chains, and they often get it wrong." What they're saying: Some lawmakers such as Kaine argued that they don't need to use AI to write legislation about it. He said he has read a lot about it and trusts his judgment more than AI. After we spoke with him, Pallone shared a statement through a spokesperson that said: "You don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated. Members of Congress don't need to spend their time talking to AI chatbots all day to know we need to rein in this dangerous technology." Friction point: But some members of Congress were irked or surprised that colleagues don't use a technology they're seeking to regulate. "Are you serious?" Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), 74, said in response to our question. "I use it for everything! I can't believe there's a senator that doesn't use AI." Yes, but: There are members of Congress who are frequent AI users, including some in Hickenlooper's age range. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, told Axios he uses AI "every day." Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), 76, went back to school to get a master's degree in machine learning and said he prefers Claude. Catch up quick: Some of the most powerful elected officials in the country have told other media outlets in the recent past that they don't use AI. In late 2025, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), 54, said in an interview that he didn't think he'd ever used AI. About the same time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to President Trump, 80, said that she didn't think Trump personally uses AI, though his social media account regularly posts AI-made content.

events.title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
events.summary: For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous , tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down. “Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “ We Must Pace the Frontier .” China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal. “The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.” Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies. “His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.” Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”) The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained. When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.” The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power. “Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.” In a recent essay , China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs. “Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.

events.title: Trump escalates war on federal data
events.summary: The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government. Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation. Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats. Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data. 🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases. The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles. Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic. 🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy , NPR reported . The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies. The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute . ⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported . For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws. The EEOC is now planning to do away with the so-called EEO-1 reports, which require companies to provide data on their workforces broken down by race, ethnicity, sex and job title. The move comes amid a broader Trump administration crackdown on DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — initiatives. At a July hearing, Andrea Lucas, an EEOC commissioner appointed by Trump, said the data collection was burdensome for employers and encouraged discrimination against white workers, per the Guardian. What they're saying: "The level of politicization in this administration is beyond anything I've seen," says Denice Ross, former U.S. chief data scientist and currently director of the Data Policy Institute at the Federation of American Scientists. "I've been doing this work for 25 years." Zoom out: Fears about the handling of data that doesn't comport with Trump's worldview have been around for years . Last year, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics hours after the agency released disappointing jobs numbers. "Today's Jobs Numbers were RIGGED in order to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad," Trump wrote. The Department of Homeland Security has stopped regularly publishing comprehensive immigration enforcement statistics, including data that allowed outsiders to assess the administration's deportation efforts. The official who oversaw DHS's independent statistics office resigned in July, The Atlantic reported . According to a tracker run by former federal government data scientists, 38 datasets have been eliminated since Trump returned to office. Hundreds of other datasets have been altered or disrupted. The other side: "The Trump administration is committed to providing the American people with timely, accurate, and relevant data that's helpful to inform meaningful research, discourse, and decision-making," White House spokesman Kush Desai said. "Ensuring public health and other critical data actually reflect reality while refusing to waste taxpayer resources on ideological pet projects are all important parts of that mission." The bottom line: "We really take data for granted," Ross said. "It's invisible infrastructure, like a bridge or cell service. We don't notice until it's gone."

events.title: BT Email users hit by barrage of unsolicited password reset PINs
events.summary: UPDATED BT Email customers say they have been bombarded with hundreds – and in one case more than 1,000 – unsolicited password reset messages, leaving the telco investigating what is causing the deluge. The reports began appearing on BT's community forums over the weekend, with customers describing sudden bursts of PIN messages arriving within minutes despite them making no attempt to reset their passwords. One customer said they received between 50 and 70 PIN texts "in the space [of] a few minutes," while a second reported more than 100. A third said the number had passed 500, and another claimed to have received more than 1,000. One BT customer who contacted The Register separately said they had received around 300 password reset emails over the previous 24 hours, typically arriving in bursts of around 50 within a minute before stopping for several hours. BT has acknowledged the problem but has yet to explain what is behind it. "We are aware that some customers have received a large number of password reset pin messages and we are actively investigating the cause of this," a BT moderator said on the company's community forum. "If you have received multiple messages like this, please ignore them and remain vigilant for any unusual activity with further messages or unexpected calls." BT added that customers' email accounts are secure and that those receiving the messages do not need to take any action. At least one customer, however, claims someone accessed their account during the PIN barrage. The user said they lost access to both their email and BT ID overnight, but managed to request a PIN before whoever was accessing the account could change the telephone number attached to it. That account has not been independently verified, and it isn't clear whether the apparent takeover was connected to the flood of PIN messages. The cause of the wider problem remains a mystery. It isn’t yet clear whether it’s the result of someone deliberately hammering a password recovery mechanism, a fault within BT's systems, or something else entirely. The Register has asked BT how many customers are affected, whether the messages are being generated by external password-reset attempts, and whether it has found any evidence of malicious activity. We've also asked the telco what rate limiting it applies to password reset requests, given reports of hundreds of PINs arriving within minutes, and whether both email and SMS messages are affected. BT says it's investigating. In the meantime, some customers are getting enough PINs to start their own lottery. ® Updated at 09.49 UTC on September 17, 2026 to add: "We are aware that a small number of customers have received repeated password reset PIN messages via text or email. We have implemented a number of mitigations to prevent further password reset messages from being sent, and we’re contacting any impacted customers to advise them to ignore the PIN messages they have received. Customers do not need to take any further action, and we continue to monitor the issue."

events.title: The public wants a say in AI development
events.summary: Democratic and Republican voters agree that the American public should decide the future of AI development, not billionaires in Silicon Valley, according to new polling shared first with Semafor. The poll was commissioned for a new organization launched by Alex Bores , who made a name for himself as a top target of the AI industry in his failed bid for Congress in New York. Though AI ranked last on a list of 13 issues that 1,502 registered voters polled this month said they care about, half said AI is moving too fast and 86% identified lack of regulation as a problem. Only 18% of those polled think the US falling behind China competitively is a problem, a risk President Donald Trump has cited in opposing regulation. While just 36% polled said they had heard about incidents like the Hugging Face hack, “support for reasonable regulations is actually quite correlated with all these other issues,” Bores told Semafor Tuesday in Washington on the sidelines of the “pro-human” summit attended by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Steve Bannon. The poll’s results, Bores argued, show that “if you show good work on AI, you’re winning over voters, even though AI isn’t their top issue.” Bores’ new organization, Who Decides, aims to help the broader Democratic coalition unite around a “shared baseline” for AI protections. The organization will help traditionally Democratic groups like labor and civil society craft AI policy messages, Bores said. “As a Democrat, I say this with love, but we turn everything into a circular firing squad, and I think it’s really, really important that on this issue, where we have powerful, well-resourced enemies that don’t want there to be any regulation whatsoever, that we are all on the same tea,” he said.

events.title: Household income hits record, but lower earners lose ground
events.summary: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements ; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show. Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs , uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net. The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's " Big Beautiful Bill" took hold. That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next. By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967. Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060. The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people. Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%. State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly. Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains. Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile. The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%. Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025. Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median household income among Hispanics, $73,260, showed no significant change from 2024. Meanwhile, 21.8% of Hispanic adults ages 19 to 64 were uninsured in 2025, down a bit from the previous year — but still the highest uninsured rate among the major racial and ethnic groups shown by Census Yes, but: Big racial income gaps remain even as some groups posted gains. Asian American households had the highest median income at $126,300 in 2025, compared with $91,930 for white households and $59,980 for Black American households. Black Americans' household income rose 4.8% from 2024 and whites' household income rose 3%, while Asian Americans' household income showed no significant change. Zoom out: A broader measure of hardship paints a less rosy picture. The Supplemental Poverty Measure , which factors in taxes, government benefits, housing, work and medical expenses, held statistically steady at 13.1% — nearly 3 percentage points above the government's official poverty rate. Medical expenses put an estimated 7.7 million more people below the supplemental poverty line in 2025, the Census Bureau said. Between the lines: Health insurance coverage held steady overall in 2025. The uninsured rate remained statistically unchanged at 7.9%, or 26.7 million people. Medicaid coverage fell 0.5 percentage points nationally, from 17.6% to 17.1% of the population — representing about 1.4 million fewer people with Medicaid coverage in 2025 than in the previous year Among adults ages 19 to 64, 17.3% had public health coverage — including Medicaid, Medicare and VA/CHAMPVA coverage — down 0.5 percentage points from 2024. Census says the decline was driven by a 0.6-point drop in Medicaid coverage among working-age adults. What we're watching: The 2025 numbers may represent the last snapshot before major federal safety-net cuts begin showing up in the Census data, Robert Greenstein, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution, tells Axios.

events.title: Tech giants launch flexible-power coalition for data centers
events.summary: A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all. The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure. The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper. What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance . State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE. The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call. The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it. Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday . More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago. In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them. How it works: Data centers have traditionally been treated as giant, round-the-clock power users. The coalition wants to change the rules so facilities that can reliably cut their grid demand when electricity supplies are tight can get connected faster and potentially avoid some costly grid upgrades. The flexibility could come from shifting or pausing AI computing jobs, tapping batteries or nearby power generation, coalition leaders said. Google has committed 1 gigawatt of power demand it can reduce when needed through utility agreements nationwide, said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation. The group plans to push the approach with federal and state regulators, regional grid operators and utilities. Yes, but: The bargain depends on data centers actually delivering the flexibility they promise. Sivaram said facilities should qualify for faster or larger connections only if their ability to cut demand is "verifiable and enforceable." Reality check: Convincing communities that this complicated solution can actually address their concerns will be a tall order. "Power-flexible data centers are a wonky topic," Sivaram told Axios. His pitch: Data centers could cut their electricity use when the grid is stressed, helping avoid costly infrastructure while bringing in revenue that can support other electricity users. The goal, Sivaram said, is to turn data centers into "good grid citizens" that communities see as assets rather than burdens. What we're watching: Whether regulators actually create the fast lane the coalition wants. Federal regulators in June directed regional grid operators to examine new options for connecting large, flexible power users, providing an opening for the approach AEMA is advocating. Editor's note: Amy Harder is a fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth, but was not involved in the polling and received no advance access beyond that provided to other journalists. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that 76% of Republicans (not 78%) support requiring data center developers to pay for grid upgrades.

events.title: Polymarket’s Next Bet? It Can Also Be a Media Company
events.summary: Every day, a newsletter from the prediction market Polymarket hits my inbox with a subject line that could easily come from any number of politics-focused newspapers or magazines. Recent entries include “Houthis Reveal New Precision Strike Capabilities,” “BREAKING: Trump Unveils Green Energy Beam,” and “World War I, 2.0?” These dispatches are roundups with breathless summaries of the day’s top stories, linking out to corresponding Polymarket markets—yes, this thing will happen; no, it won’t. As far as business news analysis goes, the newsletter is not exactly Bloomberg’s Money Stuff , or even Emily Sundberg’s Feed Me —but it’s recognizably a commercial editorial product, and one that plays an important role in the prediction market ecosystem. The industry is currently embroiled in a series of legal battles over whether prediction markets are financial services (the view held by the markets and the federal government) or gambling platforms (the position of many state authorities and regulators). The fight over what kind of companies these are could end up in the Supreme Court, but in the meantime, both Polymarket and its even-more-popular archrival, Kalshi, have successfully positioned themselves as new media organizations too. For two companies associated with risk, it’s a notably old-school hedge. All kinds of tech startups have launched editorial projects—did you know the alternative dating app Feeld has a surprisingly good magazine?—but the leading prediction markets are entrenching themselves into the mainstream media apparatus in a particularly aggressive way. A recent report noted that they’re integrated into a quarter of the top 20 companies listed in the S&P 500’s Communications Services sector. Polymarket has partnerships with Dow Jones and Substack, while Kalshi has deals with CNN, CNBC, and Fox Corp. None of the agreements facilitate trading. Instead, they’re mainly about data sharing; news outlets want to know what people are putting their money on, and prediction markets are happy to oblige. The deals showcase prediction markets as information channels—places to go to find out about what’s happening. They’ve given Polymarket and Kalshi much-needed boosts in credibility and offered a straightforward introduction to the wider public. Prediction market boosters hype these products as “truth machines,” revealing public sentiment more accurately than polling or traditional reporting; when media outlets decide the odds themselves are newsworthy , they reinforce that message. “Given the forecasting success of the markets, it's clear there is informational value,” says Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such. “And three out of four users don't trade, which suggests the informational use case is popular enough to be taken very seriously.” (Polymarket declined to comment.) Providing data is only a small part of how these companies function as new media entities. On social media, their official accounts post like news outlets, adopting a vernacular that mashes up PopCrave’s frenzied sensibility with Bloomberg’s coverage areas. (The efforts haven’t been wholly reliable: A New York Times analysis earlier this year found that Polymarket’s newsy social accounts have published “false and misleading information.”) Chief executive and founder Shayne Coplan has referred to the company’s partnership with X as “News 2.0.” In 2024, the company hinted at even more expansive ambitions, recruiting for an editor in chief role to lead “content and data journalism” efforts. It never made that hire, although political analyst and media founder Nate Silver came on later that year as an adviser. But on its careers page , the company beckons prospective employees by playing this angle up: “Become the new front page of the internet.” Kalshi is less inclined to describe itself this way. When asked if it considered itself a media company, Such, the spokesperson, tells WIRED that it does not, though the markets themselves have “quasi-media” attributes because they follow the news. “We see ourselves as a financial exchange,” he says. Sure. But why not both? Financial services companies have jumped into the media sector before, most obviously Bloomberg, which initially focused on providing market data and financial analytics before expanding to include journalism products. More recently, the online trading hub Robinhood—now also a Polymarket competitor with its own prediction market offerings—ran a media subsidiary called Sherwood before winding it down earlier this summer. Then there’s Hunterbook, which operates both an investigative outlet called Hunterbook News and a hedge fund that executes trades based on its outlet’s investigations. Polymarket doesn’t have a dedicated subsidiary or editorial arm. But it has launched a weekly podcast called What Are the Odds? in partnership with the podcast network Dear Media.

events.title: Arizona Lowered the Bar for Its English Fluency Test. Experts Say It Will Harm Students in the Long Run.
events.summary: Samantha Ramos teaches students in her English language development class at John B. Wright Elementary School in Tucson, Arizona. Cassidy Araiza for ProPublica Samantha Ramos stood at the front of her second grade classroom, a small mic clipped to her lanyard amplifying her instructions as she began a phonics lesson. “Can we get our arms ready?” asked Ramos, who’s taught at the John B. Wright Elementary School in Tucson, Arizona, for 15 years. She brought her right palm to her left shoulder as the students imitated her movements. Ramos, who specializes in teaching English as a second language, was leading a lesson that day on the short “i” sound. She told the students to pronounce each letter with a different gesture — touching the shoulder for the “w,” the elbow for the “i” and the hand for the double “l” — before sounding out the word “will.” They repeated the process for other short “i” words — “dig,” “wig” and “fit.” The lesson is part of a daily block of language instruction, ranging from two to four hours long, that Arizona students learning English as a second language are required to take. The students, most of them Spanish-speaking Latino children, remain in the program, separated for part of that time from their peers whose primary language is English, until they pass a test showing they’re fluent enough to learn in a mainstream classroom. The program is known as “structured English immersion,” or colloquially as “English-only” because all instruction is required to be in English. This limits their time for core subjects, like math and science, that are critical to academic success and college readiness. Arizona is the only state with English-only laws still in effect for its public schools. But the number of students enrolled in the curriculum has tumbled dramatically this year. At the Tucson Unified School District, where Ramos teaches, the percentage of test-taking students who scored high enough to be classified as proficient in English more than doubled — from 10% in 2025 to 24% in 2026. Rather than a big leap in fluency, however, the test results reflect the Arizona Department of Education lowering the grade needed to pass. The changes were approved by outgoing Superintendent of Public Instruction Tom Horne, a longtime Republican defender of Arizona’s English-only policies. Experts warn this change will do lasting harm to tens of thousands of Arizona students who will exit the structured English immersion program before they know the language well enough to succeed. Such students are already part of the lowest-performing group on standardized tests, and the loss of specialized instruction could further harm their long-term academic success, according to education researchers. Past attempts by the Arizona Department of Education to reclassify large numbers of children learning English as fluent prompted federal investigations by the departments of Justice and Education. Federal officials contended placing such students in classrooms where they struggled because they lacked knowledge of English violated their civil and educational rights, and Arizona agreed to a settlement more than a decade ago. What’s happening now could be a repeat of that, said Katie Bernstein, an applied linguist and professor of early childhood education at Arizona State University. “If you’re put in a class where you don’t understand what’s going on at all, you’re not learning language or content,” she said. “And so those are the worst outcomes of all, are students who are not given any language services.” Ramos teaches her students phonics during a daily block of English-language immersion. Cassidy Araiza for ProPublica Nearly 1 in 10 students enrolled in Arizona public and charter schools marked in their school registration forms they speak a language other than English at home. State law mandates that they be assessed for fluency and placed in structured English immersion, and each spring they take the Arizona English Language Learner Assessment, or AZELLA, to measure their progress in reading, writing, speaking and listening. This approach has been required since Arizona voters passed a 2000 ballot initiative, Proposition 203, banning bilingual education in public schools. Still, officials have periodically made changes to the proficiency test. The U.S. departments of Justice and Education determined the version of AZELLA administered between 2006 and 2012 — coinciding with Horne’s first two terms as the state’s top education official — was “not a valid measure of English language proficiency and readiness.” As a result, the state had removed at least 28,000 students from structured English immersion who still lacked proficiency in reading and writing the language. The Arizona Department of Education was found to be in violation of civil rights laws that ban discrimination on the basis of race and national origin by schools that receive federal funds. The state voluntarily entered a settlement , which stressed that the law requires “education agencies to take appropriate action to overcome language barriers that impede students’ equal participation in instructional programs.” Do You Have Experience With Arizona’s Structured English Immersion System, Also Called English-Only? Have stories to tell about how Arizona treats children learning English in public schools? Share your tips with Rafael Carranza at englishlearners@azluminaria.org . The settlement agreement stipulated that the state would immediately help school districts find the students who had been harmed and offer “reading and writing intervention services.” In the long term, the state was required to revamp the AZELLA test. Similar issues prompted a second voluntary settlement four years later , which instructed the state to raise the threshold for a test score to qualify as proficient in English. The state was also required to retest English-language learners using more rigorous standards, among other things. Ida Rose Florez, a psychologist and former professor and researcher at Arizona State University, conducted a study published in 2012 that found the AZELLA test was “ineffective and obsolete” and its results could be arbitrary. The research concluded there was no evidence the test could “accurately differentiate” between children who need English-language services and those who don’t. “What I examined, and what I saw, was a test that was absolutely not developed correctly,” Florez told Arizona Luminaria and ProPublica. “I don’t see any basis for validity whatsoever.” After dropping during the pandemic, AZELLA passing rates held steady at 12% statewide for three school years, including in 2025, when more than 118,000 took the test and just over 14,000 scored well enough to be reclassified as proficient. After the Arizona Department of Education lowered the score needed to pass the test, the statewide reclassification rate for 2026 jumped to 26%, according to the department’s official tally announced to teac

events.title: Justice threatens GOP showdown in West Virginia
events.summary: The News Jim Justice is getting the itch. And it could set up a battle of GOP titans. The West Virginia GOP senator is considering a run for his old job as governor in 2028, which would potentially set up a race between him and incumbent Gov. Patrick Morrisey. Justice told Semafor he’s “sure thinking about it” before quickly interjecting that he loves “what I’m doing here” in the Senate. He also jabbed at Morrisey but insisted he wants the governor to be successful: “Gov. Morrisey has a more difficult time bonding with people and everything, but beyond that, I want him to do great, I really do. I’m not in a food fight at all.” “I do love the people of West Virginia, and I spent eight years trying to build it back. Got it really going,” Justice continued. “I just want goodness for West Virginia, but I want goodness for the whole nation too. We’ll make a decision.” Know More West Virginia is a small state that’s also the home of bare-knuckled politics and big personalities. Republicans recruited Justice, a former Democrat, to run against former Sen. Joe Manchin, I-W.Va., in 2024, though Manchin ultimately decided against seeking reelection. Manchin narrowly defeated Morrisey in 2018, but Morrisey mounted a political comeback in 2024 by emerging from a crowded GOP primary and winning the governor’s mansion. A Morrisey ally told Semafor that Justice has myriad vulnerabilities and hasn’t had to win a tough GOP primary against someone like the incumbent governor (though Justice did easily defeat former Rep. Alex Mooney, R-W.Va., in 2024). The ally added that the conservative Club for Growth is already committed to opposing Justice, put Morrisey’s war chest at nearly $5 million across several political entities, and noted that Justice is in debt and is now sharing control of his family’s Greenbrier resort. But Justice said people in West Virginia are encouraging him to run: “You’re going to hear people come to you and say, ‘Boy, we’d love to have you back as governor.’ You know, that’s natural and everything. I don’t pay a whole lot of attention.” Manchin also flirted repeatedly with running for his old job as governor, which he used to call the “best job in the world.” Manchin never ran after serving in the Senate, but Senate Republicans believe Justice is more likely to run than not, according to several GOP sources. Regarding the 2028 governor race, Manchin said on Tuesday: “Can’t we get through this election before worrying about the next election?”
