events.title: A new crop of Democratic early-state kingmakers rises for 2028
events.summary: The News One Democratic lawmaker — Rep. Jim Clyburn — played a pivotal role in the party’s 2020 presidential primary. Which means you’re about to hear a lot more from Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández, Steven Horsford, and Maggie Goodlander. Not to mention Sens. Ben Ray Luján, Jacky Rosen, Maggie Hassan, and more. Democrats’ decision to bump up New Mexico to their fourth primary spot in 2028, right after the now-familiar trio of South Carolina, Nevada, and New Hampshire, bestows growing prominence and sway on congressional delegations from all four states. Populous Michigan and Virginia, fifth and sixth on the primary calendar, will be right behind them. Democrats in the previous cast of early states are going to find new opportunities to wield their clout with a field that could easily number in the dozens. And lawmakers from states newer to the early-primary lineup are already preparing to elevate what matters to their constituents, as they get wooed by presidential aspirants. “I want them to come to New Mexico and look at the issues that we face,” said Fernández, D-N.M. “I want to see the candidates inspire the kind of communities that will make a difference in both the primary election and the general election.” With competitive midterm races happening in nearly all of the early states, potential Democratic presidential candidates are already on the trail with purple-district incumbents and candidates. Other lawmakers from early-primary states are fielding calls from 2028 contenders looking to appear with them. To name just a recent few: California Gov. Gavin Newsom appeared at the opening of a state party campaign office with Horsford; Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has done events for Nevada’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee, Aaron Ford; and New Mexico candidates have seen visits by former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. “I’m not taking sides early. They’re all going to have to earn it,” said Horsford, whose district includes Las Vegas. He said he was hoping candidates would “understand that working-class people care about their healthcare, housing, childcare, elder care.” Rep. Gabe Vasquez, who represents a Trump-won New Mexico district, said Buttigieg had recently appeared with him. He named housing, water, and immigration as the top issues for candidates “to really come and understand how tough this economy truly is and what it’s going to take to fix it.” Democrats are also pouring into competitive Senate races in states like New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas is facing former Sen. John Sununu. But Luján says his colleagues are eager to visit him in New Mexico, too, even though Republicans struggled to even field a candidate against him. “Come on down and visit New Mexico, get to know the state. Get to know the people,” Luján told Semafor. “I certainly hope that whoever the next president of the United States is a Democrat and is a Democrat that understands New Mexico.” Luján’s fellow New Mexico senator, Martin Heinrich, said Democrats are still working through how they will host candidates in early-primary states in 2027 and 2028. But he said the new calendar is a big deal for New Mexico, which dropped off the swing-state map in 2008 after then-Sen. Barack Obama turned it blue. “We have a lot of really unique issues that are not something that you learn about through osmosis in other parts of the country,” Heinrich said. New Mexico will get “presidential candidates to care about water, public lands, national laboratories,” he added — “things that many of them just don’t have that much familiarity with.” Luján also said his state has great food, but cautioned candidates about a regional tripwire: feeling compelled to choose between the state’s famous green and red chiles. “It depends what they’re eating. Anyone that gives you an answer? They don’t know the state,” he said. “You can’t pick one.” Know More Democratic incumbents in tight races are hoping to reap electoral benefits from 2028 candidates who are coming through their districts. The visits tend to energize the base ahead of the midterms and may also broaden congressional candidates’ appeal. “I always look at the quality of events. Are they putting me in front of voters who I really haven’t connected with before? That’s sort of my No. 1 goal,” said Rep. Susie Lee, D-Nev., who represents a purple district. She called herself a “Buttigieg fan” this time and said she would endorse in the 2028 cycle, though she was waiting to learn more about other candidates’ positions. It helps that three early-primary states for 2028 are also hosting competitive Senate races this fall. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., just campaigned in New Hampshire, and he’ll be heading to both Michigan and South Carolina, completing the trifecta. “We’ve never had a problem with getting people to pay attention to our state because we’ve always been a swing state. And I think the calendar probably heightens it,” said Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich. “We’re a good microcosm and often canary-in-the-coal-mine on issues, so we want to be in the mix.” Room for Disagreement Not every Democrat is sold on the new calendar. Those in New Hampshire say their state law supersedes the party’s revised order, which puts South Carolina ahead of them. “I continue to remind folks that New Hampshire has a state law, so we’re going to have the first primary,” Hassan told Semafor. “We are seeing a lot of people come up and campaign and support our candidates, and we continue to think that it’s really good for candidates, especially Democratic candidates, to be on the ground doing retail politics.” Nicholas and Burgess’ View The next generation of Democrats is clearly relishing the opportunity to help their party turn the page. After generations of candidates aligned their strategies around the Iowa caucuses and the first-in-the-nation primary in New Hampshire, Democratic candidates will now have to appeal to more diverse voters and work harder to stand out from a likely crowded field. But the huge slate of candidates could also prevent a repeat of Clyburn’s success in resuscitating Joe Biden’s campaign in 2020. The senior House Democrat became a kingmaker for Biden by giving him momentum heading into Super Tuesday after Biden’s poor showing in the first three states. This time, a half-dozen states are going before Super Tuesday and some of them have tons of delegates. That means Democratic contenders have a lot more lawmakers to woo. Notable Newsom said he wouldn’t run for president if former Vice President Kamala Harris did, CNN reported .

events.title: Congress eyes final legislative push before midterms
events.summary: The House is embarking on its last days in session before breaking for the midterms, with a final vote expected Wednesday on a bill ratcheting up penalties on Russia. The procedural vote teeing up the final tally on the sanctions bill inflamed intraparty tensions when two purple-district Democrats, Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington and Jared Golden of Maine, once again broke ranks and voted with Republicans. The White House privately reached out to some Democratic lawmakers to sway them on the procedural vote with promises like infrastructure projects, according to one lawmaker. events.title: Girls flag football is fastest-growing high school sport
events.summary: Data: NFHS ; Map: Brad Jennings/Axios Girls flag football has become the fastest-growing high school sport, as tens of thousands take up a game that barely had a varsity footprint a few years ago. Why it matters: Few girls high school sports have moved from niche to mainstream so quickly, broadening athletic opportunities in the process. By the numbers: More than 102,000 girls played high school flag football in 2025-26, a 551% increase in the past four years, according to the National Federation of State High School Associations . Catch up quick: In 2024, just 12 states sanctioned high school girls flag football, viewed as a safer, more accessible version of America's most popular spectator sport. Today, 23 states plus Washington, D.C., sanction it as an official varsity sport , and 3,990 schools reported participants in 2025-26. The NFL is backing its growth, too. It has invested millions to launch and expand high school programs , and featured the sport in its Super Bowl commercials . Beyond high schools, flag football will debut at the 2028 Olympics, and at least 40 NCAA schools already offer it as a collegiate varsity sport. Reality check: It's not yet clear whether flag football is mostly creating new high school athletes or pulling girls from established sports. A recent Newsday analysis on Long Island found flag participation rising sharply while girls lacrosse, softball and track participation fell. What we're watching: Girls varsity wrestling is undergoing its own boom. All 50 states now report girls wrestling participation, and 40 state athletic associations hold girls wrestling championships, up from just five about a decade ago.

events.title: UK funds flying broadband stations with power beamed from below
events.summary: The UK's Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA) is funding projects aimed at delivering connectivity using high-flying aircraft, including technology to beam power from the ground to keep them in the air. Britain's science and technology body, inspired by America's DARPA but on a more modest budget, says it is backing 18 projects to develop aircraft capable of operating reliably and cost-effectively in the stratosphere, as part of a program known as Enduring Atmospheric Platforms. Success will be measured by whether any aircraft can continuously supply 300 W of power to a communications payload for an entire week, while holding station above the UK. The intent is to create an alternative to orbital satellites for providing connectivity to underserved parts of the UK and elsewhere in the world. These are known as high-altitude pseudo-satellites (HAPS). The agency says that satellites have been the default way to reach users or communities that are not well served by terrestrial networks, but their distance and orbits impose physical limits on what they can deliver. ARIA is allocating £70 million ($94 million) in funding over three and a half years for the projects, which will tackle the power and reliability challenges of sustained operations above the UK. The projects are split into three technical areas, with TA1 set to cover enabling technologies, TA2 comprising system integration and testing, and TA3 focused on deployment and communications. ARIA highlighted a project called Carousel from aerospace startup Menapia. This plans to produce a constellation of high-altitude multi-rotor aircraft, capable of routine operations at altitudes up to 20 km (12 miles), with the intention of forming a persistent "canopy" over the UK. Another is Enduring Drone Networks, being developed by VFP Aerospace, which is aiming for persistent presence via a relay team of units that will cycle between their service altitude and ground stations for recharging. It says it is targeting a production cost of £50,000 ($67,000) per drone. In the enabling technologies category, a firm called Hypanode Ltd is working on a fuel cell power system to deliver 20 times more energy than current battery technology. Scalable Laser Ltd is developing laser-based power beaming technology, pairing high-power laser diodes with advanced photovoltaic receivers, while Space Solar Engineering Ltd is looking at radio frequency power beaming to deliver continuous power to a HAPS aircraft. A more exotic-sounding technology is Stratospheric Navigation and Gravity (STRAT-NAV) from the University of Bath. This seeks to extend the endurance of HAPS craft by allowing them to predict and make use of atmospheric gravity waves – caused when air is forced upward by weather fronts or hills, and gravity pulls it back down, creating a ripple. "This research expands the UK's leadership in high-altitude platforms to become the place where this industry is designed, built, and scaled," says Rico Chandra, ARIA's program director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms. "Getting there means backing bold ideas, from fixed-wing solar aircraft to designs nobody predicted, including aircraft that fly on spinning wings instead of propellers." ARIA funds teams of scientists and engineers to pursue cutting-edge research. It is a non-departmental public body sponsored by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST). It was until recently chaired by entrepreneur Matt Clifford, who stepped down after taking up a role with US AI firm Anthropic. The agency was also controversially spared being asked to make savings leading up to the UK government's Spending Review last year. ®

events.title: $42b fund manager Cathie Wood sees interest rates topping 7pc on AI boom
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ARK Invest manages around $42b. Its CEO Cathie Wood believes interest rates could top 7pc Fund manager Cathie Wood tips economies to boom and prices to fall, but interest rates to surge as the AI revolution gathers pace. It could result in interest rates exceeding 7 per cent. Ms Wood does not think calls for regulation will be heeded and predicts that US President Donald Trump will veto any such efforts that might pass Congress. The manager of a $US30 billion ($42 billion) investment fund believes artificial intelligence and related disruptive technologies will lead to both deflation as well as short-term interest rates pushing 7 per cent. In Australia to spruik a new investment partnership with Australian fund manager Associate Global Partners, ARK Invest CEO and chief investment officer Cathie Wood argues that "technology is inherently deflationary" by increasing productivity and pushing down the cost of production. She believes the current AI expansion will translate to an economic boom alongside "good deflation", as opposed to the price falls generated during economic crises when demand is collapsing. "We think short rates will approximate nominal GDP growth, which was true during the industrial revolution — the last time we had a technology revolution of this size," she told ABC's The Business in a one-on-one interview during her visit. "Real growth could move into the 7 to 8 per cent range, nominal maybe the 6 to 7.5 per cent range. "Short rates would, over time, I'm not saying tomorrow, move towards that 6.5, 7.5 per cent rate. "Long rates, they'd still go up as well, but not as much." Overnight, US 10-year government bond interest rates again briefly moved above 5 per cent. Aside from a brief period in 2023, this month has been the first time that rate has breached that level since before the global financial crisis of 2008. "Once we have psychologically passed the 5 per cent yield threshold in the US 10-year … then we can see that all kinds of doors have suddenly been opened up, and all kinds of possibilities about where yields could sit are just waiting for us to explore," Rabobank global strategist Michael Every told The Business. Will rising interest rates blow up the AI boom? Conventional wisdom and previous experience have generally shown rising interest rates to be poison for the value of tech firms, especially those yet to generate profits. Financial commentator Satyajit Das recently said that he expected a financial crisis within the next two years, driven by a combination of rising interest rates and a realisation that AI was not delivering on its promised or required returns on investment. However, Ms Wood argues that major US AI companies are already starting to generate revenues above ARK's optimistic expectations. "We're all looking for proof points and we are getting some already, and they're astounding," she said. ARK's Venture Fund holds stakes in Anthropic and Open AI, which Ms Wood said is based on the belief that the trillions of dollars of investments going into artificial intelligence will ultimately pay off. "There are rumours, and we think they are well-founded, that Anthropic's gross [profit] margins are 80 per cent," Ms Wood said. "That's a software-like gross margin." When asked if those kind of profit margins are sustainable given the tendency of competition to erode them as technologies become more mature and widespread, Ms Wood argued the AI boom is "very different" from earlier boom-bust cycles such as railroads and the internet. "Between 1873 and 1893 in the United States, 200 railroads went out of business," Ms Wood explained. "There was a lot of hope and a lot of capital deployed, and investors just didn't know if it would pay off. Ultimately it did, but too late for most of those railroad companies. "In the case of AI we've already narrowed the market down so much to four big players. She said that revenue generation has so far surpassed ARK's relatively optimistic forecasts. "If it's a big surprise to us it's a shock to everybody else," Ms Wood remarked. 'If you win AI you win the 21st century' Another potential threat to the AI boom is the debate about regulation, stoked in the past week by comments from industry leaders . Michael Every believes some of those within the industry talking about the need for a slow down in AI development and increased regulation, such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, may be doing so with a strong element of self-interest. "Either they've only just watched The Terminator and The Matrix, having completely avoided those movies up until now in their life.

events.title: Abu Dhabi investment to help McLaren build next-gen SUV
events.summary: British supercar maker McLaren plans to invest £500 million ($675 million) to expand its UK manufacturing and engineering operations on the back of a larger investment commitment from Abu Dhabi’s L’imad, its main shareholder. As part of the investment, the company will speed up development of next-generation car models, including its first SUV, it said in a statement on Wednesday. A new vehicle assembly unit will also be set up in the UK and vehicle output will be increased to help it create 1,000 new direct and indirect jobs by 2032 in the UK, as well as 3,000 additional jobs across the supply chain. The company will also build engines in-house in the UK for the first time. “Over the past 20 months, L’imad has worked closely with McLaren Automotive’s management team, supporting the business in sharpening its strategic direction and positions itself for long-term growth,” said Jassem Al Zaabi, managing director and group chief executive of L’imad. “This investment reflects our confidence in its potential and our commitment to backing the business through its next chapter.” McLaren Automotive will also expand operations at the McLaren production centre in Woking, England, and its carbon-fibre manufacturing and research unit in South Yorkshire, after opening two new sites in Bicester and the Midlands recently. L’imad to boost its AD Ports stake to 98.5% The announcement comes as L’imad is set to increase its stake in AD Ports Group to 98.5 per cent after meeting all conditions to acquire the global ports operator. L’imad, through its wholly owned subsidiary ADQ, already owns 75.42 per cent of AD Ports and launched a voluntary tender offer on August 18 to acquire the remaining issued and paid-up share capital. It offered Dh6.25 ($1.70) for each share it does not already own. At close of business on September 15, “ADQ has received acceptances representing in excess of 23.08 per cent” of share capital of AD Ports, it said in a bourse filing to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where AD Ports Group shares are traded. L'imad will boost its shareholding in AD Ports on settlement of the offer, no later than October 9, it said in a statement on Wednesday. The payment to AD Ports shareholders and the process of registration of company's shares in the name of ADQ will also be completed by October 9. “All conditions of the offer have been satisfied, save for the customary notifications required to be submitted to the Capital Market Authority and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange [ADX],” it said. AD Ports, which runs about 40 terminals in the UAE and has a presence in nearly 50 markets globally, is part of L’imad’s ports & logistics platform, which also features major assets such as Etihad Rail and Aramex. L’imad, set up last year, continues to expand its investment portfolio within the UAE and abroad. Last month, L’imad also completed its acquisition of the remaining shares in Abu Dhabi National Energy Company, known as Taqa, through its subsidiary Abu Dhabi Power Corporation, taking its stake from 98.12 per cent to 100 per cent. Taqa is now awaiting regulatory approval to delist from the ADX. L’imad also owns a major stake in Abu Dhabi real estate developer Modon Holding. On Tuesday, L'imad said it was teaming up with Azerbaijan Investment Holding to pursue joint investments in the country and the wider Central Asia region. The partners are exploring investments in sectors including industry, critical minerals and related supply chains, urban and transport infrastructure, energy and digital connectivity, a L'imad statement read.

events.title: Community 'blindsided' by legislation change fears becoming ghost town
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Fears Glenden will become a ghost town after legislation change Questions remain about the future of Glenden and other resource towns. ( Supplied: Isaac Regional Council ) The state government has introduced legislation to repeal a requirement for a nearby coal mine to house its workforce in Glenden. The mayor says the council and Glenden community were "blindsided" by an abrupt policy reversal. Registrations of interest will open to buy houses, commercial buildings, and a lease of the entire town. Plans to save a small Queensland mining community from becoming a ghost town are being scrapped under proposed laws. Legislation forcing nearby coal mine workers to relocate from a work camp into the town of Glenden would be removed by amendments introduced to Queensland Parliament this week. The accommodation requirement for workers at QCoal's Byerwen mine was legislated in 2023 by the former Labor state government, following a concerted campaign by the local council and residents . The government has instead opened registrations of interest for homes, commercial buildings, and a lease of the entire town, 160 kilometres west of Mackay, to draw private investment. Isaac Regional Council Mayor Kelly Vea Vea said the community was "extremely surprised" by the decision. "The legislation that was introduced to parliament yesterday completely blindsided my council and blindsided Glenden," she said. Glenden sits on land leased by Newlands coal mine owner Glencore, which took over its assets in 2013. When the mine transitioned to closure three years ago, the Queensland government legislated plans to shut down QCoal's Byerwen camp by 2030, over fears the town could be left empty. The town of Glenden was built in the 1980s to house mine workers. ( ABC Tropical North: Melissa Maddison ) In March last year, Resources Minister Dale Last pushed back dates that had been set for gradual introduction of the workforce, citing issues with Glenden's water infrastructure. Speaking to Queensland Parliament on Tuesday, Mr Last said the laws introduced by the former Labor government were rushed. "There was no consultation, no consideration of the impact on services and no consideration of the future of that community and the impact that would have," he said. Under the new proposal, QCoal would be able to renew its mining camp lease beyond 2030. Tina Keogh lived in Glenden for 13 years, and her husband worked in the region until about a year ago. She said it was a tight-knit community where "everybody knew everybody", and she was sad to see empty homes on a recent visit. A house in Glenden that was home to the Keogh family for 13 years. ( Supplied: Tina Keogh ) "We left 10 years ago; nobody has occupied our house since we left," she said. "The people that are living [out] there that have been there for so long … they've got to find somewhere else to go. "They can't expect to hold onto a town when there's nothing there." Tina Keogh and her husband raised their young family in Glenden. Cr Vea Vea said she would meet with the resources minister to discuss the proposed legislation changes. She said she had been hoping to see government investment in infrastructure left behind by Glencore. "I'm really disappointed that the state government has chosen this path and refused to communicate this to us or the community," Cr Vea Vea said. "Every month that the state government has chosen to kick the can down the road of resolving these complex issues, families have continued to leave. "The school has continued to shrink, and the community continues to have a lack of certainty." Mr Last and QCoal were contacted for comment.

events.title: Bring on the AI swarms. They’re the only thing that can defend us now that AI is free
events.summary: Unpredictable token bills haunted the first half of 2026 as AI experimenters pushed deeper into the tech and often found useful results could only be achieved after surprising and unwelcome expenditure. We've gone from tokenmaxxers to tokenmisers, counting every character we send to AI services. That changed the way we used AI, focusing users on the ticking meter and unable to cast their eyes up and explore the possible. Those blinkers fell away in the middle of August when Alibaba delivered Qwen3.8-27B, byte-for-byte probably the most powerful language model ever created – and also capable of running on a high-spec laptop. The community of “local AI” enthusiasts noticed and have spent the intervening weeks whittling Qwen down to fit on an ever-widening array of devices, including – surprisingly – my M4 MacBook Air. Their work means millions of similar devices can now access near-frontier-level artificial intelligence from free software. The gap between my MacBook Air and a smartphone isn’t vast. As local AI developers continue whittling Qwen down to size, a few hundred million smartphones will also be capable of running top-tier AI. While that hasn't happened yet, it won't be more than six months away. At the rate things are unfolding, probably closer to six weeks. Suddenly, "good enough" AI isn't something that we will have to rent. We can have it, at no cost, on our desktops, our kitchen tables, our classrooms and in our pockets. That’s great, but also scary because we've been caught unprepared by AI effectively becoming free. Nobody yet knows what we will do with free AI, or if we are ready for it. On the positive side of the ledger, we stand to benefit from a growing “cognition surplus” that brings more thinking capacity into the home or office. Need to wrangle your way through a baroque accounting system? Give it to the AI. Sorting through twenty years of smartphone snaps? Again, let the AI do the heavy lifting. How about a personal newspaper gathered while you sleep, and presented on your tablet at the breakfast table? It's all doable now. All of that feels very much like something I remember clearly from the early 1980s, when the promise of the “home computer” was managing recipes. We knew the device would find a use, but it wasn't until the one-two punch of GUIs and the Web that most people had any real use for a home computer. That's exactly how this moment feels. Sure, managing smartphone photos will be helpful for millions, but the biggest win will be on the darker side of the ledger – where every bad actor – from script kiddies with a grudge through to the worst of the worst – now have equal access to powerful AI that will go with them everywhere. They’ll use it to lie, cheat and vex, at a speed and on a scale never before seen. To deal with that, we'll fight fire with fire. The most important job our AIs will be tasked with will be keeping us as safe as possible from other AIs. We’ll only be aware of this when it fails. But “good enough” AI and “intelligence everywhere” will enable resource pools and defensive techniques that our adversaries could never harness for themselves, so we stand a solid chance. ®

events.title: Mythos has made 2026 patching hell. It might make 2027 a breeze
events.summary: When Microsoft delivered over 970 patches last week, many saw a nightmare for beleaguered security staff. Gartner research vice president Craig Lawson thinks infosec workers might soon see sunlit uplands as their workloads ease. Lawson outlined that scenario at Gartner’s IT Symposium in Australia today and explained it by theorising that the increased volume of vulnerability discoveries made possible by Anthropic’s Mythos and other bug-hunting AI might be getting close to finding most of the flaws in established codebases. “We've never had a situation where massive codebases have been audited to that level before,” he told The Register, and offered the recent series of CVEs found in OpenBSD – which has historically been an unusually secure and stable OS – as evidence that AI bug-hunters are cleaning up. “Think about how much technical debt has been retired in products just in the last six months,” he said. Lawson pointed to the fact security vendors, who in theory know what it takes to create secure products, are also using AI to find flaws in their wares. Those discoveries, he suggested, again indicate AI is taking out potential avenues for zero-day attacks. The high number of CVEs reported in 2026 is a positive signal. Lawson thinks Mythos and its ilk may also create an invisible signal as vendors use the AI to detect more bugs in their future releases. He therefore thinks that 2027 might see CVE numbers fall as vendors finish cleaning up old codebases, and because they use AI to more thoroughly test their next releases. “2027 could be the first year we see a net drop, maybe not in aggregate vulnerabilities, but definitely in severity of flaws,” he told The Register. He thinks AI will also make defenders happy by giving them better tools. Today, he said, a red-teaming exercise is an infrequent and costly event that usually involves hiring an external provider. AI bug-hunters could mean organizations can effectively run a red team every day. And if a red team exercise produces tickets that need solving, he thinks AI will help analysts to identify fixes more quickly. “What if I could spend three minutes going to Gemini and saying ‘Write syntax for an F5 IRule’ that becomes a virtual patch? Everyone can do threat intelligence, enrichment, some of those harder tasks.” When infosec staff make those fixes, Lawson wants organizations to celebrate the impact of their work. Today, Lawson said, security operations centers measure staff by the number of tickets they process and close. He thinks a better approach is to celebrate the fact that cyber-defenders kept a hospital open or stopped a ransomware raid. ®

events.title: University of Manchester Uses NVIDIA Earth-2 to Forecast Air Pollution Across the UK
events.summary: Air pollution is a serious public health risk, contributing to an estimated 30,000 deaths in the U.K. alone last year. Data-driven insights can help — but computing air quality with traditional chemistry-based models is expensive, which limits how detailed they can be and how regularly they can be run. David Topping, a professor in the University of Manchester’s department of Earth and environmental science, saw that the NVIDIA Earth-2 family of open AI models and tools had cracked a related problem for weather forecasting — and asked whether the same generative frameworks could work for pollution fields. “The biggest challenge is the compute required to forecast air quality,” said Topping. “Once you put chemistry into weather models, they get really, really slow. So I said, why don’t we try using the generative frameworks that NVIDIA develops for climate and weather for pollution fields?” Working with the NVIDIA Earth-2 team, Topping and colleagues generated training data from existing chemistry-climate simulations, then trained Earth-2 CorrDiff — a generative downscaling model — on Isambard-AI, the U.K.’s national AI supercomputer in Bristol. The model worked on the first attempt. The team has since added Earth-2 StormCast, a model that enables time-dependent forecasts that directly use air quality observations, and showed the test-training and inference workflows running on the NVIDIA DGX Spark personal AI supercomputer. “To improve human health, it’s essential that we understand the impact of environmental stressors in the air we breathe,” said Topping. “Our U.K.-wide pollution model allows us to model potential future scenarios, such as predicting what would happen if different pollution-related government policy changes went into effect. Video credit: Bristol Centre for Supercomputing (BriCS) @ University of Bristol Another potential application is proactive air quality insights for healthcare organizations. Topping envisions a scenario where regional and national healthcare services could reach out to patients with conditions like asthma to let them know that air pollution is going to be high in their area tomorrow, or next week. The team is also exploring how the air pollution model could pair with data from edge AI devices to ingest real-time air quality data and drive real-time decision making, such as in the event of a wildfire. “The fact that this model trained in two days on Isambard-AI — and can now run on a DGX Spark sitting on a desk — changes who can do this science and how quickly,” said Niall Robinson, developer relations manager for weather and climate at NVIDIA. “We’re just at the beginning of what these open workflows can do globally.” “The ability to switch from one NVIDIA framework to another was really impressive,” said Hao Zhang, a doctoral student at the University of Manchester who trained StormCast on Isambard-AI. “We’re only just starting to explore how to use these frameworks in different ways to model complex pollution fields.” From National Supercomputer to the Desktop To retrain the Earth-2 model for air pollution, Topping and the team used a year’s worth of U.K. pollution data simulated at hourly intervals to generate a detailed, U.K.-wide pollution model at a resolution of 2-3 square kilometers. Running on a single, eight-GPU node on Isambard-AI — the U.K.’s most powerful AI supercomputer, packed with 5,448 NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips delivering 21 exaflops of AI performance — the process took just two days. “Earth-2 CorrDiff has shown an incredibly efficient use of the world-class NVIDIA hardware inside Isambard-AI,” said Simon McIntosh-Smith, director of the Bristol Centre for Supercomputing at University of Bristol and cofounder of Isambard-AI. “It’s fitting that, for a climate-based project, the GPU hours used were relatively low, requiring less power from the supercomputer to run the workloads.” In addition to providing a look back at air pollution over the past year, the model can help predict future air pollution scenarios for the U.K. The team plans to further increase the resolution of its model by incorporating additional open data, enabling researchers to understand air pollution at street scale. The same generative pollution workflow also runs on the NVIDIA GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip-powered DGX Spark desktop AI system for inference and smaller training runs. Topping now has an DGX Spark system in his office retraining models. “You can now invest a few thousand dollars to get started developing powerful AI models,” Topping said. The team plans to release open source training data and workflows for the pollution models will be released so that similar models can be trained for other countries and regions. “Our aim is to offer this workflow to the entire world,” he said. “We hope that every global country and every major city with a small burst of supercomputer AI time will be able to produce their own detailed pollution models with their own local data.” Looking five years out, Topping sees the endpoint as something simpler still: an agentic interface where a clinician or government agency asks the question and the chain of models handles everything else. “With better open access to air quality observations, someone could ask our pollution model running on DGX Spark: what’s the pollution going to be like in this neighborhood tomorrow?” he said. “And a whole chain of interactions will deliver an answer, grounded on the science these frameworks represent.” Hear more from Topping in the webinar, AI for Science: From the Lab to the Frontier , taking place September 30. events.title: Java 27 grows up, makes better choices
events.summary: If one sign of maturity is making better choices, then Java has grown up a fair bit in its version 27 release Tuesday. “JDK 27 is the release where Java stops asking you to opt in to good defaults and simply turns them on,” wrote backend engineer Arvind Kumar, on his education site Codefarm. Better default settings may not be groundbreaking, but they do make life easier for developers because they mean coders have fewer things to change. Nor should users have to grapple with new features, particularly if they are not of interest. Java 27 succeeds on both counts. Built from the now-completed Java 27 specification, JDK 27 is a short‑term release that won't get long-term support. It includes four new features, or JEPs (JDK Enhancement Proposals) that are ready for production, none of which, Kumar points out, require any immediate changes in developers' code. The release includes another five new features offered as previews for further incubation. Headers get compact In Java 27, compact headers are now available by default (JEP 534). Up until now, the developer had to set them with a flag. Now, no additional action is required. Traditionally, a Java object header takes up 96 bits in a memory heap, much of which is rarely used. With Java 27, the default is a 64-bit header. Turns out the header had too much empty space. Four bytes doesn’t sound like a change to worry over, but across millions of live objects it can lead to considerable memory savings. A run on the SPECjbb2015 Java benchmark standard found that toggling to a 64-bit header resulted in 22% less heap space and 8% less CPU time. The smaller headers appear to work in production. Amazon already runs hundreds of production services with the diminutive compact object headers. SAP has already switched to compact object headers as the default for the company’s OpenJDK fork, SapMachine. Even in its smaller size, this new layout reserves some space for future projects, such as 4 bits for Project Valhalla which aims to bring value objects to Java. Java's overseers don’t want to toss the 96-bit header layout, at least for the time being. But now developers must raise a flag if they want to use it. Quantum-proofing cryptography Looking ahead to the arrival of quantum computing, Java maintainers have implemented “post-quantum hybrid key exchange,” based on TLS 1.3 (JEP 527). Java now offers three new “hybrid” ways of exchanging keys between Java clients, servers and external TLS-compliant endpoints. Each of these approaches, which are options alongside the existing key exchange protocols, combines a traditional Ephemeral Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) algorithm with the NIST ML-KEM post‑quantum key exchange algorithm. The idea is to prepare now for future quantum attacks when the keys to traditional key exchanges could be easily cracked with quantum computing. Malicious attackers are already saving encrypted sessions with a "harvest now, decrypt later" mindset. Taking out the trash, in a good way JDK 27 also tidies up its garbage collectors, the tools that quietly identify and reclaim unused memory. It switched out the default trash bin for constrained environments – Serial – to the overall default garbage collector, called Garbage-First or G1. Garbage collectors relieve developers from manually performing this task and potentially messing it up (usually). But it comes with a cost. Aggressive memory management adds overhead. So different garbage collectors have been built to meet different performance requirements regarding throughput, latency, footprint, and startup time. Recent performance improvements in G1 effectively rendered Serial GC unnecessary, Java's bosses argue. Serial was a single-threaded app built to run on a single CPU, making it well-suited to embedded and other resource-limited environs (especially with clients with less than 1792MB of memory). Thanks to optimization over the years, “G1's performance is now sufficient to replace Serial in all situations in which the JVM would previously have selected Serial,” the maintainers write in JEP 523. With this change, embedded developers will no longer have to add explicit flags to the command line during startup. Even better, it will correct cases where G1 should have been assigned in the first place, such as for containerized apps. “A chunk of containerized Java apps has been running on [Serial] all this time, even though no one consciously made that decision,” wrote PVS-Studio technical author Egor Pishii in a post. The switchover will also help unify telemetry data collection a bit more. Preparing Java 28 The remaining production-ready feature is in-process data redaction (JEP 536), in which Java’s Flight Recorder removes all sensitive details before the recording is finalized. The previews that come with this release include lazy constants (JEP 531), pattern primitive types (JEP 532), structured concurrency (JEP 533), and a set of cryptographic objects (JEP 538). There’s also a vector API (JEP 537) still in the incubation stage. We’ll see all of these again, hopefully in a more polished form, in a later release. Work is already underway for Java 28, due in March 2027: Expect a simple JSON API as an incubating project as well as a revised Shenandoah garbage collector. ®

events.title: Saudi crown prince seeks Egypt’s backing as Houthi attacks rattle Red Sea oil routes
events.summary: Saudi Arabia’s crown prince is seeking backing from the president of Egypt, his ally across the Red Sea, as the kingdom faces increased attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels CAIRO -- Saudi Arabia’s crown prince sought backing Tuesday from the president of Egypt, his ally across the Red Sea, as the kingdom faces increased attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi shipping and infrastructure that have helped drive a surge in global oil prices. Saudi Arabia has largely been on its own in confronting the Iranian-backed rebels, who rapidly captured more territory in Yemen over the past week and strengthened their ability to choke off Saudi oil exports out of the Red Sea. The vulnerability of the kingdom’s oil production was further underscored by an attack days ago that damaged its biggest pipeline. The strike was reportedly carried out by Iran’s allied militias in Iraq. It means the East-West Pipeline will be largely shut down for weeks as it is repaired, regional officials say, likely taking several million barrels of oil a day off the market. The Houthi offensive has opened up a new front in the Mideast’s war and boosted the hand of Iran, Saudi Arabia's traditional archrival in the region, which has attacked shipping through the region's other major maritime route, the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met in Cairo with Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi. The crown prince said in a statement that they both confirmed “their shared commitment to ensuring freedom and security of maritime navigation” in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the choke point at the sea’s southern end. El-Sissi's office put out a statement expressing “Egypt’s unwavering position in supporting Saudi Arabia.” Neither side gave firm details on any future steps. While Egypt is unlikely to offer military help to Saudi Arabia, the country is influential in the Arab world and can help rally support. Egypt has been at the center of mediation efforts in the last three years of turmoil in the region, keeping open relations with all parties, including Iran and its allies. In recent days, Houthi fighters made dramatic advances, seizing the Red Sea port of Mokha and three strategic islands in and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The gains have further improved the Houthis’ position to seal off the strait to Saudi shipping, which they have been attacking since late July. Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the open ocean and, from there, to Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil customers in Asia. Saudi Arabia has so far seemed reluctant to unleash a major military campaign against the Houthis, wary of bringing greater Houthi attacks on its oil infrastructure and being dragged back into an all-out civil war in Yemen, its southern neighbor. But as Houthi attacks continue, the kingdom faces a potential decision about whether to step up its military response or seek a diplomatic solution. Saudi military spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said its air defense forces intercepted and destroyed a drone Tuesday evening before it entered the airspace over Mecca, Islam’s holiest city and a focal point for followers of the faith. It’s the birthplace of Prophet Muhammad, where Muslims believe he first received God’s revelations of the Quran, and the location of the Kaaba, the black, cube-shaped structure that Muslims around the world turn to five times a day when praying. The security of the holy city is “a red line," he said, adding that Saudi forces will not hesitate to act against “hostile and terrorist behavior." The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca. The Saudis’ most essential ally, the United States, has been unpredictable and sometimes unreliable . U.S. President Donald Trump seems reluctant to widen an already unpopular and stalemated Mideast war ahead of congressional elections. The United Arab Emirates, previously a partner in the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, has withdrawn from the war after conflicts between its allies in Yemen and Saudi Arabia’s. Yemen's U.N. Ambassador Abdullah Al-Saadi told the U.N. Security Council on Tuesday that Yemen’s armed forces are regrouping and regaining control but called for a U.N. arms embargo against the Houthis to be enforced and the council to condemn the escalation. He asked "whether the international community will accept for one of the world’s most important gateways for trade and energy to become a blackmail card in the hands of a transnational terrorist group.” Iran live updates: 'Hopefully we're toward the end of the war,' Trump says Judge blocks adding Trump tribute to Kennedy Center in scathing ruling Trump blames global diesel shortages on Ukraine, says Tehran wants a deal Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping during the war in Gaza led to a decrease in traffic through the Suez Canal, gouging Egypt’s revenues.

events.title: Ransomware activity rises across Middle East as criminal groups attack Gulf
events.summary: Ransomware activity across the Middle East has risen sharply, with organised criminal groups increasingly taking aim at Gulf businesses and sectors where disruption can put greater pressure on victims to pay, according to new research. Ransomware activity tracked by cybersecurity company CloudSEK rose from 17 incidents in April 2025 to 357 in June this year, with the company saying the increase reflected a growing focus on the region by established criminal groups. “The Gulf states were, until recently, not a primary ransomware target,” Anirudh Batra, threat researcher at CloudSEK, told The National . “What our data shows is that changed in 2025, and it changed fast.” Groups including The Gentlemen built databases of compromised network devices and repeatedly attacked Saudi businesses, while Nova operated throughout the 17-month reporting period with the Gulf as a focus, he said. “These groups are not testing the market. They have committed to it,” Mr Batra said. The growth of digital infrastructure across Saudi Arabia and the UAE has increased the number of internet-facing systems available to attackers, while unpatched firewalls and VPN gateways remain common entry points, he said. Gavin Millard, vice president of intelligence at cybersecurity company Tenable, said ransomware's rise was part of a longer global trend. “Cyber crime and the tactics they use really is a borderless activity when it comes to things like ransomware,” Mr Millard told The National . Attackers are often less interested in where a company is based than in finding “the easiest and the most profitable victims”, he said. Israel and Turkey face different threats Israel recorded the highest overall cyber-threat activity in CloudSEK's data, followed by Turkey, Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia. The figures are threat-intelligence indicators rather than confirmed, successful attacks. Mr Batra said 37.8 per cent of all hacktivist activity recorded in the region was directed at Israel, alongside sustained Iranian state-linked intelligence operations. Turkey, meanwhile, led the region for ransomware activity, with criminals attracted to its manufacturing, construction, defence and logistics sectors. “Israel is targeted because of who it is. Turkey is targeted because of what it has,” Mr Batra said. Critical infrastructure can be particularly attractive to ransomware gangs because disruption can affect services as well as computer systems. “When the impact is higher, the ransom can also be higher,” Mr Millard said. “People are going to pay more to restore infrastructure that is population-impacting than just business-impacting.” The potential cost was highlighted in the UAE on Tuesday when Dr Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, head of the UAE Cyber Security Council, revealed that a hacker had demanded more than $5 million after claiming to breach a private company, destroying data and trying to leak stolen information. UAE authorities worked with the company to contain the attack and prevent further circulation of its data, said Dr Al Kuwaiti. Mohamed Belarbi, founder and chief executive of Cypherleak, told The National last week that the greater risk was an accumulation of relatively inexpensive attacks causing local cuts, business disruption and recovery costs, rather than one catastrophic shutdown. The UAE has reported a sharp increase in cyber threats since the outbreak of the war. Dr Al Kuwaiti said in April that the country was facing about 800,000 hacking attempts a day, compared with as many as 200,000 before the conflict. The council has also reported thwarting organised attacks on the country's aviation, energy and education sectors in August, a month after it said sophisticated attacks against the financial sector had been detected and contained without disrupting services. AI reduces barrier for new hackers Iranian-linked groups feature prominently in CloudSEK's report, but it also tracked operations linked or attributed by security researchers to China and Israel, alongside North Korean and Russia-aligned activity. China-linked groups exploited vulnerabilities in network equipment to access government, telecommunications and healthcare organisations for intelligence gathering, Mr Batra said. “What we see is a genuinely complex picture,” he said, with state-linked groups pursuing different objectives while international ransomware operators attack the region for money. Artificial intelligence is adding another dimension. CloudSEK said Iran-linked MuddyWater used Google's Gemini to help develop attack tools, while APT42 used AI to produce more convincing phishing messages aimed at Israeli journalists, defence workers and academics. Mr Batra said AI's immediate impact was primarily speed and scale. It can help less-experienced operators to develop tools and enable attackers to produce convincing phishing messages across languages more quickly. AI is not, however, independently selecting targets or carrying out attacks without human direction, he said. Mr Millard agreed that AI was amplifying established methods rather than creating an entirely new form of cyber attack. “AI-enabled attacks aren't novel, and they're not indefensible,” he said. “They're just amplified in scale.” Mr Millard said AI had also significantly lowered the barrier to entry, making it “far easier for a lone wolf to have the skills and capabilities of a state-based actor”. AI can automate stages of an attack, from identifying known vulnerabilities to finding potential victims and using ransomware, reducing the time defenders have to react, he said. For businesses, Mr Millard said the answer was not trying to fix every possible weakness but identifying those that attackers are actually likely to exploit. “Compliance is not security,” he said. “No one can deal with the volume of issues that are being highlighted by these models. You have to take a more pragmatic, risk-based, threat-based approach.”

events.title: Kenilworth Dairies offers lifeline to Queensland dairy farm facing closure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Queensland dairy farm facing closure offered lifeline from Kenilworth Dairies Jason Rozynski is grateful for Kenilworth Dairies' help. ( ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols ) Kenilworth Dairies has stepped up to bottle the Rozynski family's milk. The future of the 80-year-old dairy farm will depend on public support. The milk bottled direct from the Rozynski's farm should be on the shelves within weeks. A Queensland family that feared 80 years of dairying would end after a contract was not renewed has been offered a last-minute lifeline. Kenilworth Dairies owner John Cochrane will buy and bottle some of the 10,500 litres of milk that the Rozynskis produce daily, under a new single-origin brand, One Farm. Its success, and the family's future in dairy farming, will depend on public demand for the 100 per cent Queensland milk. John Cochrane bought Kenilworth Dairies in 2017. ( ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols ) Half of the drinking milk Queenslanders consume, an estimated 250–300 million litres a year is trucked up from Victoria, where the climate makes it much cheaper to produce. Jason Rozynski hopes that with the support his family has had on social media, people will get behind their fresh locally bottled milk. "We're prepared to fight for the industry and produce high quality milk from Queensland." Jason and Angus Rozynski are prepared to fight for Queensland milk. ( ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols ) Mr Cochrane said he had been "sitting back" after processor Maleny Dairies gave the family the required three months' notice that it would not be renewing the Rozynski's contract. He expected that Lactalis, Bega, Dairy Farmers or Norco would take their milk before the September 15 deadline, but the contract ended yesterday. Queensland milk is in peak production at this time of year, and in lower demand. The Rozynski family runs brown Swiss dairy cattle. ( ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols ) Mr Cochrane stepped up to answer the Rozynski's request for help to save their two farms at Imbil in the Mary Valley, about 170 kilometres north west of Brisbane. "We're going flat chat to get this brand up and running, we're looking for markets, we're looking for retailers. "They want to help … they know their customers want Queensland local milk as well." Jason Rozyski hopes his son Angus will have a future in agriculture. ( ABC Rural: Jennifer Nichols ) Mr Cochrane said if the Rozynski's Beez Knees Brown Swiss Dairy business closed, it would have serious implications for local businesses. "Where they're getting fuel, and fertiliser and all their merchandise … all those businesses get affected severely," he said. Joe Bradley has been dairy farming for more than 50 years. ( Supplied: Joe Bradley ) Dairy farmer Joe Bradley, who advocates for the industry as the director of eastAUSmilk, said Kenilworth Dairies was "absolutely the hero" of the story. "I congratulate them on what they've done; it's a brilliant move. We could not afford to lose the Rozynski family," Mr Bradley said. Since deregulation in the year 2000, the number of dairy farms in Queensland has dried up, from 1,500 to fewer than 220. Mr Bradley said the major processors' decision not to pick up the Rozynski's milk was "a bad, bad signal for the Queensland industry". "We've got a lot of farmers at the moment who are second-guessing what they are doing, saying, 'Well, hang on, it's the Rozynski family this year, who's it going to be next year?'" Frozen, dried and fresh dairy products are produced at a factory in Casino. ( ABC Rural: Kim Honan ) Mr Cochrane reached out to Richmond Dairies in northern New South Wales to turn the remainder of the Rozynski's Mary Valley milk into ingredients for the Australian manufacturing industry and exports. Mr Rozynski said it would fetch far less than drinking milk, but could help tide them over until next year when milk was in shorter supply and there was a chance of picking up a larger processing contract in addition to Kenilworth Dairies. Mr Cochrane has invested millions of dollars into growing Kenilworth Dairies since buying the factory and agritourism business in 2017. He said taking on the Rozynski's milk would not affect his commitment to Kenilworth Dairies' own-branded milk and the farmers already supplying it. Kenilworth Dairies began bottling milk in 2020. ( Supplied: Kenilworth Dairies ) Mr Rozynski said Mr Cochrane was a valued family friend and one of his father's best mates. "John's always been there for the industry and always tried to support it," Mr Rozynski said.

events.title: Third appeal lodged against Australian-record $150m native title payout
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Andrew Forrest's Fortescue appeals $150 million Pilbara native title compensation Andrew Forrest and his flagship miner has hit back against the landmark Federal Court ruling. ( AAP: Lukas Coch ) Fortescue has become the third group to appeal a record Federal Court award of $150.3 million to Pilbara traditional owners. Both the Yindjibarndi people and the WA government have lodged filings of their own. A date for the appeals to be heard has not been set. Australia's largest ever native title payout will face appeals from three sides, with mining billionaire Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest's Fortescue becoming the latest group to challenge the landmark legal judgement. In May, the Federal Court ordered the West Australian resources giant pay a record $150.3 million to a group of traditional owners for building four iron-ore mines in WA's north without their permission. Late last month, the Yindjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation (YNAC) and WA government lodged opposite appeals to each other in quick succession. A spokesperson for Fortescue said it was forced to respond to the two appeals to protect its own legal position. "Our cross-appeal restates positions we put forward at trial and seeks clarity on aspects of the judgement that we believe are inconsistent with existing legal principles and precedent," they said. Fortescue's Solomon mine hub in the middle of WA's Pilbara region. ( AAP: Will Russell ) The spokesperson said despite the court's judgement and the company's immediate payment, it did not bring the matter to an end. "Fortescue has always wanted to resolve this long-running dispute," they said. "We paid the full compensation award within 24 hours because we wanted the money to reach the Yindjibarndi community as quickly as possible." Fortescue's Solomon Hub sits on about 135 square kilometres of Yindjibarndi exclusive native title land and has produced estimated revenue of $80 billion since 2013. Traditional owners not yet ready to end dispute with Forrest's Fortescue More than a fortnight after winning the largest native title compensation payout ever in Australia, a Yindjibarndi man returns to his country. Contributions by the flagship operation have helped company chair Andrew Forrest's personal wealth surpass $33 billion. Justice Stephen Burley found Fortescue had destroyed at least 124 spiritually significant sites in digging the mines, and permanently altered the landscape with its water extraction. He said the miner was liable for $150 million for cultural losses affecting the Yindjibarndi people and another $150,000 in economic losses, plus compound interest. When YNAC announced its appeal in August, chief executive Michael Woodley said lawyers for the native title body would target both branches of Justice Burley's verdict. Michael Woodley says YNAC's appeal will target both the cultural loses and economic losses rulings. ( ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates ) It followed a unanimous vote in Roebourne , more than 1,500 kilometres north-east of Perth, where many of the Yindjibarndi community's 500 or so members live. A successful appeal could push the compensation figure closer to the $1.8 billion YNAC had initially claimed, applying what it described as an industry-standard royalty rate. YNAC will also renew its argument that Fortescue systematically divided the Yindjibarndi people by funding a breakaway native title group and harmed their ability to practice traditional ceremonies. Documents filed to the Federal Court reveal the WA government's appeal follows similar grounds to its original case. It disputed nearly every dimension of Justice Burley's judgement and labelled the compensation for cultural loss "manifestly excessive." The State Solicitor's office wrote the Justice had failed to provide adequate reasons for a sum that was nearly three times greater than the amount awarded to the Northern Territory's Guradnji, Yanyuwa, and Yanyuwa-Marra people in February. Tony Buti says the government's appeal is seeking clarity, while court filings slam the payout as "excessive". ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) At the time, WA Attorney-General Tony Buti said the appeal sought "clarity on the law", although one critic accused the government of attempting to appear "business friendly" . The state has previously suggested that compensation should be capped at $10 million, while Fortescue put the number at $8.1 million. In a statement, YNAC chief executive Michael Woodley labelled both appeals "disappointing." "Even if it is consistent with the positions they held during the case," he said.

events.title: TypeSafe AI debuts model for machines that plays Doom
events.summary: TypeSafe AI, a startup bestowed with $40 million in funding, on Tuesday declared itself a maker of frontier models with the release of Jev, a new type of AI model intended for interaction with machines rather than people. Instead of returning natural language in response to a text-based prompt, TypeSafe AI designed Jev to return typed probabilistic decisions for use by other software or AI models. Type safety in programming is a way to catch errors that arise when software processes an unexpected type of data, as might happen if an operation tried to divide an integer by a text string. By providing typed, structured values, Jev can avoid the parsing and validating that must be done to process text responses from LLMs. This approach can be useful for scenarios where interactions with an AI system need to be constrained to a limited set of answers. It can, for example, play Doom, when fed structured data describing the player's game state. But it's more likely to be used for sorting customer service problems and other business workflows. With Jev, the developer starts with a state value, which can be a JSON object or simply a string like "My card was charged twice." The model gets presented with state information through a set of question primitives (Choice, Score, Noul), each of which returns a different type of structured response with probabilities. So a question asking the model to choose which of three departments should handle a particular customer service query might come back: {"billing": 0.08, "technical": 0.85, "sales": 0.07}, with a confidence score of 0.82. That's not very useful for a person seeking the answer to a question but for a software developer, that might be just the thing to make a particular customer service function run more reliably. Jev is a System One model, which relies on a different architecture called Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI, is a former OpenAI researcher and one of the co-inventors of reinforcement learning for human feedback (RLHF) and ChatGPT. "TypeSafe was founded to pursue an alternative path for AI research, focused on machine-native AI," said Almeida in a statement. "I spent years working on models designed to make AI better at interacting with people. But if AI is going to fundamentally change how work gets done, people can't be the only consumers of intelligence." While natural language responses from the likes of ChatGPT or Claude can be wrapped in other code to produce a constrained set of responses, Jev's appeal follows from its efficiency. TypeSafe claims that LLMs generally have variable response times that can stretch into minutes. Jev's response time supposedly ranges from 70ms-500ms, 40x-200x faster than traditional LLMs. The model achieves this speed by using parallel processing. LLMs like OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Terra predict the next text token in a sequence and thus operate sequentially. The System One architecture returns all outputs to a query at once. The demo posted on the TypeSafe website shows Jev returning a response in 0.114s, compared to 8.566 seconds for OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Terra. Then there's the issue of cost. Jev charges $0.042 / MTok for input and $0 for output. OpenAI GPT-5.6 Terra costs $2.00 / MTok and $12 / MTok for output. And compared to a top tier model like Fable 5.1, Jev costs 238x less. The name "Jev" is a reference to 19th century English economist William Stanley Jevons, known for Jevons paradox, who argued that technology efficiency related to coal usage increased coal consumption rather than reducing it. The name also reflects the AI industry's bet that greater token efficiency will increase token consumption even as token prices decline. That wager assumes the market for tokens will be as broad as the market for energy – an assumption that isn't yet settled given that many people who have access to AI tools just don't have a use for them or avoid AI tools due to moral objections. TypeSafe claims that Jev is hallucination-free, which really isn't a fair comparison as its output is not natural language. Jev instead returns structured responses with probabilities, and that does not preclude the possibility of being incorrect. TypeSafe's model won't be the source of misinformation like fabricated legal citations but it also won't be used in the same way since its responses are intended to be consumed by software. Where this becomes relevant is when handling AI agent tool calls and automation. "Having a hallucinated tool call is inconvenient in an agent, but is an absolute deal-breaker if it’s part of a system with latency guarantees or it’s buried several layers deep in a dependency chain," the company claims in its blog post. "Existing models, no matter how smart, still hallucinate and have type errors." Jev, TypeSafe claims, is well-suited for AI automation software, real-time applications that need quick decisions, AI map reduce jobs for classifying large corpora of data, verification of AI inputs, and AI model harnesses. And if it can play Doom as well and as efficiently as advertised, it may not be long before users ask Jev to make drone targeting decisions. ®

events.title: AI panic sparks rare bipartisan moment on Capitol Hill
events.summary: Lawmakers who want to regulate AI are doing something unusual as Congress barrels towards a lengthy recess with no tangible solution in sight: They're working across the aisle. Why it matters: Bipartisanship is increasingly elusive on Capitol Hill of late, but it remains a crucial first step for action in a Senate that requires 60 votes to pass most legislation. The latest example: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) are pressing congressional leadership for a vote on their bill to establish a federal program to assess and monitor AI systems. "Recent incidents of rogue AI agent swarms hacking into public websites and systems have removed lingering doubts concerning the ability of these agents to wreak havoc on our cyber infrastructure," the pair wrote in a letter first obtained by Axios. "Congress cannot delay legislating to address frontier AI risks much longer. Industry-led evaluations are not enough." State of play: Several new bipartisan efforts to regulate AI have cropped up in the week since several current and former employees at Anthropic and OpenAI went public with concerns about the existential risks posed by their own products. Reps. Russell Fry (R-S.C.) and Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) are founding a caucus focused on AI small businesses, called the Innovators Caucus, as Axios reported Monday. Among the group's stated goals is starting work on a federal framework to regulate AI, as well as bringing small businesses to the AI policymaking table. The doomsday warnings have also breathed new life into existing bipartisan proposals to mitigate the dangers of AI. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) has been publicly hawking his bill with Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) to require AI companies to include a human-activated "kill switch" in their systems. Lieu has also privately pitched Democratic leadership on creating a bipartisan AI select committee if they retake control of the House next year. Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) have also been championing their comprehensive AI regulation bill, the Frontier Act. Zoom out: It has been years since Congress passed multiple pieces of truly big bipartisan legislation, and decades since bipartisan lawmaking on marquee issues was a regular practice. The most common moments when cross-party cooperation sees a renaissance on Capitol Hill these days: crises. Consider what got passed in the 117th Congress, on the heels of the Jan. 6 attack and the COVID pandemic: $1.2 trillion in infrastructure spending , a $280 billion semiconductor and research bill and the first major gun safety law in decades, all with bipartisan majorities. Yes, but: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has signaled that his chamber will not take any action on the AI front before the House leaves for a six-week recess that doesn't end until after Election Day. Johnson said in a CNN interview Sunday that Congress should "not smother American innovation" with overly burdensome AI regulations. President Trump has gone even further in dismissing the urgency of federal AI regulations, writing in a Truth Social post Monday: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX." What to watch: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has sounded a considerably more dire note on the issue. A potential House Democratic majority next year may be the place where AI regulation finally finds its footing on Capitol Hill.

events.title: Rep. Chuck Edwards files complaint against House Ethics
events.summary: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) filed a complaint against the top Republican and Democrat on the House Ethics Committee on Tuesday, accusing the lawmakers who investigated him of breaking their own rules. Why it matters: Edwards is escalating his fight against the committee just two weeks after the House voted 413-2 to censure him over its findings that he violated House rules related to sexual harassment and a hostile workplace. Edwards' complaint asks the Office of Congressional Conduct to investigate Ethics Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.) over their handling of his case. The Ethics Committee has previously disputed Edwards' account of the process. When it released its report last month, Guest and DeSaulnier said Edwards had agreed to waive certain procedural steps after reviewing a draft of the report several days earlier. The committee's findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate. Driving the news: "There was nothing ethical about this process," Edwards said in announcing the complaint. He alleges the committee circumvented its own rules by adopting its final report and recommending his censure before receiving his formal response. Edwards has maintained that his conduct did not violate House rules, though he did apologize to his wife, family, and the two women he allegedly harassed. The committee declined to comment. Catch up quick: The Ethics report's findings corroborated several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings. He told one staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios. Edwards gave the two young female staffers numerous gifts, including jewelry worth over $1,000, as well as "designer purses, guns , shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners," the Ethics panel found. What they're saying: "He has no remorse, and now he's trying to turn the tables and say somehow ethics did something wrong," Rep. Teresa Leger- Fernandez (D-NM), the chair of the Democratic Women's Caucus, told Axios. "It just shows you how hard to touch the man is," she added of Edwards. DeSaulnier told Axios he had not yet read Edwards' complaint but was confident the committee followed the proper process.

events.title: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back
events.summary: The Epstein files fight that consumed the House last year is threatening to engulf Republicans all over again. Why it matters: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is now just one Republican away from having the support he needs to force another politically painful Epstein vote — and he and his allies are hunting for the final GOP signature. Retiring Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) signed Massie's new discharge petition Monday, joining Massie and Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.). Massie and Mace told Axios they're actively targeting retiring Republicans and members in vulnerable districts for the fourth GOP signature that will get them the magic number to force a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), one of four Republicans who bucked President Trump and GOP leadership to sign Massie's first Epstein petition last year, told Axios she's considering signing again and has been having conversations with Massie. The big picture: The push is reviving one of the most disruptive fights of Trump's second term for House Republicans. Last year's Epstein discharge petition became a months-long headache for Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and the White House before ultimately securing 218 signatures and forcing the issue onto the House floor. The bill passed with almost unanimous support in the House. The Epstein Files Transparency Act II would enforce and expand the release of remaining files at DOJ. "The Department of Justice continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files that should be released to the public. In addition, the DOJ is unlawfully maintaining heavy redactions on the files it is releasing," Massie wrote in a s tatement last month . Reality check: Even if Massie locks down the Republican support he needs this week, the House is set to leave Washington Thursday until after the November midterms, meaning any potential floor showdown would come post-election. Democrats also still need to provide the remaining signatures needed to reach the 218 required to discharge the bill, though Democratic leadership is encouraging members to sign on. Massie said he views that as just a logistical problem: "I haven't found any Democrat who's against it." Behind the scenes: Massie and Mace are focusing their recruitment efforts on Republicans who may have less to lose from crossing Trump. "I've got one hero slot left," Massie told Axios. Massie said he's talking to members in districts "where they're polling 10 points down," arguing they can either stay off the petition and risk losing anyway or sign it and make the issue part of their reelection pitch. Mace told Axios she is also "talking to Republicans who are leaving, and some Republican districts that we need to focus in on now." The intrigue: Boebert could provide the fourth Republican signature, but Massie says he doesn't expect the Republicans who took the political risk last year to do it again. "Anybody who did the first one is not obligated to put their head in the guillotine again," Massie said when asked about Boebert. "I think it's somebody else's turn." "Ralph Norman did it. He's a new one, and I think there are other new ones out there that we can get," he added. Between the lines: Massie is again accusing Johnson of manipulating the House calendar to deny him the time needed to force a vote. Johnson recently canceled two of the House's three remaining September workweeks. "He got a call from somebody that's above his pay grade that said, 'Take those two days off the calendar. Don't you dare give Massie the runway to get that plane off the ground,'" Massie said. Johnson, after calling Massie "stupid" for suggesting the House would add recess time, then formally moved to cancel session weeks, as Massie had predicted.
