events.title: ‘Now We Can Know Everything and Do Anything,’ Jensen Huang Says at Dreamforce
events.summary: That was the message NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang brought to Salesforce Dreamforce Tuesday, joining CEO Marc Benioff onstage in an appearance that coincided with the announcement of Koa — Salesforce’s first CRM reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super. Huang didn’t just take the stage. He walked into the crowd — threading through the audience at Moscone Center, mic in hand, with Benioff alongside. “We’re all following you, bro,” Benioff told Huang at one point, drawing applause. “With electricity, we could power everything,” Huang said, tracing the arc of industrial revolutions. “With the internet, you can find anything. And now, with artificial intelligence as an infrastructure layer across the planet, we can know everything and do anything.” That arc led directly to the announcement. Salesforce’s first reasoning model was built by post-training NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super on a proprietary synthetic dataset drawn from nearly three decades of enterprise CRM deployments. When Benioff asked Huang about AI safety, Huang was direct. “Safety is paramount in a lot of ways. It’s job one,” Huang said. “However, safety is an engineering problem. We’re developing computing systems after all … If you build a product or a service and you’re not confident in its functionality, capability or safety, then don’t release it.” He reiterated that innovation and leadership should coincide with safety and security . “Innovation, speed and safe products — it’s a false choice,” Huang said. “You could definitely have both at the same time. So run as fast as you can. But if you feel at any given point in time the company’s out of control, or the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right.” Throughout his talk, Huang offered a positive vision for the future of AI. He noted he was among the first to push back on the notion that AI would end the software industry. He also pushed back on the idea that AI is a threat to jobs. “As a result of our ambition, and with the productivity boost we get from AI, the sky’s the limit,” he added. “Engage AI. Don’t get left behind.” “Every company, every enterprise, every country would become an AI company,” Huang said. “It’s going to be an agentic enterprise.” “The sky is especially the limit for our Trailblazers,” Benioff said, referring to the company’s customer and developer community. “I think this technology, the way it empowers people … the technology can partner with them to do this in incredible new ways.” Because NVIDIA Nemotron is open, Salesforce was able to fine-tune and run the model entirely within its own infrastructure. Salesforce controls the weights, the model runs on Salesforce’s systems and no customer data is used during training or inference. “Not a single byte of customer data was used,” said Rohan Kumar, Salesforce’s president of platform and engineering, who introduced Koa before Huang took the stage. Open models went from 30% at the beginning of last year to now some 70%, Huang explained. “People are both adopting closed models at exponential rates, but also building their own custom AIs — because every single software company is an AI company, and every single enterprise is going to be an agentic and AI enterprise.” NVIDIA is one of them — running on Salesforce across sales, service, marketing and operations, and currently piloting Agentforce for customer-support workflows. Koa was built using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with NVIDIA NeMo RL, NeMo Gym and NeMo AutoModel. The training corpus covers synthetic enterprise scenarios across 14+ industries — manufacturing, financial services, healthcare and travel. In Salesforce’s CRM Bench, a model benchmark that includes a suite of real-world tasks like updating an opportunity, routing a case, or scheduling a follow-up, Koa already matches or exceeds leading model performance on CRM actions with 3x fewer errors. Koa is already running inside Salesforce, powering an employee agent in Slack, and is moving into customer pilots in October as a customer-selectable model in Agentforce, starting with Formula 1, UChicago Medicine, Baxter Credit Union, 1-800Accountant, Engine and Xero. General availability is expected winter 2026 in U.S. regions. events.title: US 10-year yield hits highest level since 2007
events.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended his bond buyback program in contentious congressional hearings Tuesday, as the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since the 2007 global financial crisis. Bessent suggested the spike could have been worse without Treasury’s intervention; he also defended a separate operation to prop up the Japanese yen as preventing Tokyo from selling its US debt, which would have pushed yields higher . “Bessent’s intervention risks whipping up a blaze that could cause damage well beyond America ,” PIMCO’s former CEO argued in The Economist, as a surge in global bond yields prompted central banks to coalesce around monetary tightening. US Federal Reserve watchers put the odds of a rate hike Wednesday at 92% . — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: How Ed Sheeran's tour imploded over a geopolitical fight
events.summary: Ed Sheeran's world tour spiraled into chaos this week after one opener was removed, every remaining opening act quit and stadiums threatened to pull the plug on the tour. Why it matters: The turmoil reveals the power dynamics behind major concert tours, showing how even a global star like Sheeran can be forced to take a back seat on decisions about his own shows. Driving the news: All four of Sheeran's remaining supporting acts announced Tuesday that they were dropping out. Irish musicians Aaron Rowe and Beoga , as well as Danish band Lukas Graham , said Tuesday they were leaving the tour. Rowe was set to replace Macklemore as the opener for the U.S. shows, AP reports. Finneas , who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, also announced he was exiting the concert series, saying on Instagram that "artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed." Catch up quick: The moves came one day after rapper Macklemore, who was scheduled for most of the remaining tour dates, was dropped after using his sets to voice support for Palestinians and condemn the war in Gaza during shows on Sept. 4-5 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore told the MetLife crowd on Sept. 4 that he wanted to do the tour so he could "say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine.'" His performance included images of war-torn Gaza playing on the video board. The tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone Monday that concert venues threatened to cancel shows unless Macklemore was dropped from the tour after his pro-Palestinian comments. Zoom in: Macklemore said the decision came after he spoke with Sheeran, alleging that the headliner faced pressure from stadium owners including Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium. According to Macklemore, Sheeran is typically "apolitical" and the recent round of backlash "challenged" him "in a way it never had before." The other side: Sheeran shared on Instagram Tuesday that the decision to remove Macklemore from the tour came not from him, but from the promoters. "I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living." Sheeran also wrote on Instagram that he didn't want his Loop Tour drawn into a public discussion around the war in Gaza. "I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," Sheeran wrote on IG. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated." He added: "I have my personal views on the devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care. Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own personal way." Zoom out: The turmoil over Sheeran's concert tour raises broader questions about political speech at concerts. As Rolling Stone notes, several stadiums that opposed Macklemore's appearance are publicly owned. One such venue is Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which faced calls to cancel Ye's shows earlier this year due to his past antisemitic comments. The bottom line: Sheeran has tried to keep politics off his stage. The fight over Gaza has now made that neutrality difficult to maintain.

events.title: Top Oversight Dem Opens Investigation of Donald Trump Jr.’s Russian Oligarch-Funded Wedding
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, at an event at the White House in June. Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee launched an investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s relationship with a Russian oligarch who paid for much of Trump Jr.’s wedding earlier this year. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., sent two letters on Monday to the White House and Trump Jr. requesting records related to Trump Jr.’s financial relationship with the oligarch, Umar Kremlev. “The secretive, close relationship between the son of a sitting U.S. President and a member of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious national security and public corruption concerns,” Garcia wrote. Garcia told Trump Jr. it “may be the most serious allegation against you to date.” The letter to Trump Jr. asked for documents including Trump Jr.’s communications with Kremlev and “financial records of all purchases made for your wedding by foreign nationals.” “Paper Trail” Podcast Learn more about this story on ProPublica’s podcast “ Paper Trail .” Trump Jr. did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Garcia’s investigation. The letters were prompted by a ProPublica investigation published Monday , which revealed that Kremlev secretly covered hundreds of thousands of dollars of expenses for Trump Jr.’s wedding. That included renting out a private island in the Bahamas for multiple nights. The wedding guest list numbered around 50, including Jared Kushner and other members of the Trump family. Kremlev, who first met Trump Jr. recently, also attended the intimate affair with a large group of other Russians. Kremlev is close to Putin and serves as the head of the International Boxing Association, a scandal-plagued sports group that has been financed by the Russian state-owned energy giant Gazprom. The wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions. Kremlev’s press office previously told ProPublica that he and Trump Jr. “have a friendly relationship” and that they don’t talk politics. After ProPublica’s story was published, Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, released a joint statement confirming Kremlev’s role. “Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us,” they said in a statement published on her Instagram account. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.” They added, “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive.” The couple also drew a distinction between the ceremony itself, which was just family, and the rest of the wedding weekend. In a statement released by the White House after the story was published, President Donald Trump echoed that. “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding,” he said. “It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal!” The couple exchanged vows on Friday, May 22, on a private island in the Bahamas. The wedding festivities then continued for two days. The Saturday, May 23, event, which Kremlev paid for, was held on the same island as the ceremony. (“Night 2. One Love!” Bettina Trump posted about the Saturday festivities on Instagram.) The Sunday reception was held a roughly 10-minute boat ride away on a neighboring private island, rented out by Kremlev. At the Sunday reception, the couple had their first dance, with Bettina Trump wearing her wedding dress, and ate a five-tier wedding cake topped with a miniature bride and groom.  Afterward, the couple’s wedding planner talked to Hello! magazine about planning the three-day affair with Bettina Trump. “She wanted a progression,” said the planner, Lewis Miller. “The ceremony was very serene and pretty and soft, and the dinner was very elegant, and then the next night was much more colorful, and then the last night was more kind of cool and fun tropical vibes.” Read More Donald Trump Jr.’s Bahamas Wedding Was Secretly Bankrolled by Russian Oligarch Close to Putin The post Top Oversight Dem Opens Investigation of Donald Trump Jr.’s Russian Oligarch-Funded Wedding appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: The vulnpocalypse rains iBugs down on Apple with record-setting number of patches
events.summary: Apple has addressed more than 260 CVEs across all of its operating systems, browsers, and other software products, marking the largest single patch cycle in Cupertino's history. While this CVE count is hardly notable compared to some vendors - hello, Microsoft’s record-breaking 974 bugs disclosed earlier this month - it does set a company record for Apple. It also reflects the new reality of AI-driven bug hunting, as models become exponentially better and faster at finding security vulnerabilities. However, the flip side of the AI coin we were promised - that models would also excel at writing patches and automatically fixing software and systems - yeah, that hasn't happened yet. The silver lining for everyone updating their Apple products right now (including this humble vulture): none of the vulnerabilities are listed as being under active exploitation. Of course, that may change very quickly as attackers are, at this very moment, looking to exploit the newly disclosed bugs, too. And we promise you that they are using AI. Apple’s latest mobile and operating system versions, iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, released on Monday, also address a record 122 and 204 security vulnerabilities, respectively, across phone, iPad, and computer operating systems. Of these hundreds of CVEs, however, there are only ten (by our count) that AI is directly credited with finding. iOS 27 fixes 122 flaws Just two of the iPhone and iPad CVEs fixed with iOS 27 credit a coding agent or AI assistant with finding them. These include CVE-2026-65410, a vuln that exists in iPhone and iPad AVE video encoders, that can cause unexpected system termination. Apple credited AI-bug-finding firm Calif, along with Claude and Anthropic Research, with finding and reporting this security flaw. Then there's CVE-2026-65409, a type-confusion issue in iOS’ Foundation framework that can be abused to cause a denial of service, also found by Calif - specifically human researcher Bruce Dang - in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research. Some of the more interesting and serious iOS bugs fixed with the newest update aren’t listed as found by AI. These include CVE-2026-43689, a privilege-escalation flaw that could allow an app to gain root access. Apple credited Nosebeard Labs’ Andreas Jaegersberger and Ro Achterberg with reporting this bug. Additionally, CVE-2026-65406, a logic-issue flaw due to improper validation in Background Assets, could be abused to access sensitive user data. Background Assets is an Apple framework that lets you download large files and content in the background before a user opens the app for the first time. Baidu Security researcher Ye Zhang spotted this one. macOS 27 patches 204 vulns Meanwhile, the new macOS 27 update that addresses 204 vulns also fixes both the AI hunted bugs: CVE-2026-65410 and CVE-2026-65409. Plus, it credits AI helpers with discovering eight others, including one especially nasty flaw that could lead to remote code execution through the CUPS printer interface. Let’s start with that one. CVE-2026-43692 is a validation issue in CUPS that can be exploited by a remote user to either terminate the app or execute malicious code. Aaron Grattafiori and the Nvidia AI Red Team receive credit for disclosing this flaw. CVE-2026-64790 in CUPS can be exploited to gain elevated privileges. Grattafiori and the Nvidia AI Red Team again get credit for the win. CVE-2026-43791, a validation issue in StorageKit, can be abused to read files. Grattafiori, the Nvidia AI Red Team, Meridian Miftari, and Amy from amys.website disclosed this flaw to Apple. CVE-2026-43690 is a race-condition bug in the Server Message Block (SMB) network communication protocol. A local user can exploit the flaw to read kernel memory. Calif’s Bruce Dang, with Claude and Anthropic Research, found this one. CVE-2026-43719 is another SMB use-after-free bug, discovered by Calif’s Dang and Jakob Pammer, Claude, and Anthropic. “Mounting a maliciously crafted SMB network share may lead to system termination,” Apple warned. CVE-2026-65376 is yet another SMB issue - this one an out-of-bounds-read flaw reported by Dang, Claude, Anthropic, and 재영 정. CVE-2026-65374 is a memory-corruption issue in the WebDAV protocol that can lead to code execution. Dang, Claude, Anthropic, and He Wei (ギカク) receive credit for finding this bug. CVE-2026-65375, also in WebDAV, can cause unexpected system termination. Apple credited Dang, Claude, Anthropic, and Devcore Research Team’s YingMuo. CVE-2026-43677 is an out-of-bounds write issue in WebDAV with a slew of researchers receiving credit for finding it. In addition to the usual trio (Dang, Claude, and Anthropic), bubu, Omar Cerrito, HE WEI（ギカク), Roman Zabicki, Richard Zana, Chris Bailey - Short Circuit, Aswin Kumar Gokulakannan, and Surya Narayan Kushwaha are on the list.®

events.title: Investors see surge in US Treasury yields emerging as new market risk
events.summary: The recent rise in US bond yields is emerging as a new source of investor anxiety after the 10-Year Treasury rose to a level not seen in almost two decades. A Bank of America fund manager survey on Tuesday said 33 per cent of respondents saw a “disorderly rise in bond yields” as the biggest market risk, replacing artificial intelligence. The survey was released a day after the yield on the 10-year Treasury passed 5 per cent. The 10-year yield rose to as high as 5.041 per cent earlier in the day – its highest since July 2007 – pushing up borrowing costs for consumers and companies. The rise in bond yields dragged down Wall Street's main indexes, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average suffering a loss of 328 points, or 0.63 per cent. Analysts have attributed the recent increase in bond yields to rising oil prices and inflation fears stemming from the Iran war, concerns about the US fiscal direction and spending by AI companies. Investors are now increasingly looking to the Federal Reserve to clamp down on inflation. Traders have all but locked in that the US Fed will raise interest rates by 25 basis points on Wednesday, with the UAE Central Bank likely to follow because of the dirham’s peg to the dollar. The rise in US Treasury yields come as some energy exporters in the Gulf lose out on revenue from the Iran war, which could make it more expensive to borrow. For countries with lower revenue and higher spending needs, government reserve funds and possibly sovereign wealth funds could be called on to assist with projects, said Rachel Ziemba, founder of geopolitical risk firm Ziemba Insights. “And so those issues, more so than where US rates are, are arguably more important,” she said. Ms Ziemba also said the region has been investing more in US equities and private equity, rather than in Treasury bonds and similar dynamics. “And I think that trend is likely to continue,” she said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the recent rise in bond yields on “global issues”, with the rise in US Treasury yields occurring alongside others across advanced economies as part of a broader global bond rout. Mr Bessent acknowledged the recent increase also reflected the “need to address the [US] deficit”, which recently passed $40 trillion. Mr Bessent told politicians during his testimony on Capitol Hill that the buyback programme was a success, repeating his claim the US bond market has been the best-performing in the developed world since President Donald Trump began his second term. The Treasury Department last week announced it was seeking to buy back $6 billion of government debt, triple the size of its normal operations, in an effort to calm the market. The department previously announced it would double the size of the programme. “There is a counter-factual of what would it ​have done – and we then proceeded to have the two most successful Treasury auctions that we've ‌had in 20 years,” he said. Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, said he believes low interest rates over the past 10 years have warped perceptions about the current Treasury levels. “If you look across history, a 10-year 5 per cent Treasury is not unusual, he said. “I think people need to be recalibrated.”

events.title: House quashes another Trump impeachment push with Dem help
events.summary: The House voted for the third time in two years to quash a rogue effort by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump. Why it matters: As with the last two times, the vote divided House Democrats. Some sided with Green, but others voted "present" or actively helped GOP leadership defeat the effort. Green frustrated his Democratic colleagues by forcing the vote without support from party leadership, with one telling Axios the move was "fucked up." The Texas Democrat defended his attempts to impeach Trump over killings committed by federal immigration officials, calling it a "life and death" matter. Driving the news: The House voted 232-147 for Republican leadership's measure to table — effectively, kill — Green's motion to force a vote on impeaching Trump, with 47 members voting "present." Between the lines: Some Democrats who voted with Green privately sneered before the vote that it was a distraction from party messaging on the House's last in-session week before the midterm. Green pushed back by saying the lawmakers who criticized him "don't have the courage to stand up and face me" and challenging them to debate the matter publicly.

events.title: AI networking startups race to replace Nvidia's NVLink
events.summary: As Nvidia expands its influence through its NVLink Fusion tech, rival networking vendors are scrambling to bring alternative interconnects and switches to market. At the AI Infra Summit this week, Delos Data and Cornelis Networks officially entered the scale up networking race. Scale-up fabrics, like NVLink, are what have allowed Nvidia to make eight, 72, and now 576 GPUs behave as one enormous AI accelerator. To catch up, rivals like AMD have embraced emerging protocols like Ultra Accelerator Link. Today, these protocols are largely being tunneled over standard Ethernet switches. For instance, AMD is using Broadcom’s 102.4 Tbps Tomahawk 6-based switches connecting to custom I/O dies on the MI455X. Purpose-built UALink switches and physical interconnects remain elusive, but that won’t be the case for long if Cornelis and Delos have their way. The two companies are approaching this challenge from a few different angles, including standardization, software optimization, and physical hardware. Setting the standard for the Never-Nvidia network At AI Infra on Monday, HPC-centric networking vendor Cornelis introduced the Active Compute Fabric (ACF), which seeks to establish an open architecture for scale up and scale out networking that integrates programmable compute into the fabric. The standard signals Cornelis’ entry into the scale up networking arena. Spun out of Intel in 2020, Cornelis’ Omni-Path tech was originally designed as a scale-out interconnect for high-performance computing applications, including supercomputers like Trinity and Lynx. With the imminent launch of the company’s 800 Gbps-capable CN6000-series switches and NICs, the company has its sights set not only on bringing its tech to a broader audience through the open Ultra Ethernet protocol, but also on scale-up networking. ACF expands on the mission of technologies like UALink and the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking, another scale up networking protocol, to set a baseline for in-network compute capabilities across a wide range of hardware, not just Cornelis’ own CN-series parts. One of the key technologies behind Nvidia’s NVSwitch ASICs is support for SHARP, which allows for things like in-network collectives to be offloaded to the switch ASICs, freeing up GPU compute and cutting down on communication overheads. Collective acceleration isn't new by any means, with major networking vendors from Broadcom to Cisco having implemented it in some capacity. As an open architecture, ACF appears to set a least common denominator so that customers deploying these systems know exactly what they’re getting. However, it doesn’t stop there. Cornelis sees opportunities to accelerate a variety of other functions. We’ve detailed a few below: KV cache offloading used to store and retrieve model state across multiple sessions. MoE expert dispatch to reduce duplicate transfers and communication overhead for mixture-of-experts models during inference and training. Message passing interface offload for HPC-centric applications. In fabric checkpointing for failure recovery during training and other large workloads. “Communications overhead and synchronization can leave expensive accelerators underutilized,” the company explained. These in-network accelerators “allow the network to operate on data as it moves through the system.” According to Cornelis, the savings potential from reclaiming that idle compute is significant. “In a 100,000 GPU system, Cornelis modeling of public data shows that roughly half of all GPU hours are spent waiting for data, worth about $1.68 billion a year in wasted capacity and 500 GWh of power.” As usual, take these claims with a grain of salt. However, reclaiming GPU idle time would equate to significant savings. Eliminating all the bottlenecks that contribute to them is easier said than done. A new kind of NIC for the AI age While Cornelis champions its ACF architecture, Delos Data, a startup founded by former Barefoot Networks and Intel execs, aims to tackle the physical layer with a series of new network reference designs. Marketed under its Nonstop AI portfolio, the network interfaces span the full gamut of connectivity from co-packaged interconnects to more traditional NICs. The idea, the company explains, is to provide customers with a system-level blueprint for speeding up data movement between endpoints and enabling larger compute domains scaling beyond a single rack. Delos’ data interface will be offered in three form factors. The first is an I/O die capable of more than 30 Tbps of aggregate bandwidth or about 8 TB/s in either direction. That’s more than double the interconnect bandwidth of either Nvidia's or AMD’s latest accelerators, which cap out at 3.6 TB/s. Just how competitive that ends up being will depend on when Delos’ I/O chiplets actually see deployment. That timeline is going to depend heavily on integration since those I/O dies need to be integrated directly into the accelerator package, which requires a high-degree of co-design. Critically, Delos isn't trying to trap its customers in a walled garden to the same extent that Nvidia does with its NVLink Fusion I/O dies or IP. At least as of writing, NVLink Fusion still requires customers to buy NVSwitches for scale up networking. Delos’ chiplets are protocol agnostic. They don’t care whether you’re using ESUN, UALink, or something else. Chip designers that'd rather focus their efforts and capital on the AI bits of their accelerators – which, it turns out, applies to most hyperscalers – could simply license Delos' chiplet design. This protocol agnosticism also extends to Delos’ near-packaged optics (NPO) tech, which will integrate a 10-plus Tbps data interface — that’s 2.5 TB/s bidirectional bandwidth in Nvidia speak — with optics engines from leading optics suppliers. Rack scale systems, like Nvidia’s NVL72, have largely relied on copper interconnects up to this point due to power constraints. As systems grow from 72 GPU rack systems to row-scale clusters with 576 and eventually 1,152 GPUs, optics become unavoidable. While integrating optics directly into the accelerators is possible using tech available today, the blast radius of a failed optical module is considerable. NPO offers an alternative. Copper interconnects are used within the rack, with optics provided via user-serviceable NPO modules between racks. Finally, Delos is working on a 400-plus Gbps NIC, which like the rest of its data interface offerings is protocol agnostic. This is arguably the least surprising entry in the entire lineup. Scale out networks are still going to be required for large training clusters as well as for front-end access and storage networks. events.title: Crypto industry’s top legislative priority implodes
events.summary: The cryptocurrency industry just lost the lead of a lifetime. Just last year, banks were so terrified of digital asset companies’ war chest that they scrambled to overhaul their own lobbying . But on Tuesday, senators failed to advance the firms’ top legislative priority, shrugging off the threat of tens of millions of dollars that still could hit them this fall . President Donald Trump’s crypto adviser had hoped for Republican unity , but even that couldn’t materialize, as baked-in allegiance to banks drove three Republicans to vote no; all Democrats voted no out of concern the bill wouldn’t rein in Trump. Odds are high lawmakers won’t take up another permanent overhaul of crypto regulation until Trump leaves office. “The amount of money the crypto industry spent on lobbying firms for such a staggering defeat would have been better spent curing cancer,” one lobbyist told Semafor after the vote. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Your AI agents' reports and questions have a new inbox, courtesy of AWS
events.summary: AWS engineers have published an open-source AI agent management tool that treats tasks and permission requests just like emails that fill up an inbox. Pizza Bot was announced on AWS’ open-source blog last week, where it was billed by its developers as a way to more easily manage agent tasks without constantly having to check a chat window to see if a task was completed or on hold because more permission was needed. “You don’t send an email and then sit watching the outbox until the reply lands,” the Pizza Bot team wrote. “Pizza Bot is shaped like an email client for the same reason: a thread is a unit of work you come back to rather than a session you have to attend.” Like the modern email services it mimics, Pizza Bot organizes communications with AI agents into message threads. Finished tasks, along with detailed result writeups you’d expect from a colleague you’ve delegated your work to, end up in the Unread category, while anything you need to make a decision on is shunted to the Action category. Asynchronous agent communication is likely to be a godsend for those balancing multiple tasks assigned to digital delegees, as the Pizza Bot team describes it. “Live chat assumes both parties are present, which holds for a quick exchange and breaks the moment a task takes several minutes,” the Pizza Bot maintainers wrote. Just like you don’t want to stare over the shoulder of the poor IT sod you sent off to do a task while you watch YouTube videos, no one wants to sit there and watch an AI agent do web research, or whatever. “Pizza Bot treats an agent the way you’d treat a colleague who has gone off to do the work: it comes back when there’s something to read, or something only you can decide,” the PB team added. Internal tool goes open source Pizza Bot, named for Amazon’s “two-pizza team” model (i.e., small, autonomous teams small enough to be fed by two pizzas), began life inside Amazon as an internal tool for AI agent uses other than software development. According to its developers, non-coding uses they were exploring internally continually had the same requirements, namely working in the background autonomously and only bugging their user when they were done or had a question. “None of those describe how anyone uses a chat window,” the Pizza Bot team explained. “They describe how people already work with each other.” Email, they added, was the perfect design paradigm for internal use, and seeing whether it would work for everyone else meant opening the project to open source contributions. As mentioned, Pizza Bot is open source - you can snag a copy for Windows, macOS, and Linux from its GitHub repo. It runs on-device, stores all its communication threads locally in SQLite files, and doesn’t transmit anything off device unless you grant permission for it to do so. Prompts and attachments are sent to model providers, naturally, but even that’s not necessary: Pizza Bot also supports Ollama, allowing users to run compatible open-weight AI models locally. Pizza Bot doesn’t ship with a lot of capabilities, as its maintainers noted that Amazon-specific skills and MCP servers were left out when they rebuilt it as an open source project for public release. Out of the box, however, it can list, read, write, edit, and search files, delegate tasks to specialist agents, and run a sandboxed JavaScript interpreter. It also ships with a browser automation skill and a guide skill that lets users ask about Pizza Bot’s capabilities. Claude Code-compatible .mcp.json files are supported and can be dropped straight in, as can skills, the team noted. One word of caution to anyone who wants to try it: The devs make clear this is a piece of open source software, not an officially supported AWS product. “There’s no AWS support or service-level agreement behind it,” they note. If you’re gonna bake a pie with this bot, you’ve been warned. ®

events.title: Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board votes to close building
events.summary: The Kennedy Center's board voted Tuesday to close the iconic performing arts center's main building for a renovation project championed by President Trump , multiple outlets reported and a source familiar confirmed to Axios. Why it matters: Trump's attempts to put his name on the building , which memorializes former President John F. Kennedy, have fueled an ongoing legal and political battle. The decision came hours after a federal judge again said the center could not put Trump's name on the building . Driving the news: Trump said in a Truth Social post that the renovation "cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name." He said that if the ruling is not in his allies' favor or is not overturned by the Supreme Court , "the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place." Catch up quick: A resolution from the board, filed in the ongoing legal fight with Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over the Center, cited "water intrusion and deterioration of the center's physical plant" that it said "caused a partial ceiling collapse," arguing the safety risk "greatly outweighs any reputational risk associated with closing the main building." A second resolution filed in the case listed ways Trump could be "legally and appropriately recognized" on the building, after a federal judge ruled that only Congress can change its name. Zoom out: The resolution states that without his name on the building, it's "unlikely" Trump "will provide the fundamental oversight of the renovation of the main building." It listed options for text on the exterior marble beneath the center's name, including "A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump" or "Renovation, Restoration, and support by President Donald J. Trump." Friction point: U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper blocked the center from closing earlier this year, finding that "the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center" and "based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided presentation of information." But in that order, he said his injunction would not prevent "capital repair work," nor would it "categorically prohibit the Board from closing the Center should it come to this decision anew after independently balancing its multiple obligations to the Center in a prudent fashion." Catch up quick: The renovation project would address issues like corrosion and rehabilitating the building's iconic theaters and Grand Foyer, Axios previously reported. The draft resolution proposes sending marquee events offsite, while continuing some programming at the REACH — an indoor–outdoor space. Beyond infrastructure renovations, Trump ally and board member Paolo Zampolli outlined his luxury vision for the space to Axios' Cuneyt Dil, including expanding the outdoor park to create a "concert hub," and building a marina. What we're watching: For now, those ideas aren't part of the board's resolution — but the center's future under Trump remains in flux, in part because of an ongoing legal challenge to the president's takeover. And while Trump allies position him as the center's financial savior, the Washington Post reported that ticket sales plunged after the board of trustees voted to name the center after him. events.title: Low-quality casino sites conceal highly dangerous threat actors
events.summary: If your employees are visiting Chinese-language gambling or adult sites, they may not just be wasting time and money, but potentially encountering serious malware hidden behind domains that look like mostly harmless entertainment at first glance. A report from Infoblox urges the security community to pay closer attention to these websites, because some double as command-and-control (C2) infrastructure for espionage and malware distribution. Zach Edwards, staff threat researcher at Infoblox, suggests security researchers and the media have ignored these sites because the story is complicated and confusing. Infoblox says it tracks about 1.7 million Chinese-language casino websites that facilitate illegal gambling. These support North Korean money laundering and tax avoidance, among other dubious activities. And these casino sites can be difficult to distinguish from one another. They tend to use variations of common templates in terms of design and function. Many operate like a legal casino would, just relying on the advantage of house odds to profit. While these sites provide illegal gambling and adult entertainment for online visitors from China and Asia, some rely on US cloud providers for computing infrastructure. "Major US hosting companies (Amazon, Microsoft, Cloudflare, and Google) continue to host infrastructure associated with these domains," the Infoblox report explains. "One likely explanation is account theft at those providers, a practice documented previously as 'infrastructure laundering.'" That refers to hosting companies like Funnull that have reportedly rented IP addresses from Amazon Web Services and Microsoft and made those resources available to clients carrying out illegal activities. According to a July 2026 report from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), disparate crime syndicates increasingly use common infrastructure for cybercrime, while online scams resulted in estimated losses of between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion in 2025 across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. A subset of casino sites offer scam gambling, or "scambling." Visitors place bets but can't get their money out if they win. And then there's a subset of sites used by China-aligned threat groups. "China-aligned APT groups have been running the PeckBirdy framework since 2023, hiding their malware C2 domains inside low-quality Chinese-language casino websites," Infoblox said. PeckBirdy, as noted by Trend Micro researchers in January, is a script-based framework that attackers can load through compromised websites. In one campaign, attackers injected scripts into gambling sites that loaded PeckBirdy and displayed fake software update pages designed to entice victims to download malware. The problem is that each of these three types of sites, though they change frequently, looks similar. Infoblox notes that just over 3 percent of its enterprise customers resolved at least one PeckBirdy C2 domain. "The most important thing for defenders to do is stop ignoring casino domains," Infoblox argues. "An alert on a Chinese-language casino or adult domain that gets closed as an employee browsing violation is precisely the outcome the PeckBirdy operators are counting on. The decoy works because the dismissal is reasonable – these domains genuinely are, most of the time, exactly what they appear to be." Security analysts who review suspicious network contacts are advised to check whether these casino domains include malicious payloads before closing the review ticket. ®

events.title: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI
events.summary: 2026 midterm elections: Helping voters navigate election information in the age of AI Sep 15, 2026 | By Ginny Badanes, General Manager, Tech for Society, Microsoft As Americans prepare to vote this November, artificial intelligence is changing how many people find and understand election information. Some voters are deliberately turning to AI tools with questions about candidates, ballot measures, election procedures, and issues that matter to their communities. Others are encountering AI-generated summaries at the top of search results. In either case, AI is increasingly becoming a front door to election information. This shift is happening quickly. More than 30% of the U.S. working-age population now uses AI (Microsoft AI Diffusion Index, Q1 2026; Microsoft, AI Adoption Across the United States ) . These tools can help people understand complicated topics, compare information, and explore unfamiliar issues. But election information can also present some challenges for AI. It is highly local, changes quickly, and can be incomplete, contested, or stripped of essential context. The answer is not to steer voters away from AI, it is to help people use it wisely, particularly when the information may influence aspects of their voting experience, such as how, when, and where they cast their ballot. That is why, on National Voter Registration Day , a day when our brands and products come together to encourage civic participation , we’re launching the next phase of our voter education initiative, Check. Recheck. Vote . This year, the campaign will equip voters with practical AI literacy skills for the 2026 election season. We launched Check. Recheck. Vote. in 2024 to help voters recognize the risks posed by deceptive AI-generated content. Deepfakes and other deceptive media remain a serious concern. But in conversations with voters and election organizations, we are also hearing about a broader and more immediate challenge. Millions of people now encounter election information through AI-generated answers, and many are not sure how to determine whether those answers are current, complete, or reliable. The updated campaign gives voters three straightforward steps: Check the sources and citations behind an AI-generated answer. Look for where the information came from, who published it, and when it was last updated. Be cautious when an answer provides no sources. Recheck important details by visiting the original sources and comparing what other credible sources say. This is especially important for fast-changing or location-specific information. Vote based on current information from your state or local election website, including official guidance on registration, voting options, deadlines, and polling locations. At the center of the campaign is a new 75-second video that shows how an AI-generated answer can appear during an ordinary election-related search, explains where these answers can fall short, and offers simple steps voters can take before relying on them. The campaign website pairs the video with practical guidance and links to authoritative election resources, including state-by-state voting information and tools for educators. We are working with the National Association of Secretaries of State (NASS) and the National Association of State Election Directors (NASED) to scale the reach of this campaign across all fifty states and the territories and to point voters to accurate information directly from state and local election officials so they can participate with confidence. We believe that civics and voter education start well before a citizen is old enough to vote. That’s why we are also investing in efforts to extend AI voter literacy education in the classroom. The campaign website includes a classroom activity to help students examine how AI may shape the election information they encounter, practice verifying claims, and keep their own judgment at the center of the process. We are also amplifying our impact on this important issue by supporting the News Literacy Project . We’re also proud to announce today that, in partnership with iCivics, we are launching Village Square – a new Minecraft Education civic learning experience that helps students explore how communities make decisions and solve shared challenges. The game brings concepts such as dialogue, participation, and collective decision-making to life through immersive gameplay. Village Square gives educators and families an engaging, nonpartisan way to help young people practice listening to different perspectives, weighing trade-offs and working together to build stronger communities. Finally, we know that credible local reporting remains essential to informed civic participation, and that reporting is under strain in many communities. In Washington state, Microsoft is partnering with the Associated Press Fund for Journalism to expand election coverage for 10 local newsrooms operating 14 news websites. Participating newsrooms receive access to AP election results and race calls, vote tabulations, state-specific maps and graphics, and resources that help local journalists connect national and statewide developments to the communities they serve. The newsrooms represent communities from Seattle to Spokane and the Wenatchee Valley. Their work complements the reporting of the Associated Press, helping trusted, fact-based election coverage and results reach communities that might otherwise lack access. This investment reflects a broader reality. Voters need more than information. They need reliable sources that can provide context, ask hard questions, correct mistakes, and explain what national developments mean at the local level. Microsoft’s Support for the 2026 Midterms Voters aren’t the only ones navigating this AI moment, so are the people running campaigns and conducting elections, all while facing an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. Microsoft has long supported the security and resilience of campaigns and elections. In 2018, we launched AccountGuard to help political campaigns and democracy-focused organizations defend against cyberattacks, and during the 2024 election cycle we joined dozens of other technology companies in the Tech Accord to Combat Deceptive Use of AI in 2024 Elections . Here’s how that commitment continues today: Equipping election officials. With The Elections Group, International IDEA, Ready for Tuesday and Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Lab, we launched the free, open-source AI + Elections Skills Hub : prompts, sample AI agents, and draft policies for responsible adoption. It’s already reached 1,000+ officials across 45 states. Strengthening cybersecurity. We’ve deployed Microsoft Sentinel to several state and local election offices for stronger threat detection, and we’re also supporting select election and political stakeholders with MDASH to find and fix software vulnerabilities faster. Countering bomb hoaxes.

events.title: Scoop: Trump pollster gives GOP a data center survival guide
events.summary: President Trump's longtime pollster is offering Republican candidates a detailed playbook for neutralizing Democratic attacks over AI data centers — down to what language they should and shouldn't use. Why it matters: Republican strategists say GOP candidates have been all over the map in responding to the backlash to data centers. The goal is to put Republicans on offense after months of playing defense on the issue. Driving the news: Pollster Tony Fabrizio warns in a two-page memo obtained by Axios that "unqualified support for building more AI data centers is a losing position." Fabrizio specifically advises candidates not to say, "I support building more data centers," warning: "It will be clipped and show up in ads." Instead, he tells Republicans to support AI infrastructure only if developers pay for their own power needs, protect consumers from higher utility bills and safeguard local water and natural resources. Fabrizio argues that candidates must make clear those conditions are enforceable, rather than voluntary commitments from tech companies. "This converts the candidate from a defender of technology companies into the person imposing rules on them," Fabrizio writes in the memo, which was sent Monday. Fabrizio offers a three-step script for candidates. First, "validate" voters' concerns about higher utility bills, the power grid and water use. Second, "draw the line" by vowing not to support projects that force families to subsidize them or allow tech companies to harm surrounding communities. Finally, argue that projects should move forward only if companies provide their own power, protect ratepayers and safeguard local water. "The order matters," Fabrizio writes. "It adopts voters' concerns as the approval standard instead of asking them to set those concerns aside." Fabrizio warns against generic support for "more data centers," leading with jobs or China, dismissing local concerns or defending individual projects before their costs and resource demands are known. By the numbers: Fabrizio's polling shows voters are far more receptive to data center construction with conditions than unrestricted development. Sixty-one percent of registered voters favor allowing construction with conditions, compared with 28% who favor prohibiting data centers altogether. His polling also finds voters oppose additional data center construction without conditions by 65% to 24%. The background: Fabrizio is a central player in Trump's midterm political operation, helping shape the polling and strategy guiding the GOP's campaign to retain control of Congress. Yes, but: Trump remains an enthusiastic booster of data centers even as Republicans grapple with growing voter concerns about their local impact. "I'm telling you, it's all a hoax. The data centers are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy, and it's the oil of the next 20, 25 years," Trump said Monday.

events.title: Trump considered dangerous, corrupt by majority in new poll
events.summary: Data: The Economist/YouGov ; Chart: Avery Lotz A slight majority of registered voters describe President Trump as corrupt and dangerous, a recent poll found, while just 14% say he isn't divisive. The big picture: Simply put, polling hasn't been pretty for the president — or for his Iran war , tariffs or other top priorities . Still, with the midterms weeks away, Trump has centered himself, making the election a referendum on his presidency . By the numbers: " Corrupt" (53%) and "dangerous" (51%) led the list of descriptors voters applied to Trump in the Sept. 11-14 The Economist-YouGov poll of 1,461 U.S. registered voters. Those words were followed by "out-of-touch" (47%), "cruel" (46%) and "bold" (45%). Just 18% said they'd use the word "steady" to describe the president. Worth noting: Democrats are testing an anti-corruption midterm message as Americans' perceptions of government corruption hit a 20-year high , per Gallup's trend , and polls show Americans believe the president has inappropriately profited from cryptocurrency while in office. The results broke sharply by party — 91% of Democrats and 62% of independents said Trump was corrupt, compared with 10% of Republicans. Republicans weren't universally positive: Less than half (49%) said they'd use the word "honest" to describe the president. Just 10% said it didn't describe him, while 41% had no opinion. Similarly, 38% of Republicans said he was steady, while 53% said they had no opinion. What they're saying: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement that "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars." Ingle also accused Democrats in Congress of failing to stop waste, fraud and abuse in government. Zoom out: Trump's approval rating ticked up from the lowest point of his political career, recorded last month in Reuters-Ipsos' trend , this month. Some 35% of Americans approved of his performance, up from 33% in the late August poll, per Reuters. Between the lines: The last thing many Republicans want, Axios' Marc Caputo reports , is for Trump to make the midterms a vote on his popularity (or lack thereof). Still, Trump headlined both nights of the party's midterm convention in Dallas and pledged a $5,000 dividend to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans keep control of Congress — a plan that would cost more than $1 trillion. Friction point: YouGov's polling found that a majority signaled they believe it's unlikely Trump actually follows through with the idea, which Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has said would require congressional approval. More than four in 10 (41%) said he definitely wouldn't do it, while an additional 16% said he probably wouldn't. More said it was a bad idea (45%) than those who said it was a good idea (38%). Methodology: This Economist-sponsored poll was taken September 11-14, 2026. Respondents were selected from YouGov's opt-in panel to be representative of adult U.S. citizens, and screened for voter registration. The margin of error is ± 3.3%. events.title: Microsoft’s partners debut new Windows PCs at IFA
events.summary: More choice and possibility with Windows PCs at IFA Mark Linton, Corporate Vice President, Windows & Devices This year at IFA, I saw the Windows ecosystem doing what it does best: bringing innovation to life through products and experiences for every person, purpose, and price point. Our partners introduced new Windows PCs, spanning dependable everyday devices, beautifully crafted premium designs, new and immersive gaming systems, commercial devices designed to help organizations work securely and productively, and powerful tools for developers, creators, and AI power users. Together, these announcements demonstrated the breadth of what’s possible with a Windows PC. This matters because people are being thoughtful about when, where, and how they spend. We know that a new PC is a meaningful purchase, and that customers want to feel confident that they choose the right PC for them. They want to know that it will deliver a better experience today while continuing to meet their needs for years to come. Windows PCs from our partners give people more ways to find the right device without compromising on what matters most to them. For more than 40 years, our goal has been to put a computer on every desk and in every home. We know the PC is personal and the place you go to play, create, build, connect and learn. Some prioritize battery life and portability, while others need greater performance for gaming or creative work. And increasingly, people are also looking for useful AI experiences that are easy to use and fit seamlessly into their existing workflows. And of course, everyone needs to find the right device at the right price for them. IFA showed how our partners are meeting those different needs. The strength of Windows is choice, and the latest Windows PCs bring together modern design, stronger performance, built-in security and useful AI experiences available at different price points. For those who have been holding on to an older PC, the choice and value available today makes it a good time to find the right device. IFA also demonstrated how Windows is evolving for the next era of computing. The latest OpenClaw Windows App makes it easier to configure and run AI models locally on supported NV IDIA RTX Spark Windows PCs. It builds on the secure agent-execution foundation we introduced at Microsoft Build, helping agents work within defined boundaries while taking advantage of the computing power available on the device. We are also making it easier for developers to turn ideas into reality with new ready-to-code Windows experiences for next-generation devices. By pre -installing the essential tools and pre-configuring Windows settings for development on developer class devices with 64GB+ unified memory and 250gbps memory bandwidth, developers can jump right in . Project Zenith devices enable developers to run capable coding models locally and unmetered, helping lower token costs , experiment more freely, and stay in their flow. Project Zenith shows how Windows and our ecosystem partners are bringing these innovations together to create more capable, purpose-built experiences. Check out the la test a nnounceme nts and activity from our partners at IFA. As the fourth-generation Vero consumer laptop, the device debuts a new chassis design incorporating post-industrial recycled aluminum, low-carbon aluminum, and PCR plastic, along with greatly expanded repairability features. For uncompromising performance and all-day productivity, it is powered by Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors with up to 180 platform TOPS. Designed for creators who need both performance and mobility, the ProArt P16 is the thinnest 16-inch RTX Spark laptop at just 12.9 mm, while the P14 is the lightest ProArt laptop ever at 1.48 kg, complemented by large 99Wh and 90Wh batteries and ASUS Lumina Pro OLED displays with up to 1,600-nit brightness and professional-grade color accuracy. ASUS brought these capabilities to life through its first global live showcase of agentic AI solutions for creators and developers, demonstrating how ProArt PCs can connect local AI, ASUS applications, and customizable workflows to transform creation, development, and production. At just 1.15 kg and 13.5 mm thin, the refined aluminum build slips easily into a bag and travels well from class to coffee shop to couch. Available in 14- and 15-inch configurations, the lineup offers a choice of Snapdragon X or AMD Ryzen AI 400 Series processors.

events.title: How the Copilot Creators Collective is shaping the future of creativity and AI literacy
events.summary: The New Media Movement: How the Copilot Creators Collective is Shaping the Future of Creativity and AI Literacy A year ago, Microsoft brought together a group of Filipino creators around a shared question: what becomes possible when creativity, community, and AI come together? That question became the starting point for the Copilot Creators Collective, a community built around a clear mission: to help more Filipinos understand, explore, and use AI responsibly through the voices of creators they trust. One year later, that mission has been brought to life by CCC members who are not only experimenting with Microsoft Copilot in their own work, but also translating AI into stories, conversations, and learning moments that feel practical, familiar, and human. At the heart of the Collective is Microsoft’s vision of empowering every person and organization on the planet to achieve more. For the CCC, that vision extends from creators to the communities they reach. Through campaigns, learning sessions, and creator-led storytelling, members have helped broaden AI literacy and advocate for responsible AI use by showing how Copilot can support real moments in work, life, education, creativity, and learning. “Over the past year, the Copilot Creators Collective has shown us what happens when Filipino creators are given the space, tools, and community to explore AI with purpose,” said Josh Aquino, Head of Communication of Microsoft Philippines. “But the Collective was never built for creators alone. It was built so more Filipinos could see AI in the context of everyday life—through people they trust, stories they relate to, and examples that show how Copilot can help them create, learn, work, and solve problems responsibly.” One Year of Learning, Experimenting, and Creating Together In its first year, the CCC’s mission moved from idea to action through the creators who carried it into different communities. Across learning spaces, workplace conversations, and education campaigns, members helped make AI feel less abstract and more useful to the people it was meant to serve. At the YSEALI Bootcamp for Digital Creators, Isa Rodriguez, CJ Salvador, and Jax Reyes brought creator-led perspectives to a regional initiative designed to equip young Southeast Asian leaders with digital storytelling and responsible technology skills. Organized in partnership with the U.S. Department of State through the Young Southeast Asian Leaders Initiative, the bootcamp gathered 81 Attendees from across the region, representing multiple nations and communities. The initiative provided a platform for CCC members to show how Microsoft 365 and Copilot can support productivity, content creation, and responsible experimentation. Their participation showed how AI literacy can start with people who understand the realities of digital storytelling and can speak to peers in a way that feels grounded, practical, and approachable. That same role came through in Microsoft’s Work Trend Index campaign, which emphasized that while AI is already embedded in everyday work, the next frontier is helping people and organizations turn individual experimentation into trusted, repeatable, and scalable ways of working. Through this campaign, Trixie Esguerra-Bugia helped make insights on AI adoption, productivity, and the future of work more relatable for everyday professionals and creators. Her own use of Copilot reflects the practical value she helps audiences see: it supports the behind-the-scenes work that makes content creation possible, from organizing shot lists to checking grammar and refining outlines. For creators working as one-human teams, she shows how AI can serve as a digital assistant that brings more structure and confidence to everyday work. In education, Alvin Santos and Reb Atadero helped bring the same message to Filipino teachers and learners through Microsoft’s campaign in partnership with the Department of Education. Leveraging DepEd’s nationwide network, the campaign showed how free tools such as Copilot Chat and Reading Progress can address classroom needs at scale. In just 21 weeks, it reached 3,431 students across eight regions, analyzed 8,381 reading submissions, trained 2,002 teachers, and achieved 91.5 percent teacher satisfaction. By connecting AI to everyday teaching, literacy, and student support, Alvin and Reb helped frame it as a practical aid for educators and learners alike. Alvin’s own experience reinforces this point: he has used Copilot as a creative sounding board and to develop lesson plans tailored to French non-native English speakers. The Collective’s work also shows how AI can support more ambitious ideas behind the scenes. Ceej Tantengco-Malolos experienced this while organizing an art exhibit for women’s sports. With Copilot and a small team, she created display mockups, drafted media invitations, and built a promotional plan for an event that might have otherwise felt difficult to take on. Her example adds another layer to the CCC’s first-year story: responsible AI is not only about learning the tool, but using it to bring meaningful ideas to life. Other members of the Collective echo this sense of possibility. Buji Babiera shared how Copilot helped him gather themes from different parts of the world for a local story under a tight deadline. Abi Maravilla described Copilot as a sounding board that helps simplify the complex and organize ideas without becoming overwhelmed. Andi Lopez shared how it helps turn scattered thoughts into something clearer and more meaningful, while also supporting work such as marketing pitch decks and data analysis for esports commentary. Seen together, these efforts move the CCC’s story forward from experimentation to impact. In its first year, the Collective helped broaden AI literacy by meeting Filipinos where they are: creators learning to work more efficiently, professionals navigating the future of work, educators looking for practical classroom support, and communities discovering how AI can help them start, organize, teach, create, and solve problems more responsibly. One year in, the Copilot Creators Collective stands as both a milestone and a starting point. Its first year shows how Filipino creators are already using AI to work more efficiently, think more expansively, and tell stories with greater confidence. It also shows that the future of creativity will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by people: creators who ask better questions, share what they learn, and use new tools to bring more thoughtful ideas into the world. “My first year with the Copilot Creator Collective was marked with remarkable firsts. It was my first time working with Microsoft Copilot and AI in general” said Alvin Santos. “And also, my first to be part of a project that fostered long-lasting partnerships with the brand and a thoughtfully curated bunch of amazing content creators. I’m raring to see what’s in store for the 2nd year!

events.title: Iranian spies hit Windows machines with Chosen Brick data-stealing malware
events.summary: Iranian state cyber actors are targeting individuals using social messaging apps to deploy surveillance and data-stealing malware on their Windows machines, three Western governments warned. In all observed cases, Chosen Brick has infected Windows systems exclusively. Iran has used it since at least 2025 to take over individuals’ devices, stealing their contacts, emails, and social media messages, which allows the spies to track people’s movements, the FBI, UK National Cyber Security Centre, and the Netherlands’ General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) said on Tuesday. “Iran almost certainly uses cyber activity to support the repression of individuals who are seen as a threat to the regime, such as dissidents, activists and journalists,” the security advisory said. “In some cases, the Iranian intelligence services have plotted to kidnap or conduct lethal operations against individuals internationally, who they perceive as enemies of the regime.” These attacks typically begin with WhatsApp and Telegram messages, purportedly coming from individuals and organizations that the victim knows and trusts. The Iranian spies do a significant amount of research to prepare for these social engineering campaigns. By the time they send the initial message via a social media app, they have “extensive” knowledge of the targeted individual, their contacts, and relevant industry organizations to make the phony messages more believable, according to the agencies. After building rapport with the mark, the attackers convince them to download and open a file that appears to be a legitimate application. Specifically: Pictory, RunwayML, Norton Antivirus, Telegram, Adobe Flash Player, and KeePass are among the legitimate applications the malicious files have been made to resemble, the government agencies said. Upon opening the file, the malware executes without the victim’s knowledge, and will survive a reboot of the target device. Chosen Brick also adds exclusions to Microsoft Defender antivirus in an attempt to evade detection, and then connects to Telegram for command-and-control (C2) communications using a victim-specific Telegram bot. While the malware hasn’t yet been observed to automate lateral movement across the network, this is “technically possible,” the advisory noted. It does, however, download additional malware and set up persistence for new payloads on infected devices, using the same registry key that Chosen Brick uses to establish its own persistence on a Windows device: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Other features include enumerating running processes and system information, capturing screen and audio content, stealing emails, along with Telegram and WhatsApp data from web browsers, and wiping the computer system. “Organizations that are concerned Chosen Brick has been executed should contact their IT providers, either internal or external, to investigate,” the US, UK, and the Netherlands warned. “As this actor targets personal devices, not just corporate devices, organizations are recommended to circulate this with their staff that are likely to be targeted and support them in checking their personal devices too.” The Western agencies’ latest Iran alert follows a series of water and energy cyberattacks that researchers and media reports have linked to Iran, although the US and UK governments have stopped short of formally attributing them, as the military conflict between Iran and the US approaches its seventh month. In August, America’s lead cybersecurity agency, CISA, disclosed that the July cyberattacks that disrupted American water utilities across 12 states targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems. CISA did not, however, attribute the campaign to Iran or anyone else. Around the same time, a suspected Iran-linked cyberattack also shut down a small UK power plant. Also in August, five US agencies warned that attackers are using AI-generated exploitation scripts to break into internet-exposed Siemens S7 Series programmable logic controllers (PLCs) at water, manufacturing, energy, and other critical facilities. “This is not a theoretical risk – it is an active threat,” the feds warned. ®

events.title: New AI tool lets influencers ‘scale themselves like software’
events.summary: The News The tech-focused creator Emily Higgins is speaking directly into the camera about the importance of a good hook for a social media video — she does what looks like three takes, each with a slightly different script. But Higgins only filmed one video. The other two were AI-edited, using a new tool from New York-based tech-media startup Avail that allows brands to create dozens of variants of video ads recorded by human influencers. The creatorAPI platform, which launched Tuesday, points to a social-media future in which content created or augmented with AI is increasingly common. It’s also a response to the rise of so-called “synthetic influencers,” completely fake avatars that can hawk goods on the internet. Instead, the tool will allow creators to “scale themselves like software,” said Avail CEO Chris Giliberti. It’s designed so the human creator authorizes all of their different videos: Brands can fix recording mistakes, test out different intros, or create variations that target different geographies or audiences. Using a technique known as “dark posting,” all the different ads won’t show up on the creator’s profile, but will proliferate into users’ feeds. Avail put together a cocktail of third-party AI models to create the tool. Know More Giliberti acknowledged the tool could be controversial, given how difficult it is for an untrained eye to tell the differences between AI-edited videos and the growing public pushback to anything tinged with AI, especially in the creative space. “There’s this purity that people expect from creatives, like they’re always the last people that are allowed to adopt productivity tools,” he said. “I just think it’s really unfortunate that software engineers are able to crank out 10 times more code with [AI] tools and that’s palatable... but the second a creator adopts a tool like this, they’re shamed for it.” Notable As the technology improves, using AI to edit video for translation purposes is increasingly common: Amazon last week rolled out alternate-language versions of a popular German soap opera that were made using AI lip-dubbing.

events.title: The Guardian view on the Bank of England’s £120bn bill: power without accountability | Editorial
events.summary: Quantitative tightening has blurred the line between monetary and fiscal policy, leaving ministers accountable for decisions they cannot directly control When Labour made the Bank of England independent in 1997, the idea was that the Bank set interest rates while the Treasury taxed and spent. Monetary policy was in Threadneedle Street, fiscal policy in Whitehall. But in August the Bank of England quietly slipped out that its key policy could cost the Treasury £120bn . That policy – quantitative tightening (QT) – clearly ought to be rethought and the policy of the Treasury indemnifying the Bank for its losses ended . Last year, ministers paid the Bank £17bn to cover these arguably notional losses – an amount considerably larger than the budget of the Ministry of Justice, which is dealing with a real prisons crisis. Bank independence was constructed for a world in which monetary policy decisions had predictable and indirect fiscal effects. The financial crisis, Covid, war and fractious trade disputes have contributed to ending that world. The Bank bought up government bonds to support the economy via its quantitative easing (QE) programme. But the constitutional settlement – of an independent central bank working out on its own what to do with those bonds – has not caught up. The game is surely up when a former Bank deputy governor, Charlie Bean , acknowledges that independence cannot justify effectively giving power to an unelected monetary policy committee (MPC) over decisions with great consequences for public spending. events.title: Slowing AI development could boost hyperscaler balance sheets
events.summary: Any slowdown in AI spending would let hyperscalers catch their financial breath and ease their reliance on borrowing to fund their buildouts. A Semafor review of analyst estimates finds that at current projections, as tracked by S&P Capital IQ, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft are expected to spend $66 billion more on capital spending (nearly all of it AI-related) than they earn in cash from operations over the next six quarters. Debt, stock sales, and complex deals that shift that spending off their balance sheets are filling the gap. Even a 10% pullback in capex flips that to a $74 billion surplus; a 20% pullback puts them more than $200 billion in the black. These companies might still choose to tap outside funding — “always spend other people’s money” remains a cardinal rule of corporate finance — but they wouldn’t be forced to. They could spend some time rebuilding balance sheets that have become stretched by breakneck spending or restoring stock buybacks that have largely been sacrificed on the AI altar. — Jake Angelo

events.title: AI is doing what Wall Street couldn't
events.summary: Liz’s view Chuck Prince, CEO of Citigroup from 2003 to 2007, is remembered for one quote that captured the greed and spinelessness of Wall Street bosses chasing riches while steering the global economy toward a cliff: “As long as the music is playing, you’ve got to get up and dance. We’re still dancing.” (Prince later clarified that his comments were about private-equity buyouts, not subprime mortgages, but they became indelibly attached to the production of toxic housing bonds.) Today’s music is AI, not subprime mortgages, and it’s still playing. But this crop of Chuck Princes seems willing to consider stepping off the dance floor. I’m still not sure what Dario Amodei’s idea to “pace the frontier” actually means in practice — slower Wi-Fi at the Anthropic office? Tying the developers’ shoelaces together? — but it’s clearly a warning issued at the cost of some short-term riches, which is more than Prince ever managed. Prince knew how dangerous Wall Street’s subprime addiction was but couldn’t quit. Some peers knew too, and quietly did: JPMorgan began exiting subprime lending in late 2006, and Goldman Sachs’ strong-arm collateral demands ensured it was not stuck holding what Jeremy Irons’ Dick Fuld-esque character in the film would later call “the biggest bag of odorous excrement ever assembled in the history of capitalism.” Both firms paced their own frontiers. Neither did anything to stop the overall machine. The loudest alarms back then came from outsiders — misfit investors like Michael Burry and academics like Raghuram Rajan — who got plenty of grief for their candor . The calls this time are coming from inside the house. Notable Read Amodei’s full essay , calling on AI labs to “ pace the frontier. ”
